claims.label: External conditions alone cannot explain complex coadaptations
claims.statement: Complex adaptations and coadaptations between organisms, such as the woodpecker's feeding structures or the misseltoe's dependence on particular trees, birds and insects, cannot be accounted for by the direct effects of external conditions such as climate and food.
claims.quote: it is preposterous to attribute to mere external conditions, the structure, for instance, of the woodpecker, with its feet, tail, beak, and tongue, so admirably adapted to catch insects under the bark of trees.
claims.chapter: Introduction

claims.label: Overproduction plus slight profitable variation leads to natural selection
claims.statement: Because more individuals of each species are born than can survive, there is a recurring struggle for existence, so any individual that varies even slightly in a way profitable to itself has a better chance of surviving and thus of being naturally selected.
claims.quote: As many more individuals of each species are born than can possibly survive; and as, consequently, there is a frequently recurring struggle for existence, it follows that any being, if it vary however slightly in any manner profitable to itself, under the complex and sometimes varying conditions of life, will have a better chance of surviving, and thus be _naturally selected_.
claims.chapter: Introduction

claims.label: Natural selection causes extinction of less improved forms and divergence
claims.statement: Natural selection almost inevitably causes much extinction of less improved forms of life and produces divergence of character.
claims.quote: we shall then see how Natural Selection almost inevitably causes much Extinction of the less improved forms of life and induces what I have called Divergence of Character.
claims.chapter: Introduction

claims.label: Species are not immutable but descend from other, mostly extinct, species
claims.statement: Species are not independently created and immutable; species of the same genus are lineal descendants of some other, generally extinct, species, just as varieties of one species descend from that species.
claims.quote: I am fully convinced that species are not immutable; but that those belonging to what are called the same genera are lineal descendants of some other and generally extinct species, in the same manner as the acknowledged varieties of any one species are the descendants of that species.
claims.chapter: Introduction

claims.label: Natural selection is the main but not exclusive means of modification
claims.statement: Natural selection has been the main, but not the only, cause of the modification of species.
claims.quote: Furthermore, I am convinced that Natural Selection has been the main but not exclusive means of modification.
claims.chapter: Introduction

claims.label: Domesticated forms vary more among individuals than wild species do
claims.statement: Individuals of the same variety of long-cultivated plants and domesticated animals generally differ much more from each other than individuals of any one species or variety in nature.
claims.quote: they generally differ much more from each other, than do the individuals of any one species or variety in a state of nature.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Greater domestic variability is caused by changed, less uniform conditions
claims.statement: The greater variability of domestic productions is due to their being raised under conditions of life less uniform than, and somewhat different from, those of their parent species in nature.
claims.quote: I think we are driven to conclude that this greater variability is simply due to our domestic productions having been raised under conditions of life not so uniform as, and somewhat different from, those to which the parent-species have been exposed under nature.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Variability arises mainly from effects on reproductive elements before conception
claims.statement: The most frequent cause of variability is that the male and female reproductive elements have been affected by the conditions of life before conception, the reproductive system being more sensitive to changed conditions than any other part of the organisation.
claims.quote: But I am strongly inclined to suspect that the most frequent cause of variability may be attributed to the male and female reproductive elements having been affected prior to the act of conception.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Inherited effects of use and disuse modify domestic animals
claims.statement: Habitual use and disuse of parts produce inherited changes in domestic animals; for example, domestic ducks have lighter wing bones and heavier leg bones relative to the skeleton than wild ducks because they fly less and walk more.
claims.quote: I find in the domestic duck that the bones of the wing weigh less and the bones of the leg more, in proportion to the whole skeleton, than do the same bones in the wild-duck; and I presume that this change may be safely attributed to the domestic duck flying much less, and walking more, than its wild parent.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Selecting one trait unconsciously modifies other correlated parts
claims.statement: Because of laws of correlation of growth, when man selects for and augments any peculiarity, he almost certainly also modifies other parts of the structure without intending to.
claims.quote: Hence, if man goes on selecting, and thus augmenting, any peculiarity, he will almost certainly unconsciously modify other parts of the structure, owing to the mysterious laws of the correlation of growth.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Inherited peculiarities appear in offspring at the age they appeared in parent
claims.statement: A peculiarity tends to appear in the offspring at the same period of life at which it first appeared in the parent, though sometimes earlier.
claims.quote: A much more important rule, which I think may be trusted, is that, at whatever period of life a peculiarity first appears, it tends to appear in the offspring at a corresponding age, though sometimes earlier.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Domestic races differ like congeneric species, but usually less
claims.statement: Apart from their lesser uniformity, their often monstrous development of one part, and their fertility when crossed, domestic races of a species differ from each other in the same manner as closely allied species of a genus in nature, though in most cases to a lesser degree.
claims.quote: domestic races of the same species differ from each other in the same manner as, only in most cases in a lesser degree than, do closely-allied species of the same genus in a state of nature.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Any wild species domesticated as long would vary as much as existing domestics
claims.statement: Domesticated species were not chosen for an unusual inherent tendency to vary; any comparable set of wild animals and plants, bred under domestication for as many generations, would on average vary as much as the parent species of existing domesticated productions have.
claims.quote: I cannot doubt that if other animals and plants, equal in number to our domesticated productions, and belonging to equally diverse classes and countries, were taken from a state of nature, and could be made to breed for an equal number of generations under domestication, they would vary on an average as largely as the parent species of our existing domesticated productions have varied.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Domestic dogs descend from several wild species
claims.statement: Domestic dogs have probably descended from several distinct wild species rather than from a single one.
claims.quote: from geographical and other considerations, I think it highly probable that our domestic dogs have descended from several wild species.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: All domestic pigeon breeds descend from the rock-pigeon
claims.statement: All domestic pigeon breeds, however different, have descended from the rock-pigeon (Columba livia) and its geographical sub-species, not from several aboriginal wild stocks.
claims.quote: I can feel no doubt that all our domestic breeds have descended from the Columba livia with its geographical sub-species.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Domestic breeds arise mainly by man's accumulation of successive variations
claims.statement: Domestic breeds were not produced suddenly in their present useful form; their key cause is man's accumulative selection, nature supplying successive variations and man adding them up in directions useful to him.
claims.quote: The key is man’s power of accumulative selection: nature gives successive variations; man adds them up in certain directions useful to him.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Races differ most in the parts man selects
claims.statement: Continued selection of slight variations in one part valued by man, such as leaves, flowers or fruit, produces races that differ from each other chiefly in that part, while other parts differ only slightly.
claims.quote: as a general rule, I cannot doubt that the continued selection of slight variations, either in the leaves, the flowers, or the fruit, will produce races differing from each other chiefly in these characters.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Unconscious selection over centuries modifies any breed
claims.statement: Unconscious selection, in which people simply breed from their best animals without aiming to change the breed, would over centuries improve and modify any breed, as methodical breeders have done within their lifetimes.
claims.quote: Nevertheless I cannot doubt that this process, continued during centuries, would improve and modify any breed, in the same way as Bakewell, Collins, etc., by this very same process, only carried on more methodically, did greatly modify, even during their own lifetimes, the forms and qualities of their cattle.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Slow accumulated change hides the wild parents of old cultivated plants
claims.statement: Because a large amount of change has been slowly and unconsciously accumulated in long-cultivated plants, in many cases their wild parent-stocks can no longer be recognised.
claims.quote: A large amount of change in our cultivated plants, thus slowly and unconsciously accumulated, explains, as I believe, the well-known fact, that in a vast number of cases we cannot recognise, and therefore do not know, the wild parent-stocks of the plants which have been longest cultivated in our flower and kitchen gardens.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Domestic races differ greatly externally but little internally
claims.statement: Because man can select mainly on externally visible deviations, domestic races differ greatly in external characters and relatively slightly in internal parts or organs.
claims.quote: We can, I think, further understand the frequently abnormal character of our domestic races, and likewise their differences being so great in external characters and relatively so slight in internal parts or organs.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Keeping large numbers of individuals favours successful selection
claims.statement: Because useful variations appear only occasionally, keeping a large number of individuals greatly increases the chance of useful variations appearing and is of the highest importance to success in selection.
claims.quote: But as variations manifestly useful or pleasing to man appear only occasionally, the chance of their appearance will be much increased by a large number of individuals being kept; and hence this comes to be of the highest importance to success.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Accumulative selection is the predominant cause of change in domestic races
claims.statement: Among the causes of change in domestic races, including conditions of life, use and disuse, correlation and crossing, the accumulative action of selection, whether methodical or unconscious, is by far the predominant power.
claims.quote: Over all these causes of Change I am convinced that the accumulative action of Selection, whether applied methodically and more quickly, or unconsciously and more slowly, but more efficiently, is by far the predominant Power.
claims.chapter: Ch. I: Variation under Domestication

claims.label: Individual differences supply the material for natural selection
claims.statement: The slight individual differences among members of a species provide the materials that natural selection accumulates, in the same way that man accumulates individual differences in domestic productions.
claims.quote: These individual differences are highly important for us, as they afford materials for natural selection to accumulate, in the same manner as man can accumulate in any given direction individual differences in his domesticated productions.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Polymorphic genera vary in traits of no use, unfixed by selection
claims.statement: In polymorphic genera such as Rubus, Rosa and Hieracium, the inordinate variation concerns structures that are of no service or disservice to the species and so have not been seized on and made definite by natural selection.
claims.quote: I am inclined to suspect that we see in these polymorphic genera variations in points of structure which are of no service or disservice to the species, and which consequently have not been seized on and rendered definite by natural selection
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Doubtful forms of mobile animals are rare within a country but common between areas
claims.statement: Among highly locomotive animals that unite for each birth, doubtful forms ranked as species by some and varieties by others are rarely found within the same country but are common in separated areas.
claims.quote: Amongst animals which unite for each birth, and which are highly locomotive, doubtful forms, ranked by one zoologist as a species and by another as a variety, can rarely be found within the same country, but are common in separated areas.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: No clear line separates species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences
claims.statement: No clear line of demarcation exists between species and sub-species, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences; they blend into one another in an insensible series.
claims.quote: Certainly no clear line of demarcation has as yet been drawn between species and sub-species—that is, the forms which in the opinion of some naturalists come very near to, but do not quite arrive at the rank of species; or, again, between sub-species and well-marked varieties, or between lesser varieties and individual differences.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Natural selection turns slight varieties into more distinct ones and species
claims.statement: Individual differences lead to slight varieties, these to more distinct and permanent varieties, then to sub-species and species, the passage being mainly due to natural selection accumulating structural differences in definite directions, so that a well-marked variety is an incipient species.
claims.quote: I attribute the passage of a variety, from a state in which it differs very slightly from its parent to one in which it differs more, to the action of natural selection in accumulating (as will hereafter be more fully explained) differences of structure in certain definite directions.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: The term species is arbitrary and not essentially different from variety
claims.statement: The term species is given arbitrarily, for convenience, to a set of closely resembling individuals and does not differ essentially from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.
claims.quote: I look at the term species, as one arbitrarily given for the sake of convenience to a set of individuals closely resembling each other, and that it does not essentially differ from the term variety, which is given to less distinct and more fluctuating forms.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Dominant species, widespread and abundant, produce the most varieties
claims.statement: The dominant species, those that range widely over the world, are most diffused in their own country and are most numerous in individuals, most often produce well-marked varieties.
claims.quote: Hence it is the most flourishing, or, as they may be called, the dominant species,—those which range widely over the world, are the most diffused in their own country, and are the most numerous in individuals,—which oftenest produce well-marked varieties, or, as I consider them, incipient species.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Species of larger genera more often present varieties
claims.statement: Within a country, a larger proportion of the species in larger genera present varieties than of the species in smaller genera, and those that vary have on average more varieties.
claims.quote: it has invariably proved to be the case that a larger proportion of the species on the side of the larger genera present varieties, than on the side of the smaller genera.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Small genera often grow large while large genera peak, decline and vanish
claims.statement: Over geological time small genera have often increased greatly in number of species, and large genera have often reached a maximum, declined and disappeared.
claims.quote: geology plainly tells us that small genera have in the lapse of time often increased greatly in size; and that large genera have often come to their maxima, declined, and disappeared.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Where many species of a genus have formed, many are still forming
claims.statement: On the view that species are strongly marked varieties, where many species of a genus have been formed, on average many new species should still be forming.
claims.quote: All that we want to show is, that where many species of a genus have been formed, on an average many are still forming; and this holds good.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Species in large genera differ from one another by small amounts
claims.statement: In large genera the amount of difference between species is often exceedingly small, so that their species resemble varieties more than do species of small genera.
claims.quote: Now Fries has remarked in regard to plants, and Westwood in regard to insects, that in large genera the amount of difference between the species is often exceedingly small. I have endeavoured to test this numerically by averages, and, as far as my imperfect results go, they always confirm the view.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Species of large genera cluster unequally around certain species
claims.statement: Species of large genera are not equally distinct from one another but are clustered in little groups around certain other species, as varieties are clustered around their parent species.
claims.quote: As Fries has well remarked, little groups of species are generally clustered like satellites around certain other species.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Species very closely allied to others have restricted ranges, like varieties
claims.statement: Species that are very closely allied to other species, and so resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges, similar to the restricted ranges of acknowledged varieties.
claims.quote: But there is also reason to believe, that those species which are very closely allied to other species, and in so far resemble varieties, often have much restricted ranges.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Analogies between species of large genera and varieties support descent
claims.statement: The analogies between species of large genera and varieties (more varieties, small and unequal differences, restricted ranges) are understandable if species once existed as varieties, and inexplicable if each species was independently created.
claims.quote: And we can clearly understand these analogies, if species have once existed as varieties, and have thus originated: whereas, these analogies are utterly inexplicable if each species has been independently created.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant
claims.statement: Because the dominant species of larger genera vary most and varieties become new species, larger genera tend to become larger, and dominant forms tend to become more dominant by leaving many modified, dominant descendants.
claims.quote: The larger genera thus tend to become larger; and throughout nature the forms of life which are now dominant tend to become still more dominant by leaving many modified and dominant descendants.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: Variation under Nature

claims.label: Overproduction makes a struggle for existence inevitable
claims.statement: Because all organisms tend to increase at a high (geometrical) rate, more individuals are produced than can survive, so every species must undergo a struggle for existence with members of its own species, with other species, or with physical conditions.
claims.quote: A struggle for existence inevitably follows from the high rate at which all organic beings tend to increase.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species
claims.statement: The extraordinarily rapid increase and wide spread of introduced (naturalised) animals and plants in new countries is explained by geometrical increase under favourable conditions with reduced mortality, not by any rise in their fertility.
claims.quote: In such cases the geometrical ratio of increase, the result of which never fails to be surprising, simply explains the extraordinarily rapid increase and wide diffusion of naturalised productions in their new homes.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Average abundance depends only indirectly on fecundity
claims.statement: The average number of individuals of an animal or plant species depends only indirectly on how many eggs or seeds it produces; high fecundity mainly compensates for heavy destruction, usually early in life.
claims.quote: So that in all cases, the average number of any animal or plant depends only indirectly on the number of its eggs or seeds.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Predation, more often than food supply, sets average numbers
claims.statement: Although food sets the upper limit to a species' increase, very often it is destruction by predators rather than food supply that determines the species' average numbers.
claims.quote: The amount of food for each species of course gives the extreme limit to which each can increase; but very frequently it is not the obtaining food, but the serving as prey to other animals, which determines the average numbers of a species.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Periodic extreme cold or drought is the most effective check
claims.statement: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodic seasons of extreme cold or drought are the most effective of all checks on increase.
claims.quote: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodical seasons of extreme cold or drought, I believe to be the most effective of all checks.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Competitors decline poleward, so climate acts more directly there
claims.statement: The number of species, and therefore of competitors, decreases going northward, so that going north or up a mountain one more often finds stunted forms caused by the direct harmful action of climate than going south or downhill.
claims.quote: for the number of species of all kinds, and therefore of competitors, decreases northwards; hence in going northward, or in ascending a mountain, we far oftener meet with stunted forms, due to the _directly_ injurious action of climate, than we do in proceeding southwards or in descending a mountain.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring competitors
claims.statement: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring their competitors and enemies; for example, many garden plants that tolerate the local climate never become naturalised because they cannot compete with native plants or resist native animals.
claims.quote: That climate acts in main part indirectly by favouring other species, we may clearly see in the prodigious number of plants in our gardens which can perfectly well endure our climate, but which never become naturalised, for they cannot compete with our native plants, nor resist destruction by our native animals.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Many species need a large local stock to persist
claims.statement: In many cases a large number of individuals of a species, relative to the number of its enemies, is necessary for the species to survive, which explains why rare plants can be very abundant in the few spots where they occur.
claims.quote: On the other hand, in many cases, a large stock of individuals of the same species, relatively to the numbers of its enemies, is absolutely necessary for its preservation.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Balanced struggles keep communities uniform over long periods
claims.statement: Although competition between organisms constantly recurs with shifting outcomes, the opposing forces are so finely balanced that community composition stays roughly the same for long periods, even though a trifling change could tip the balance toward one organism.
claims.quote: Battle within battle must ever be recurring with varying success; and yet in the long-run the forces are so nicely balanced, that the face of nature remains uniform for long periods of time, though assuredly the merest trifle would often give the victory to one organic being over another.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Chains of interaction link distant species' abundances
claims.statement: Very different organisms are linked by chains of interaction, so that the abundance of one species can determine the frequency of another through intermediate species; for example, cats may control the frequency of red clover and heartsease by way of field-mice and humble-bees.
claims.quote: Hence it is quite credible that the presence of a feline animal in large numbers in a district might determine, through the intervention first of mice and then of bees, the frequency of certain flowers in that district!
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Struggle is most severe between members of the same species
claims.statement: The struggle for existence is almost always most severe between individuals of the same species, because they live in the same places, need the same food and face the same dangers; between varieties of a species it is nearly as severe.
claims.quote: But the struggle almost invariably will be most severe between the individuals of the same species, for they frequent the same districts, require the same food, and are exposed to the same dangers.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Congeners compete more severely than species of different genera
claims.statement: Because species of the same genus are usually similar in habits and constitution and always in structure, competition between them is generally more severe than between species of different genera.
claims.quote: As species of the same genus have usually, though by no means invariably, some similarity in habits and constitution, and always in structure, the struggle will generally be more severe between species of the same genus, when they come into competition with each other, than between species of distinct genera.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Each organism's structure is shaped by its relations to other organisms
claims.statement: The structure of every organism is related, in essential but often hidden ways, to the structure of the other organisms with which it competes, from which it must escape, or on which it preys.
claims.quote: A corollary of the highest importance may be deduced from the foregoing remarks, namely, that the structure of every organic being is related, in the most essential yet often hidden manner, to that of all other organic beings, with which it comes into competition for food or residence, or from which it has to escape, or on which it preys.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Few species reach range edges where climate alone kills them
claims.statement: Only a few plants or animals extend their ranges so far that they are destroyed by the severity of climate alone; competition continues everywhere except at the extreme limits of life.
claims.quote: we have reason to believe that only a few plants or animals range so far, that they are destroyed by the rigour of the climate alone.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: Struggle for Existence

claims.label: Natural selection preserves favourable and destroys injurious variations
claims.statement: Because more individuals are born than can survive, individuals with any advantage, however slight, have the best chance of surviving and reproducing, while injurious variations are eliminated; this preservation of favourable and rejection of injurious variations is natural selection.
claims.quote: This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Neutral variations escape selection and remain fluctuating
claims.statement: Variations that are neither useful nor harmful are not acted on by natural selection and stay variable, which may explain the variability of so-called polymorphic species.
claims.quote: Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: No native biota is so well adapted that it cannot be improved
claims.statement: No country's native inhabitants are so perfectly adapted that none could be improved, as shown by introduced species having established firmly in every country.
claims.quote: No country can be named in which all the native inhabitants are now so perfectly adapted to each other and to the physical conditions under which they live, that none of them could anyhow be improved; for in all countries, the natives have been so far conquered by naturalised productions, that they have allowed foreigners to take firm possession of the land.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection
claims.statement: Seemingly trivial characters such as colour can be shaped by natural selection; colours that match the background, as in green leaf-eating insects and heather-coloured grouse, protect their bearers from predators that hunt by sight.
claims.quote: When we see leaf-eating insects green, and bark-feeders mottled-grey; the alpine ptarmigan white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather, and the black-grouse that of peaty earth, we must believe that these tints are of service to these birds and insects in preserving them from danger.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Natural selection can modify organisms at any age
claims.statement: Because variations arising at a particular life stage tend to be inherited at the same stage, natural selection can modify organisms at any age, for instance adapting larvae independently of adults.
claims.quote: natural selection will be enabled to act on and modify organic beings at any age, by the accumulation of profitable variations at that age, and by their inheritance at a corresponding age.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons
claims.statement: Fighting between males for females is perhaps most severe in polygamous animals, and the males of such species are the most often equipped with special weapons.
claims.quote: The war is, perhaps, severest between the males of polygamous animals, and these seem oftenest provided with special weapons.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Female choice over many generations can produce male ornaments
claims.statement: Female birds, by choosing the most melodious or beautiful males over thousands of generations, can produce a marked change in male song or plumage.
claims.quote: I can see no good reason to doubt that female birds, by selecting, during thousands of generations, the most melodious or beautiful males, according to their standard of beauty, might produce a marked effect.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Sex differences in species with shared habits are mainly sexually selected
claims.statement: When males and females of a species share the same general habits of life but differ in structure, colour or ornament, those differences were mainly caused by sexual selection, although not all such differences are.
claims.quote: Thus it is, as I believe, that when the males and females of any animal have the same general habits of life, but differ in structure, colour, or ornament, such differences have been mainly caused by sexual selection
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted
claims.statement: A flower and a bee can slowly become modified and adapted to each other, at the same time or one after the other, by the continued preservation of individuals with mutually favourable slight differences in structure.
claims.quote: Thus I can understand how a flower and a bee might slowly become, either simultaneously or one after the other, modified and adapted in the most perfect manner to each other, by the continued preservation of individuals presenting mutual and slightly favourable deviations of structure.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Natural selection works only by accumulating very small modifications
claims.statement: Natural selection acts only by preserving and accumulating very small inherited modifications, each profitable to its bearer, and so excludes continued creation of new organisms or large sudden changes of structure.
claims.quote: Natural selection can act only by the preservation and accumulation of infinitesimally small inherited modifications, each profitable to the preserved being
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it
claims.statement: In animals and plants, crosses between different varieties or between different strains of the same variety give vigour and fertility to the offspring, while close interbreeding reduces vigour and fertility.
claims.quote: a cross between different varieties, or between individuals of the same variety but of another strain, gives vigour and fertility to the offspring; and on the other hand, that _close_ interbreeding diminishes vigour and fertility
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed
claims.statement: It is a general law of nature that no organism fertilises itself for an unlimited number of generations; an occasional cross with another individual, perhaps at long intervals, is indispensable, even in hermaphrodites.
claims.quote: it is a general law of nature (utterly ignorant though we be of the meaning of the law) that no organic being self-fertilises itself for an eternity of generations; but that a cross with another individual is occasionally—perhaps at very long intervals—indispensable.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants
claims.statement: Trees, across all plant orders, have separate male and female flowers more often than other plants do, which helps pollen move between trees (though Hooker reported the rule fails in Australia).
claims.quote: That trees belonging to all Orders have their sexes more often separated than other plants, I find to be the case in this country
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations
claims.statement: A large number of individuals favours natural selection because it gives a better chance for profitable variations to arise within a given period, compensating for lower variability in each individual.
claims.quote: A large number of individuals, by giving a better chance for the appearance within any given period of profitable variations, will compensate for a lesser amount of variability in each individual, and is, I believe, an extremely important element of success.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species
claims.statement: Although small isolated areas can favour new species, modification is generally faster on large areas, and forms produced there, having beaten many competitors, spread most widely and give rise to the most new varieties and species.
claims.quote: Finally, I conclude that, although small isolated areas probably have been in some respects highly favourable for the production of new species, yet that the course of modification will generally have been more rapid on large areas; and what is more important, that the new forms produced on large areas, which already have been victorious over many competitors, will be those that will spread most widely
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Freshwater biotas evolve and go extinct more slowly, keeping relict forms
claims.statement: Because all freshwater basins together form a small area, competition among freshwater organisms has been less severe, so new forms have arisen more slowly and old forms have been exterminated more slowly there, which is why fresh water holds ancient and anomalous forms.
claims.quote: All fresh-water basins, taken together, make a small area compared with that of the sea or of the land; and, consequently, the competition between fresh-water productions will have been less severe than elsewhere; new forms will have been more slowly formed, and old forms more slowly exterminated.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Natural selection acts slowly, intermittently and on few species at a time
claims.statement: Natural selection always acts very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of a region at the same time.
claims.quote: On the other hand, I do believe that natural selection will always act very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of the same region at the same time.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction
claims.statement: Because every area is already fully stocked, as a favoured form increases in number the less favoured forms decrease and become rare, and rarity precedes extinction.
claims.quote: it follows that as each selected and favoured form increases in number, so will the less favoured forms decrease and become rare. Rarity, as geology tells us, is the precursor to extinction.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives
claims.statement: Because the most closely related forms compete most severely, each new variety or species, while forming, presses hardest on its nearest relatives and tends to exterminate them.
claims.quote: Consequently, each new variety or species, during the progress of its formation, will generally press hardest on its nearest kindred, and tend to exterminate them.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Divergence of character maximises the life an area supports
claims.statement: The greatest amount of life can be supported in an area by great diversification of structure among its inhabitants.
claims.quote: The truth of the principle, that the greatest amount of life can be supported by great diversification of structure, is seen under many natural circumstances.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders
claims.statement: Where organisms compete most closely, as on a small patch of ground, the advantages of diversification mean that the coexisting inhabitants generally belong to different genera and orders.
claims.quote: where they come into the closest competition with each other, the advantages of diversification of structure, with the accompanying differences of habit and constitution, determine that the inhabitants, which thus jostle each other most closely, shall, as a general rule, belong to what we call different genera and orders.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
claims.statement: Floras gain far more new genera than new species from naturalised plants, relative to the native numbers of genera and species, so naturalised plants tend to differ from the natives at the genus level.
claims.quote: floras gain by naturalisation, proportionally with the number of the native genera and species, far more in new genera than in new species.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Intermediate forms and parent species tend to go extinct
claims.statement: In a fully stocked country, improved descendants of a species tend to supplant their predecessors, so the intermediate forms between earlier and later states, and the original parent species itself, generally tend to become extinct.
claims.quote: Hence all the intermediate forms between the earlier and later states, that is between the less and more improved state of a species, as well as the original parent-species itself, will generally tend to become extinct.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups
claims.statement: Extinct species, though generally in the same orders, families or genera as living ones, are often somewhat intermediate in character between existing groups, because they lived when the branching lines of descent had diverged less.
claims.quote: the diagram throws light on the affinities of extinct beings, which, though generally belonging to the same orders, or families, or genera, with those now living, yet are often, in some degree, intermediate in character between existing groups
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Differences between varieties grow into differences between species and genera
claims.statement: Through natural selection and divergence of character, the small differences between varieties of a species steadily increase until they equal the larger differences between species of the same genus, or even between genera.
claims.quote: Thus the small differences distinguishing varieties of the same species, will steadily tend to increase till they come to equal the greater differences between species of the same genus, or even of distinct genera.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Very few species of past periods have living descendants
claims.statement: Like a tree in which only a few early twigs grew into surviving branches, very few of the species that lived in long-past geological periods now have living modified descendants, and many whole orders, families and genera have died out entirely.
claims.quote: Of the many twigs which flourished when the tree was a mere bush, only two or three, now grown into great branches, yet survive and bear all the other branches; so with the species which lived during long-past geological periods, very few now have living and modified descendants.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: Natural Selection

claims.label: Variability is induced by changed conditions acting on the reproductive system
claims.statement: Deviations of structure arise in some way from the conditions of life to which parents and their ancestors have been exposed over several generations, acting chiefly by disturbing the reproductive system; hence variability is greater under domestication or cultivation than in nature.
claims.quote: But the much greater variability, as well as the greater frequency of monstrosities, under domestication or cultivation, than under nature, leads me to believe that deviations of structure are in some way due to the nature of the conditions of life, to which the parents and their more remote ancestors have been exposed during several generations.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Direct effects of climate and food on organisms are small
claims.statement: The direct effect of differences in climate, food and similar conditions on an organism's structure is very small in animals and perhaps somewhat larger in plants, and cannot account for the complex co-adaptations between organisms.
claims.quote: How much direct effect difference of climate, food, etc., produces on any being is extremely doubtful. My impression is, that the effect is extremely small in the case of animals, but perhaps rather more in that of plants.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Flightlessness of birds on predator-free oceanic islands is caused by disuse
claims.statement: The nearly wingless condition of several birds living on oceanic islands that lack beasts of prey has been caused by disuse of the wings.
claims.quote: I believe that the nearly wingless condition of several birds, which now inhabit or have lately inhabited several oceanic islands, tenanted by no beast of prey, has been caused by disuse.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Wingless Madeira beetles result mainly from selection against being blown to sea
claims.statement: The high proportion of flightless beetles on windswept islands such as Madeira is mainly due to natural selection favouring individuals that fly least and so avoid being blown out to sea, probably combined with disuse.
claims.quote: these several considerations have made me believe that the wingless condition of so many Madeira beetles is mainly due to the action of natural selection, but combined probably with disuse.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Blindness in cave animals results from disuse
claims.statement: Because useless eyes are unlikely to be harmful in total darkness, the loss of eyes in most cave-dwelling animals is due to disuse alone rather than to natural selection.
claims.quote: As it is difficult to imagine that eyes, though useless, could be in any way injurious to animals living in darkness, I attribute their loss wholly to disuse.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Cave animals are related to surface fauna of their own continent
claims.statement: Blind cave animals of America should be most closely allied to other inhabitants of America, and those of Europe to inhabitants of Europe, rather than the cave faunas of the two continents being specially similar to each other.
claims.quote: Notwithstanding such modifications, we might expect still to see in the cave-animals of America, affinities to the other inhabitants of that continent, and in those of Europe, to the inhabitants of the European continent.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Species ranges are limited by competition as much as by climate
claims.statement: Species in nature are limited in their geographic ranges by competition with other organisms at least as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.
claims.quote: We have reason to believe that species in a state of nature are limited in their ranges by the competition of other organic beings quite as much as, or more than, by adaptation to particular climates.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Homologous parts tend to vary together
claims.statement: Parts of the body that are homologous and alike early in embryonic development, such as left and right sides or fore and hind limbs, tend to vary in a correlated way.
claims.quote: The several parts of the body which are homologous, and which, at an early embryonic period, are alike, seem liable to vary in an allied manner
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Taxonomically important characters may be useless products of correlated growth
claims.statement: Structural differences that systematists treat as highly important, such as differences between outer and inner seeds of Umbelliferae, may arise entirely from unknown laws of correlated growth without being of any use to the species.
claims.quote: Hence we see that modifications of structure, viewed by systematists as of high value, may be wholly due to unknown laws of correlated growth, and without being, as far as we can see, of the slightest service to the species.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Natural selection reduces superfluous parts without compensatory enlargement
claims.statement: Natural selection will in the long run reduce any part of the organisation once it becomes superfluous, saving nutriment, without necessarily causing another part to enlarge; and it can enlarge an organ without requiring reduction of an adjoining part.
claims.quote: Thus, as I believe, natural selection will always succeed in the long run in reducing and saving every part of the organisation, as soon as it is rendered superfluous, without by any means causing some other part to be largely developed in a corresponding degree.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Parts repeated many times in an individual are variable in number
claims.statement: When a part or organ is repeated many times in one individual, such as snake vertebrae or stamens of polyandrous flowers, its number is variable, whereas parts present in small numbers are constant in number.
claims.quote: when any part or organ is repeated many times in the structure of the same individual (as the vertebræ in snakes, and the stamens in polyandrous flowers) the number is variable; whereas the number of the same part or organ, when it occurs in lesser numbers, is constant.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Parts unusually developed relative to congeners are highly variable
claims.statement: A part developed to an extraordinary degree or in an extraordinary manner in one species, compared with the same part in closely allied species, tends to be highly variable within that species; the rule does not apply when the unusual part is shared by a whole group.
claims.quote: _A part developed in any species in an extraordinary degree or manner, in comparison with the same part in allied species, tends to be highly variable_.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Specific characters are more variable than generic characters
claims.statement: Characters that distinguish species within a genus are more variable within species than characters shared by all species of the genus, because the former have varied since the species branched from a common progenitor.
claims.quote: It is notorious that specific characters are more variable than generic.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Congeners differ more in secondary sexual characters than in other parts
claims.statement: Secondary sexual characters are highly variable, and species of the same group differ from one another more in their secondary sexual characters than in other parts of their organisation.
claims.quote: species of the same group differ from each other more widely in their secondary sexual characters, than in other parts of their organisation
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Long-lost characters reappear through a tendency transmitted each generation
claims.statement: When a character lost in a breed reappears after many generations, the cause is a tendency to produce that character transmitted in every generation which at last prevails under favourable conditions, not a sudden resemblance to a distant ancestor.
claims.quote: When a character which has been lost in a breed, reappears after a great number of generations, the most probable hypothesis is, not that the offspring suddenly takes after an ancestor some hundred generations distant, but that in each successive generation there has been a tendency to reproduce the character in question, which at last, under unknown favourable conditions, gains an ascendancy.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra descend from a striped common ancestor
claims.statement: The domestic horse, ass, hemionus, quagga and zebra are descended from a common ancestor that was striped like a zebra, which explains the occasional appearance of stripes in horses, asses and their hybrids.
claims.quote: For myself, I venture confidently to look back thousands on thousands of generations, and I see an animal striped like a zebra, but perhaps otherwise very differently constructed, the common parent of our domestic horse, whether or not it be descended from one or more wild stocks, of the ass, the hemionus, quagga, and zebra.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Related species with shared constitution produce analogous variations
claims.statement: Species that inherit nearly the same constitution from a common parent and are exposed to similar influences tend to produce analogous variations, so that a variety of one species may resemble another species of the same genus.
claims.quote: Species inheriting nearly the same constitution from a common parent and exposed to similar influences will naturally tend to present analogous variations
claims.chapter: Ch. V: Laws of Variation

claims.label: Formation of a new form exterminates its parent and transitional varieties
claims.statement: Because each new form tends in a fully stocked country to supplant and exterminate its less improved parent and other competing forms, the parent and all transitional varieties are generally exterminated by the process that forms the new species.
claims.quote: Hence, if we look at each species as descended from some other unknown form, both the parent and all the transitional varieties will generally have been exterminated by the very process of formation and perfection of the new form.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Zones of overlap between representative species are narrow
claims.statement: Where closely allied or representative species replace each other over a continuous area, the neutral territory between them is generally narrow compared with the territory occupied by each, and species become somewhat abruptly rarer towards their range limits.
claims.quote: Hence the neutral territory between two representative species is generally narrow in comparison with the territory proper to each.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Intermediate varieties are numerically rarer than the forms they connect
claims.statement: Where varieties intermediate between two other forms occur in nature, they are generally much rarer numerically than the forms they connect, because they inhabit narrower intermediate zones.
claims.quote: generally when varieties intermediate between two other forms occur, they are much rarer numerically than the forms which they connect.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Common forms improve faster and supplant rare intermediate forms
claims.statement: Forms existing in larger numbers have a better chance in any given period of presenting favourable variations for natural selection, so they are improved faster and supplant the less numerous intermediate varieties between them.
claims.quote: For forms existing in larger numbers will always have a better chance, within any given period, of presenting further favourable variations for natural selection to seize on, than will the rarer forms which exist in lesser numbers.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Bat flight arose from an apparatus for gliding
claims.statement: Bats were derived from gliding animals, and the wing membrane extending to the tail and hind legs in some bats is a trace of an apparatus originally built for gliding rather than flight.
claims.quote: In bats which have the wing-membrane extended from the top of the shoulder to the tail, including the hind-legs, we perhaps see traces of an apparatus originally constructed for gliding through the air rather than for flight.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Habits can change without corresponding change of structure
claims.statement: Species sometimes have habits that do not match their structure, such as upland geese with webbed feet that rarely enter water or ground-living woodpeckers, showing that habits can change before structure changes.
claims.quote: In such cases, and many others could be given, habits have changed without a corresponding change of structure.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Complex eyes can be built by selection through graded useful steps
claims.statement: Natural selection could have converted a simple optic nerve coated with pigment and covered by transparent membrane into a highly perfect eye through a series of graded steps, each useful to its possessor, as shown by the graduated diversity of eyes in living crustaceans.
claims.quote: I can see no very great difficulty (not more than in the case of many other structures) in believing that natural selection has converted the simple apparatus of an optic nerve merely coated with pigment and invested by transparent membrane, into an optical instrument as perfect as is possessed by any member of the great Articulate class.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Theory fails if a complex organ could not arise by slight steps
claims.statement: If any complex organ were shown to exist that could not possibly have been formed by numerous, successive, slight modifications, the theory of natural selection would break down; no such case is known.
claims.quote: If it could be demonstrated that any complex organ existed, which could not possibly have been formed by numerous, successive, slight modifications, my theory would absolutely break down.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Lung-bearing vertebrates descend from an ancestor with a swimbladder
claims.statement: All vertebrates with true lungs have descended from an ancient ancestor that had a swimbladder used for flotation, which natural selection converted into a lung.
claims.quote: I can, indeed, hardly doubt that all vertebrate animals having true lungs have descended by ordinary generation from an ancient prototype, of which we know nothing, furnished with a floating apparatus or swimbladder.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Selection can independently produce similar organs in distantly related beings
claims.statement: Natural selection, acting on analogous variations, has sometimes modified parts in nearly the same way in two distantly related organisms, as with electric organs in unrelated fishes, so that similar organs need not be inherited from a common ancestor.
claims.quote: so natural selection, working for the good of each being and taking advantage of analogous variations, has sometimes modified in very nearly the same manner two parts in two organic beings, which owe but little of their structure in common to inheritance from the same ancestor.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Few organs lack any known transitional grade
claims.statement: Despite the small proportion of living and known forms relative to extinct and unknown ones, it is rare to find an organ toward which no transitional grade is known to lead.
claims.quote: I have been astonished how rarely an organ can be named, towards which no transitional grade is known to lead.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Most of an organism's structure is due to inheritance, not current use
claims.statement: The chief part of each organism's structure is simply inherited, so that many structures, such as the shared bones of monkey arm, horse leg, bat wing and seal flipper, have no direct relation to the species' present habits of life.
claims.quote: by far the most important consideration is that the chief part of the organisation of every being is simply due to inheritance; and consequently, though each being assuredly is well fitted for its place in nature, many structures now have no direct relation to the habits of life of each species.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: No structure exists solely for the good of another species
claims.statement: Natural selection cannot produce any structure in one species exclusively for the good of another species, though it can produce structures that harm other species; proof of such a structure would refute the theory.
claims.quote: Natural selection cannot possibly produce any modification in any one species exclusively for the good of another species
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Selection makes organisms only as perfect as their local competitors
claims.statement: Natural selection only makes each organism as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of its own country, so endemic species of a region such as New Zealand may yield to species introduced from a larger region.
claims.quote: Natural selection tends only to make each organic being as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of the same country with which it has to struggle for existence.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Traits from laws of growth are later co-opted by descendants
claims.statement: Many modifications arose wholly from laws of growth and were at first of no advantage to a species, but were later taken advantage of by its further modified descendants, as skull sutures that arose in egg-laying animals were later used in mammalian birth.
claims.quote: we may confidently believe that many modifications, wholly due to the laws of growth, and at first in no way advantageous to a species, have been subsequently taken advantage of by the still further modified descendants of this species.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Nature makes no leaps when past as well as present forms are included
claims.statement: The rule that nature makes no leaps is not strictly true of living organisms alone, but if all past organisms are included it must be strictly true.
claims.quote: This canon, if we look only to the present inhabitants of the world, is not strictly correct, but if we include all those of past times, it must by my theory be strictly true.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Unity of type is explained by unity of descent
claims.statement: The fundamental agreement in structure among organisms of the same class, independent of their habits of life, is explained by their common descent.
claims.quote: On my theory, unity of type is explained by unity of descent.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: Difficulties on Theory

claims.label: Instincts arise mainly by selection of accidental variations, not inherited habit
claims.statement: Complex instincts originate chiefly through natural selection preserving and accumulating slight accidental variations of instinct; the inherited effects of habit play only a subordinate role.
claims.quote: But I believe that the effects of habit are of quite subordinate importance to the effects of the natural selection of what may be called accidental variations of instincts
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Complex instincts are reached by gradations visible in related species
claims.statement: Complex instincts are built up by slow, gradual steps, so gradations leading to them should be found among the instincts of related species in collateral lines of descent; instincts, like bodily organs, do not change by leaps.
claims.quote: The canon of “Natura non facit saltum” applies with almost equal force to instincts as to bodily organs.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: No instinct exists for the exclusive good of another species
claims.statement: No animal performs an instinctive action solely for the benefit of another species, although each species takes advantage of the instincts of others.
claims.quote: Although I do not believe that any animal in the world performs an action for the exclusive good of another of a distinct species, yet each species tries to take advantage of the instincts of others
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Instincts vary within species in a state of nature
claims.statement: Instincts vary within species under natural conditions, for example the migratory instinct varies in extent and direction and may be lost entirely, and nest construction varies between regions.
claims.quote: instincts certainly do vary—for instance, the migratory instinct, both in extent and direction, and in its total loss.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Fear of man is acquired slowly by animals exposed to human persecution
claims.statement: Fear of humans is slowly acquired by animal populations persecuted by man, so animals on uninhabited islands are tame and heavily hunted large birds are wilder than small ones.
claims.quote: But fear of man is slowly acquired, as I have elsewhere shown, by various animals inhabiting desert islands
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Domestic instincts arise from habit and from human selection of chance variations
claims.statement: Under domestication new instincts have been acquired and natural instincts lost partly through inherited habit and partly through human selection, methodical or unconscious, of chance mental peculiarities, usually with both acting together.
claims.quote: Hence, we may conclude, that domestic instincts have been acquired and natural instincts have been lost partly by habit, and partly by man selecting and accumulating during successive generations, peculiar mental habits and actions, which at first appeared from what we must in our ignorance call an accident.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Cuckoo brood parasitism evolved from occasional laying in other birds’ nests
claims.statement: The brood-parasitic instinct of the European cuckoo was generated by natural selection from an ancestor that built its own nest but occasionally laid eggs in other birds’ nests, where the fostered young fared better.
claims.quote: By a continued process of this nature, I believe that the strange instinct of our cuckoo could be, and has been, generated.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Slave-making in ants arose from capturing pupae as food
claims.statement: The slave-making instinct of ants arose when pupae of other species, originally collected as food, were reared and proved useful as workers, and natural selection strengthened this habit until some species became wholly dependent on slaves.
claims.quote: the habit of collecting pupæ originally for food might by natural selection be strengthened and rendered permanent for the very different purpose of raising slaves.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Hive-bee comb building evolved by gradual modification of simpler bee instincts
claims.statement: The cell-making instinct of the hive-bee was acquired through natural selection by slight successive modifications of simpler instincts, of the kind seen in a graded series from humble-bees through Melipona to the hive-bee.
claims.quote: By such modifications of instincts in themselves not very wonderful,—hardly more wonderful than those which guide a bird to make its nest,—I believe that the hive-bee has acquired, through natural selection, her inimitable architectural powers.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Hive-bee cells form by bees sweeping equal spheres and building at intersections
claims.statement: Hexagonal hive-bee cells result from many bees standing at equal distances from one another, each excavating equal spherical hollows, and building up or leaving unexcavated the planes where these spheres would intersect.
claims.quote: The work of construction seems to be a sort of balance struck between many bees, all instinctively standing at the same relative distance from each other, all trying to sweep equal spheres, and then building up, or leaving ungnawed, the planes of intersection between these spheres.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: The hive-bee comb is maximally economical of wax
claims.statement: The comb of the hive-bee is absolutely perfect in economising wax, so natural selection, driven by the saving of wax, could carry comb architecture no further.
claims.quote: Beyond this stage of perfection in architecture, natural selection could not lead; for the comb of the hive-bee, as far as we can see, is absolutely perfect in economising wax.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Selection on the family explains traits of sterile social-insect workers
claims.statement: Traits of sterile workers in social insects can evolve because selection acts on the family: fertile parents whose colonies produce sterile members with a useful modification flourish and transmit the tendency to produce such members.
claims.quote: selection may be applied to the family, as well as to the individual, and may thus gain the desired end.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Neuter insects of one nest should show graded structural differences
claims.statement: If worker modifications spread gradually through selection of fertile parents, sterile workers of the same species in the same nest should sometimes show gradations of structure, and such gradations are in fact often found.
claims.quote: On this view we ought occasionally to find neuter-insects of the same species, in the same nest, presenting gradations of structure; and this we do find, even often
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Discrete worker castes arose by selection eliminating intermediate forms
claims.statement: Distinct castes of sterile workers in one nest arose when a graduated series of workers was first formed and then selection on the fertile parents favoured production of the most useful extreme forms until intermediates were no longer produced.
claims.quote: a graduated series having been first formed, as in the case of the driver ant, and then the extreme forms, from being the most useful to the community, having been produced in greater and greater numbers through the natural selection of the parents which generated them; until none with an intermediate structure were produced.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Allied species in distant regions retain nearly the same instincts
claims.statement: Closely allied but distinct species living in distant parts of the world under different conditions often retain nearly the same instincts, which is explained by inheritance from a common ancestor.
claims.quote: This theory is, also, strengthened by some few other facts in regard to instincts; as by that common case of closely allied, but certainly distinct, species, when inhabiting distant parts of the world and living under considerably different conditions of life, yet often retaining nearly the same instincts.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: Instinct

claims.label: Sterility of first crosses differs from sterility of hybrids
claims.statement: The sterility of first crosses between pure species, whose reproductive organs are perfect, is a different phenomenon from the sterility of their hybrids, whose reproductive organs are functionally impotent.
claims.quote: Pure species have of course their organs of reproduction in a perfect condition, yet when intercrossed they produce either few or no offspring. Hybrids, on the other hand, have their reproductive organs functionally impotent
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Close interbreeding lowers fertility while occasional crossing raises it
claims.statement: Close interbreeding lessens fertility, while an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases it; this explains much of the declining fertility of hybrids kept for successive generations.
claims.quote: that close interbreeding lessens fertility, and, on the other hand, that an occasional cross with a distinct individual or variety increases fertility
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Hybrid sterility can be removed under domestication
claims.statement: Because many domestic animals are believed to descend from two or more distinct species that are now fully fertile together, sterility between species is not indelible but can be removed by domestication.
claims.quote: we must look at sterility, not as an indelible characteristic, but as one capable of being removed by domestication.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Some sterility in crosses between species is very general but not universal
claims.statement: Some degree of sterility in first crosses between species and in their hybrids is an extremely general result, but it is not absolutely universal.
claims.quote: Finally, looking to all the ascertained facts on the intercrossing of plants and animals, it may be concluded that some degree of sterility, both in first crosses and in hybrids,is an extremely general result; but that it cannot, under our present state of knowledge, be considered as absolutely universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Difficulty of first cross and sterility of hybrids correspond only loosely
claims.statement: Species that are hard to cross generally produce very sterile hybrids, but the correspondence between the difficulty of a first cross and the sterility of the resulting hybrids is by no means strict.
claims.quote: Hybrids from two species which are very difficult to cross, and which rarely produce any offspring, are generally very sterile; but the parallelism between the difficulty of making a first cross, and the sterility of the hybrids thus produced—two classes of facts which are generally confounded together—is by no means strict.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Cross fertility is largely governed by systematic affinity
claims.statement: The fertility of first crosses between species and of their hybrids is largely, though not strictly, governed by systematic affinity, so that species of distinct families never produce hybrids while closely allied species generally cross easily.
claims.quote: Now the fertility of first crosses between species, and of the hybrids produced from them, is largely governed by their systematic affinity.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Reciprocal crosses between the same two species often differ greatly in success
claims.statement: The ease of crossing two species often differs greatly depending on which species is the father and which the mother, showing that crossing capacity depends on imperceptible differences confined to the reproductive system.
claims.quote: There is often the widest possible difference in the facility of making reciprocal crosses.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Cross sterility is incidental on reproductive differences, not specially endowed
claims.statement: The sterility of first crosses and of hybrids is not a quality specially endowed to keep species distinct but is incidental on unknown differences, chiefly in the reproductive systems, of the species crossed.
claims.quote: The foregoing rules and facts, on the other hand, appear to me clearly to indicate that the sterility both of first crosses and of hybrids is simply incidental or dependent on unknown differences, chiefly in the reproductive systems, of the species which are crossed.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Early embryo death is a frequent cause of sterility in first crosses
claims.statement: A very frequent cause of sterility in first crosses between species is the early death of the embryo, which may be exposed to unsuitable conditions within the mother or the egg or seed.
claims.quote: the early death of the embryo is a very frequent cause of sterility in first crosses.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Hybrid sterility resembles sterility caused by unnatural conditions
claims.statement: The sterility of hybrids closely resembles the sterility induced in pure species by unnatural conditions of life: in both cases the reproductive system is disturbed independently of general health, by disturbed conditions in one case and by two organisations compounded into one in the other.
claims.quote: Thus we see that when organic beings are placed under new and unnatural conditions, and when hybrids are produced by the unnatural crossing of two species, the reproductive system, independently of the general state of health, is affected by sterility in a very similar manner.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Slight changes of conditions and slight crosses both increase vigour and fertility
claims.statement: Slight changes in conditions of life benefit organisms, and crosses between slightly different members of the same species give vigour and fertility to offspring, whereas greater changes and wider crosses tend to cause sterility.
claims.quote: Hence it seems that, on the one hand, slight changes in the conditions of life benefit all organic beings, and on the other hand, that slight crosses, that is crosses between the males and females of the same species which have varied and become slightly different, give vigour and fertility to the offspring.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: Hybridism

claims.label: Fertility of crossed varieties is not universal nor a species criterion
