claims.statement: The ostrich probably, and the moa certainly, reached a size at which flight by muscular action with ordinary bird anatomy became physiologically impossible, and a bird as large as a man could not fly.
claims.quote: It is not improbable that the ostrich has already reached a magnitude, and we may take it for certain that the moa did so, at which flight by muscular action, according to the normal anatomy of a bird, has become physiologically impossible.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Giant Carboniferous insects and pterodactyls imply a denser ancient atmosphere
claims.statement: The giant wingspans of Carboniferous dragonflies and the small bodies and huge wings of pterodactyls, which seem beyond present mechanical limits, can be explained if the Carboniferous and Jurassic atmosphere was notably denser, for example through more carbonic acid.
claims.quote: we have only to suppose that in carboniferous and jurassic days the terrestrial atmosphere was notably denser than it is at present, by reason, for instance, of its containing a much larger proportion of carbonic acid, and we have at once a means of reconciling the apparent mechanical discrepancy.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Similarly built animals should jump to the same absolute height regardless of size
claims.statement: Because the impulse of a leap is proportional to muscle volume and so to body mass, the take-off velocity is independent of size, and similarly built animals should jump to the same actual height rather than the same relative height; longer levers in larger animals give them some advantage.
claims.quote: in other words, that all animals, provided always that they are similarly fashioned, with their various levers etc., in like proportion, ought to jump, not to the same relative, but to the same actual height.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Speed varies as the square root of linear size in swimming, flight and walking
claims.statement: Leaving aside differences in mechanical construction, swimming (Froude's law), flight (minimum stable speed) and walking (the leg swinging as a pendulum) all give the same result: an animal's velocity tends to vary as the square root of its linear dimensions.
claims.quote: the general result, attained under very different conditions and arrived at by very different modes of reasoning, is in every case that the velocity tends to vary as the square root of the linear dimensions of the organism.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Doubling gravity would make terrestrial animals short-legged or serpent-like
claims.statement: The form and actions of terrestrial animals are conditioned by the strength of gravity: if it were doubled, bipedal form would fail and most land animals would resemble short-legged saurians or serpents; if halved, animals would be lighter, more active and need less heart, lungs and blood.
claims.quote: Were the force of gravity to be doubled, our bipedal form would be a failure, and the majority of terrestrial animals would resemble short-legged saurians, or else serpents.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Folded surfaces such as villi and brain convolutions keep surface in step with mass
claims.statement: Throughout morphology, surface tends to keep pace with volume through changes of form, such as intestinal villi and folds, the shark's spiral valve, and brain convolutions whose complexity is correlated with animal size, so that a roughly constant ratio of surface to mass is maintained.
claims.quote: Throughout the whole field of morphology we may find examples of a tendency (referable doubtless in each case to some definite physical cause) for surface to keep pace with volume, through some alteration of its form.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Form of small organisms is set by surface tension, not gravity, favouring spheres
claims.statement: The form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity and mainly due to surface tension, acting either now or at an earlier stage before the form was made rigid, so small organisms tend strongly toward spherical and other simple surface-tension forms that do not occur in the external form of large animals.
claims.quote: In like manner we shall find that the form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity, and largely if not mainly due to the force of surface-tension
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Form follows growth rates in large organisms but not in minute ones
claims.statement: Large and small organisms differ in kind in how form arises: in large organisms form is the direct result of unequal growth rates in different directions, but in minute organisms and individual cells intermolecular forces outweigh gravity and form is not simply correlated with growth.
claims.quote: But it is by no means true that form and growth are in this direct and simple fashion correlative or complementary in the case of minute portions of living matter.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Cell division restores the ratio of surface to mass
claims.statement: Cell division keeps the ratio between a cell's surface and its mass approximately constant and restores the balance of surface energy with the cell's other energies; cleavage of an egg increases surface without increasing volume or mass.
claims.quote: In short, however it may be brought about, the phenomenon of division of the cell will be precisely what is required to keep approximately constant the ratio between surface and mass, and to restore the balance between the surface-energy and the other energies of the system.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Cells of each kind vary little about a mean size, whatever the body size
claims.statement: Cells of each kind vary little about a characteristic mean size and have absolute size limits, so dwarf and giant individuals of a species (e.g. Crepidula, sea-urchin larvae) differ in cell number rather than cell size.
claims.quote: An immediate and remarkable result of the principles just described is a tendency on the part of all cells, according to their kind, to vary but little about a certain mean size, and to have, in fact, certain absolute limitations of magnitude.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: Ganglion-cell size varies little; larger species have ganglia with more cells
claims.statement: Across animals large and small, ganglion (nerve) cells vary in size only within narrow limits, and smaller species have simpler ganglia containing fewer cells than larger species.
claims.quote: we may (with Enriques) lay it down as a general law that among animals, whether large or small, the ganglion-cells vary in size within narrow limits; and that, amidst all the great variety of structural type of ganglion observed in different classes of animals, it is always found that the smaller species have simpler ganglia than the larger, that is to say ganglia containing a smaller number of cellular elements.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: The smallest organisms approach molecular size, so they cannot be much smaller
claims.statement: Because a micrococcus 0.15 µm across contains only some tens of thousands of protein molecules, the smallest known organisms approach molecular dimensions, and organisms cannot be subdivided indefinitely or be much smaller than those already discovered.
claims.quote: it will still be clear that the smallest known bodies which are described as organisms draw nigh towards molecular magnitudes, and we must recognise that the subdivision of the organism cannot proceed to an indefinite extent, and in all probability cannot go very much further than it appears to have done in these already discovered forms.
claims.chapter: Ch. II: On Magnitude

claims.label: External form results from the ratio of growth rates in different directions
claims.statement: Except for certain very minute organisms whose form is set directly by molecular forces, the external form of an organism is accounted for by the ratio between its rates of growth in different directions.
claims.quote: It is the ratio between the rates of growth in various directions by which we must account for the external forms of all, save certain very minute, organisms.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Constant growth-rate ratios preserve form; changing ratios produce development
claims.statement: When the ratio between growth rates in different directions stays constant, an organism grows in bulk with little or no change of form; such constancy seldom lasts more than a season, and when the ratio alters the organism undergoes development, a steady and persistent change of form.
claims.quote: It may sometimes be a very _constant_ one, in which case the organism, while growing in bulk, suffers little or no perceptible change in form; but such equilibrium seldom endures for more than a season, and when the _ratio_ tends to alter, then we have the phenomenon of morphological “development,” or steady and persistent change of form.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Embryonic folds arise from local differences in growth rate of a uniform sheet
claims.statement: The foldings of the blastoderm that produce the neural and amniotic folds result from unequal rates of growth, local accelerations and retardations, in what is at first an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue, in the way that a sheet buckles when parts of it expand or contract.
claims.quote: the various foldings of the blastoderm, by which the neural and amniotic folds were brought into being, were essentially and obviously the resultant of unequal rates of growth,—of local accelerations or retardations of growth,—in what to begin with was an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Differences between related forms emerge gradually and are small in the young
claims.statement: Because form differences are attained by growth at specific velocities over long periods, differences between any two related individuals or species must appear gradually and be little apparent in the young, and animals of very different adult size differ less and less in size and form when traced back through foetal stages.
claims.quote: it is accordingly obvious that in any two related individuals (whether specifically identical or not) the differences between them must manifest themselves gradually, and be but little apparent in the young. It is for the same simple reason that animals which are of very different sizes when adult, differ less and less in size (as well as in form) as we trace them backwards through the foetal stages.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Human stature grows fast in infancy, steadily in childhood, then quickens in the teens
claims.statement: The human curve of growth in stature shows rapid increase in infancy, a long period of slower, nearly steady growth in early boyhood, a marked quickening in the early teens, and finally a gradual arrest as full height is reached.
claims.quote: The curve of growth for length or stature in man indicates a rapid increase at the outset, that is to say during the quick growth of babyhood; a long period of slower, but still rapid and almost steady growth in early boyhood; as a rule a marked quickening soon after the boy is in his teens, when he comes to “the growing age”
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Adult human stature declines well before fifty and markedly by old age
claims.statement: Full adult stature in man lasts only for a time: it begins to decrease well before fifty, is notably lessened by sixty, and is much reduced in extreme old age, so that growth takes a negative value.
claims.quote: We should see that a man’s full stature endures but for a spell; long before fifty it has begun to abate, by sixty it is notably lessened, in extreme old age the old man’s frame is shrunken and it is but a memory that “he once was tall.”
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Weight tends to vary as the cube of linear dimensions during growth
claims.statement: Whatever the law of increase in a linear dimension, volume and therefore weight tend to vary as the cube of linear dimensions, which mainly (though not wholly) explains why the human weight curve differs in shape from the stature curve.
claims.quote: whatever be the law of increment in a linear dimension, the law of increase in volume, and therefore in weight, will be that these latter magnitudes tend to vary as the cubes of the linear dimensions.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Boys and girls share a growth-velocity curve differing mainly in phase
claims.statement: The curves of growth velocity in boys and girls are of very similar shape but differ in amplitude and especially in phase, the girl's adolescent acceleration beginning and ending earlier than the boy's.
claims.quote: In short, throughout all this period, it is a very _similar_ curve in the two sexes; but it has its notable differences, in amplitude and especially in _phase_.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: All animals pass through the same phases of growth: slow start, early peak, slowdown
claims.statement: In long-lived and short-lived animals alike, growth begins slowly, reaches its maximum velocity early, and then slows down (with temporary accelerations) toward a point where it ceases.
claims.quote: Whether the animal be long-lived, as man or the elephant, or short-lived, like horse or dog, it passes through the same phases of growth. In all cases growth begins slowly; it attains a maximum velocity early in its course, and afterwards slows down (subject to temporary accelerations) towards a point where growth ceases altogether.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Cold-blooded animals approach a maximal size only asymptotically
claims.statement: In cold-blooded animals such as fishes the slowing of growth is greatly protracted, so that size seems never to reach a maximum but only to approach a limit asymptotically.
claims.quote: But especially in the cold-blooded animals, such as fishes, the slowing-down period is very greatly protracted, and the size of the creature would seem never actually to reach, but only to approach asymptotically, to a maximal limit.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth
claims.statement: The size an animal finally attains results from both its rate and its duration of growth: some species are larger because they grow faster (rabbit versus guinea-pig), others because they grow for longer (man versus rabbit).
claims.quote: The size ultimately attained is a resultant of the rate, and of the duration, of growth. It is in the main true, as Minot has said, that the rabbit is bigger than the guinea-pig because he grows the faster; but that man is bigger than the rabbit because he goes on growing for a longer time.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Human length growth peaks in velocity around the fifth month before birth
claims.statement: The human curve of growth in length has a point of inflection about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: before it growth velocity continually increases, and after it, though growth remains rapid, velocity falls away.
claims.quote: It will at once be seen that there is a “point of inflection” somewhere about the fifth month of intra-uterine life: up to that date growth proceeds with a continually increasing velocity; but after that date, though growth is still rapid, its velocity tends to fall away.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Variability of stature and weight tracks the rate of growth
claims.statement: The coefficient of variability of human stature and weight falls when the rate of growth diminishes and rises again during the adolescent acceleration, so that variability is a function of the rate of growth.
claims.quote: We see, in short, that the amount of _variability_ in stature or in weight is a function of the _rate of growth_ in these magnitudes, though we are not yet in a position to equate the terms precisely, one with another.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Growth rate is interrupted at physiological epochs such as birth, puberty, metamorphosis
claims.statement: Curves of growth show well-marked interruptions or changes of rate at physiological epochs such as birth and puberty, in man and in other animals, and most strikingly in animals that undergo a regular metamorphosis.
claims.quote: Just as the human curve of growth has its slight but well-marked interruptions, or variations in rate, coinciding with such epochs as birth and puberty, so is it with other animals, and this phenomenon is particularly striking in the case of animals which undergo a regular metamorphosis.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Metamorphosis is often, perhaps always, accompanied by loss of bulk and weight
claims.statement: Negative growth, an actual loss of bulk and weight, often and perhaps always accompanies metamorphosis, as in the eel, the silkworm before pupation and the frog tadpole.
claims.quote: The negative growth, or actual loss of bulk and weight which often, and perhaps always, accompanies metamorphosis, is well shewn in the case of the eel.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Organ size bears no constant ratio to body size through life, especially the brain
claims.statement: There is no simple and constant relation, holding throughout life, between the size of the whole body and that of organs such as brain, heart and liver; the brain in particular falls from about one-eighth of body weight at birth to about one-fiftieth at twenty-five.
claims.quote: It is plain, then, that there is no simple and direct relation, holding good _throughout life_, between the size of the body as a whole and that of the organs we have just discussed; and the changing ratio of magnitude is especially marked in the case of the brain
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Plaice weight-length coefficient peaks near the size of sexual maturity
claims.statement: In plaice the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 is not constant but rises to a maximum and then slowly declines with increasing size, the maximum falling near 30 cm, about the size at which sexual maturity begins.
claims.quote: we see that _k_ is by no means constant, but steadily increases to a maximum, and afterwards slowly declines with the increasing size of the fish
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Seasonal cycle in fish weight at fixed length is caused by spawning
claims.statement: In plaice of fixed length, weight falls from about November to March or April and is restored between May or June and November, a periodic change caused wholly by spawning and the subsequent rebuilding of tissues and gonads, so that the spawning season can be determined from length and weight alone.
claims.quote: With unchanging length, the weight and therefore the bulk of the fish falls off from about November to March or April, and again between May or June and November the bulk and weight are gradually restored. The explanation is simple, and depends wholly on the process of spawning, and on the subsequent building up again of the tissues and the reproductive organs.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Each part has its own specific growth rate, on which specific morphology depends
claims.statement: A large part of an organism's specific morphology depends on there being, besides an aggregate rate of growth of the whole, a characteristic specific rate of growth for each part or organ, so that small changes in these local rates soon produce striking differences of form.
claims.quote: a very large part of the specific morphology of the organism depends upon the fact that there is not only an average, or aggregate, rate of growth common to the whole, but also a variation of rate in different parts of the organism, tending towards a specific rate characteristic of each different part or organ.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Common temperate plants share a growth optimum near 26 °C
claims.statement: The optimum temperature for growth is much the same, about 26 °C, for the common plants of temperate climates, and considerably higher for plants of warmer regions such as melon and maize.
claims.quote: this optimum temperature is very much the same for all the common plants of our own climate which have as yet been studied; in them it is somewhere about 26° C. (or say 77° F.), or about the temperature of a warm summer’s day
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Growth has a van’t Hoff temperature coefficient like a chemical reaction
claims.statement: Van’t Hoff’s law, that reaction velocity is multiplied by a constant factor for each degree of temperature rise, applies with qualifications to growth, so that growth has a temperature coefficient (about 2 to 3 per 10 °C, of the same order as chemical reactions).
claims.quote: Van’t Hoff’s law, which has become a fundamental principle of chemical mechanics, is likewise applicable (with certain qualifications) to the phenomena of vital chemistry; and it follows that, on very much the same lines, we may speak of the “temperature coefficient” of growth.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Optimum temperature curves arise from acceleration combined with cumulative damage
claims.statement: Growth rate has an optimum temperature because temperature both accelerates growth according to van’t Hoff’s law and progressively damages or fatigues the organism, so the optimum curve is a complex resultant rather than a primary phenomenon.
claims.quote: It would seem to be this double effect of temperature in the case of the organism which gives us our “optimum” curves, which are the expression, accordingly, not of a primary phenomenon, but of a more or less complex resultant.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Seasonal growth in fish and man follows a damped sine curve
claims.statement: In fishes such as plaice and haddock, and in man, growth is slower in winter than in summer, as if an annual sine curve were superimposed on the growth curve, and the amplitude of this fluctuation dies away as growth slows, giving a damped sine curve.
claims.quote: in short, our phenomenon is simply expressed by what is known as a “damped sine-curve.” Exactly the same thing occurs in man, though neither in his case nor in that of the fish have we sufficient data for its complete illustration.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity
claims.statement: Century-smoothed annual ring widths of Arizona yellow pines show that the climate of Arizona over the past 500 years fluctuated with a regular period of almost exactly 150 years, probably mainly in moisture rather than temperature.
claims.quote: from which we seem compelled to draw the direct conclusion that the climate of Arizona, during the last 500 years, has fluctuated with a regular periodicity of almost precisely 150 years.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Growth rate depends largely on water uptake (turgor) as well as metabolism
claims.statement: A large part of growth, in animals and more conspicuously in plants, depends on turgor and osmotic conditions: the velocity of growth depends largely on the amount of water taken into the cells as well as on chemical metabolism.
claims.quote: A large part of the phenomenon of growth, both in animals and still more conspicuously in plants, is associated with “turgor,” that is to say, is dependent on osmotic conditions; in other words, the velocity of growth depends in great measure (as we have already seen, p. 113) on the amount of water taken up into the living cells
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water
claims.statement: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.
claims.quote: _Pari passu_ with these changes, there is a marked change in the relative lengths of the fore and hind portions of the body, that is to say, of the “cephalothorax” and abdomen: the latter growing relatively longer, the salter the water.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: The organic curve of growth resembles the velocity curve of chemical autocatalysis
claims.statement: The normal curve of growth of an organism closely resembles the velocity curve of an autocatalytic chemical reaction, with a phase of increasing acceleration, a phase in which limiting conditions reduce acceleration, and usually a final phase of retardation and loss of mass; but only a resemblance, not an identity, can yet be asserted.
claims.quote: it is sufficiently clear that the normal “curve of growth” of an organism, in all its general features, very closely resembles the velocity-curve of chemical autocatalysis.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Internal secretions and other substances accelerate growth and alter proportions
claims.statement: Substances inside and outside the organism, such as thyroid and pituitary secretions or iodine compounds, can accelerate growth in a way that changes not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
claims.quote: We may take it, then, as an established fact, whose full extent and bearings are still awaiting investigation, that there exist substances both within and without the organism which have a marvellous power of accelerating growth, and of doing so in such a way as to affect not only the size but the form or proportions of the organism.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Natural selection removes forms rather than originating them
claims.statement: Since forms, including exaggerated ones such as the great Secondary reptiles and Tertiary mammals, can arise from changes in growth, natural selection is needed to explain their disappearance rather than their appearance; in general its function is not to originate but to remove.
claims.quote: And we then, I think, draw near to the conclusion that what is true of these is universally true, and that the great function of natural selection is not to originate, but to remove
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Velocity of regenerative growth varies inversely as about the square of time
claims.statement: After its early maximum, the velocity of regenerative growth (tadpole tails) falls off inversely as some power of the time since injury, approximately as 1/T^2, so that V T^2 is nearly constant.
claims.quote: And in this particular case, the equation _V_ _T_^2 = constant, holds very nearly true; that is to say the velocity varies, or tends to vary, inversely as the square of the time.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Regeneration is ordinary growth, with the same curve as growth from zero
claims.statement: Regeneration is a particular case of growth obeying the same laws; the regeneration curve (short latent period, rapid rise to a maximum velocity, then slow decline) only appears different because ordinary growth curves start at birth, and a complete growth curve from zero has the same essential features.
claims.quote: A complete curve of growth, starting from zero, has the same essential characteristics as the regeneration curve.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Claw reversal after amputation depends on regeneration versus growth rates
claims.statement: Whether an amputated large crustacean claw regenerates as the large claw, or the claws exchange roles, depends on the ratio between the regenerative growth rate of the amputated claw and the growth rate of the uninjured claw, since claw form follows claw size.
claims.quote: It depends upon the respective rates of growth, upon a ratio between the rate of regeneration and the rate of growth of the uninjured limb
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Reproduction by fission is a physical tendency to segment plus regeneration
claims.statement: Reproduction by fission in worm-like animals consists essentially of the physical tendency of a long semi-fluid tube to break into segments, combined with ordinary regeneration, which explains its occurrence in zoologically unrelated animals and its absence in some close relatives.
claims.quote: If we add to this natural tendency towards fission of a cylindrical or tubular worm, the ordinary phenomenon of regeneration, we have all that is essentially implied in “reproduction by fission.”
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Growth velocity peaks and falls because surface resistance suddenly increases
claims.statement: The abrupt change from increasing to decreasing growth velocity is more likely due to a sudden increase of resistance, such as the formation of a comparatively firm skin during histological differentiation, than to a decline of internal growth forces; the later slowing reflects waning growth forces against rising superficial resistance.
claims.quote: I take it that the sudden arrest of velocity is much more likely to be due to a sudden increase of resistance than to a sudden diminution of internal energies: in other words, I suspect that it is coincident with some notable event of histological differentiation, such as the rapid formation of a comparatively firm skin
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Form changes follow the same route in individual development and racial history
claims.statement: Changes of form produced by varying rates of growth are the same phenomenon in individual development and in the differences between species; a transformation from one form to another follows the same course whether it happens within a lifetime or over ancestral history, which accounts for much of von Baer's law of recapitulation.
claims.quote: From one form, or ratio of magnitude, to another there is but one straight and direct road of transformation, be the journey taken fast or slow; and if the transformation take place at all, it will in all likelihood proceed in the self-same way, whether it occur within the life-time of an individual or during the long ancestral history of a race.
claims.chapter: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

claims.label: Cell structure matters only as the visible expression of forces and energy
claims.statement: The study of visible cell structure has little value except as part of a dynamical investigation, because the activities of a cell are due to energy and forces, not to particular material particles or structures as such.
claims.quote: In short it would seem evident that, except in relation to a dynamical investigation, the mere study of cell structure has but little value of its own.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Mitotic figures require a polarised force like magnetism, not mechanical traction
claims.statement: The spindle and asters of dividing cells are lines of force of a bipolar field made visible by more permeable particles, like iron filings between magnet poles, and they cannot be explained by mere mechanical traction on a protoplasmic web but require some polarised and polarising force analogous to magnetism or electricity.
claims.quote: any explanation which is based, like Rhumbler’s, on mere mechanical traction, is obviously inadequate, and we shall find ourselves limited to the hypothesis of some polarised and polarising force, such as we deal with, for instance, in the phenomena of magnetism or electricity.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: The nucleus is spherical because it is an immiscible fluid drop under uniform tension
claims.statement: The nucleus is almost always spherical because its fluid substance does not mix with the surrounding protoplasm, so it is bounded by a film of uniform surface tension and immersed in a medium transmitting uniform fluid pressure; where the cytoplasm becomes more solid (as in muscle cells or mucus-laden epithelial cells) the pressure becomes unsymmetrical and the nucleus is deformed.
claims.quote: So long as the fluid substance of the nucleus is qualitatively different from, and incapable of mixing with, the fluid or semi-fluid protoplasm which surrounds it, we shall expect it to be, as it almost always is, of spherical form.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Morphological polarity of the cell is the outward sign of a dynamical polarity
claims.statement: The visible polarity of a cell (symmetry of structure about an axis, such as nucleus–centrosome or free–attached surface) is the outward expression of a real polarised distribution of forces, whose lines of force are made visible where particles of matter become strung together under those forces.
claims.quote: The _morphological_ “polarity” is accompanied by, and is but the outward expression (or part of it) of a true _dynamical_ polarity, or distribution of forces; and the “lines of force” are rendered visible by concatenation of particles of matter, such as come under the influence of the forces in action.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: The alveolar meshwork of nucleus and cytoplasm is a surface-tension froth
claims.statement: The alveolar 'reticulum' seen in the nucleus and cytoplasm is a froth or foam produced by the interacting surface tensions of two intermixed fluids of similar density striving to separate, and is not inherent in the nature of protoplasm.
claims.quote: This phenomenon is nothing else than what we call in ordinary language, a “froth” or a “foam.” It is a surface-tension phenomenon, due to the interacting surface-tensions of two intermixed fluids, not very different in density, as they strive to separate.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Fine internal networks and granules seen in fixed cells are largely artefacts
claims.statement: Fixation preserves the general outward form of small organisms and cells, but the minute internal networks and granules described as the structure of protoplasm are to a large extent artefacts of coagulating fixatives, although larger structures such as nucleus, vacuoles, centrosomes and the spindle are really present in the living cell.
claims.quote: While this assumption is reasonable and justified as regards the general outward form of small organisms or of individual cells, enough has been done of late years to shew that the case is totally different in the case of the minute internal networks, granules, etc., which represent the alleged _structure_ of protoplasm.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Chromatin behaves as a diamagnetic body and moves to the equatorial plane
claims.statement: In the bipolar field between the centrosomes the nucleus as a whole behaves as a body more permeable than the cytoplasm and is drawn in between the poles, whereas its chromatin, once broken up, behaves like a diamagnetic body, is repelled to the weaker parts of the field, and so collects in a peripheral circle on the equatorial plane.
claims.quote: the fact is that the chromatin substance now _behaves_ after the fashion of a “diamagnetic” body, and is repelled from the stronger to the weaker parts of the field.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Differences of electric potential play a great part in cell division
claims.statement: Differences of electric potential between cell constituents, and between parts of the egg, play a great part in cell division; the potential difference between animal and vegetative poles of a fertilised egg fluctuates or reverses at successive segmentations, and the electrical difference of chromatin is greatest at mitosis.
claims.quote: Among other investigations, all leading towards the same general conclusion, namely that differences of electric potential play a great part in the phenomenon of cell division
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Every cell division results from conflict between surface tension and opposing forces
claims.statement: In all cells the mechanical process of division must be explained as the result of a conflict between surface tension and its opposing forces, the division plane being set in the equatorial plane of the polar field.
claims.quote: in all cells whatsoever, the process of division must somehow be explained as the result of a conflict between surface-tension and its opposing forces.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Entry of the first spermatozoon raises the surface tension of the egg
claims.statement: Because later spermatozoa fail to enter the egg after the first, an immediate consequence of sperm entry is an increase in the surface tension of the egg.
claims.quote: other spermatozoa, subsequent to the first, fail to effect an entry, we may safely conclude that an immediate consequence of the entry of the spermatozoon is an increase in the surface-tension of the egg
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: The pronuclei travel curved paths and meet before reaching the centre of the egg
claims.statement: Given an attraction between the male and female pronuclei and a force drawing them toward the egg centre, their paths lie within the triangle formed by the two bodies and the centre, are curved (convex toward the line joining them) unless they start on a diameter, and the pronuclei meet a little before the centre and then travel straight to it.
claims.quote: (2) unless the two bodies happen to lie, to begin with, precisely on a diameter of the cell, their paths until they meet one another will be curved paths, the convexity of the curve being towards the straight line joining the two bodies; (3) the two bodies will meet a little before they reach the centre;
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Mitotic phenomena follow from simple physical assumptions and have secondary significance
claims.statement: Most if not all of the intracellular phenomena of mitosis follow inevitably from very simple assumptions about the physical constitution of the cell and a simple distribution of polarised forces within it, and are likely to prove of only remote and secondary biological significance.
claims.quote: Most, if not all of them, would seem to follow immediately and inevitably from very simple assumptions as to the physical constitution of the cell, and from an extremely simple distribution of polarised forces within it.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen
claims.statement: Although chromosome number is constant within a species, the range of numbers across plants and animals is small: few organisms have fewer than six chromosomes in the germ-nuclei and fewer still have more than sixteen.
claims.quote: (as regards the germ-nuclei) few organisms have less than six chromosomes, and fewer still have more than sixteen
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Details of mitosis vary among close relatives and are not specific to the organism
claims.statement: The details of mitosis (presence of visible caryokinesis, position of the field of force, number of chromosome groups, chromosome form and arrangement) vary greatly even among closely related organisms or within one species, and are not specifically related to the organism in which they occur.
claims.quote: there seem to be strong grounds for believing that these and many similar phenomena are in no way specifically related to the particular organism in which they have been observed, and are not even specially and indisputably connected with the organism as such.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Early embryological categories seldom coincide with phylogenetic classification
claims.statement: Early embryological data, up to and well beyond segmentation, are a subject for physiological and physical investigation, and their categories (yolk content, chromosome form and number, radial, bilateral or spiral cleavage) will only seldom and accidentally coincide with the natural or phylogenetic classification of the systematist.
claims.quote: But we have little right to expect, and in point of fact we shall very seldom and (as it were) only accidentally find, that these embryological categories coincide with the lines of “natural” or “phylogenetic” classification which have been arrived at by the systematic zoologist.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Surface tension gives the cell its outline and morphological individuality
claims.statement: The cell is a sphere of action of localised forces, of which surface tension gives the cell its outline and individuality; partial versus total segmentation of eggs, and unicellular versus multicellular organisation, differ in whether surface tensions succeed in forming visible separations between cells.
claims.quote: surface-tension is the particular force which is especially responsible for giving to the cell its outline and its morphological individuality.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: The centrosome is essentially a centre of force, not necessarily a material body
claims.statement: The centrosome is essentially a dynamic centre of force, which may or may not consist of a visible concentration of matter but tends to produce one, as shown by cells that live without visible centrosomes and centrosomes that disappear and form anew.
claims.quote: We may safely take it that the centrosome, or the “attraction sphere,” is essentially a “centre of force,” and that this dynamic centre may or may not be constituted by (but will be very apt to produce) a concrete and visible concentration of matter.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: A continuous field of force shapes the whole organism regardless of its cells
claims.statement: The multicellular organism is not a colony of independent cells: a continuous field of force runs through the entire organism, not restricted to protoplasmic continuity, and shapes it independently of the number, size and form of its cells.
claims.quote: And such a continuous field of force, somehow shaping the whole organism, independently of the number, magnitude and form of the individual cells, which enter, like a froth, into its fabric, seems to me certainly and obviously to exist.
claims.chapter: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

claims.label: Fluid protoplasm growing by imbibition produces rounded rather than plane surfaces
claims.statement: Because protoplasm is fluid and grows by imbibition (intussusception) rather than by deposition of particles on a surface, freely growing organisms tend to have swelling, rounded contours, and plane surfaces are rare in them unless produced by pressure.
claims.quote: So far then, as growth goes on, unaffected by pressure or other external force, the fluidity of protoplasm, its mobility internal and external, and the manner in which particles move with comparative freedom from place to place within, all manifestly tend to the production of swelling, rounded surfaces, and to their great predominance over plane surfaces in the contour of the organism.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Surface tension is probably the paramount force determining cell form
claims.statement: Of the physical forces that determine the forms of cells, solitary or in contact, surface tension is of great and probably paramount importance, usually acting together with gravity, mechanical pressure and osmosis.
claims.quote: Among the forces which determine the forms of cells, whether they be solitary or arranged in contact with one another, this force of surface-tension is certainly of great, and is probably of paramount importance.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Organic symmetry reflects equilibrium and is absent without it, as in amoeba
claims.statement: Symmetry is highly characteristic of organic forms because they are figures of equilibrium governed by a principle of minimal energy, as in liquid films; symmetry is lacking only where equilibrium is lacking, as in the amoeba.
claims.quote: Such symmetry is in a high degree characteristic of organic forms, and is rarely absent in living things,—save in such cases as amoeba, where the equilibrium on which symmetry depends is likewise lacking.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Rounding off of protoplasm is due to surface tension, not vital contractility
claims.statement: When a drop of protoplasm, or the tip of an amoeba's pseudopodium, rounds itself off, this is a simple consequence of surface tension and not of any special vital contractility.
claims.quote: When any drop of protoplasm, either over all its surface or at some free end, as at the extremity of the pseudopodium of an amoeba, is seen likewise to “round itself off,” that is not an effect of “vital contractility,” but (as Hofmeister shewed so long ago as 1867) a simple consequence of surface tension
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Plasmodial taxes towards moisture, warmth and food parallel surface-tension phenomena
claims.statement: The movements of a plasmodium (Aethalium) towards damp, warm or nutritious spots and away from sugar or salt solutions can each be accounted for by local changes of surface tension, as in inanimate drops moving on a warmed or chemically altered surface.
claims.quote: When we find that a plasmodium of Aethalium, for instance, creeps towards a damp spot, or towards a warm spot, or towards substances that happen to be nutritious, and again creeps away from solutions of sugar or of salt, we seem to be dealing with phenomena every one of which can be paralleled by ordinary phenomena of surface tension
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Resting cells are spherical; the amoeboid phase is one of activity and unequal tensions
claims.statement: In naked protoplasmic cells the amoeboid form marks a phase of activity with unequal surface tensions, whereas the spherical form marks a phase of rest when internal homogeneity and minimal potential energy are attained, at which time the cell also becomes encysted.
claims.quote: In the case of the naked protoplasmic cell, as the amoeboid phase is emphatically a phase of freedom and activity, of chemical and physiological change, so, on the other hand, is the spherical form indicative of a phase of rest or comparative inactivity.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: A yeast bud arises where surface tension locally and suddenly diminishes
claims.statement: A bud appears on a yeast cell because the surface tension diminishes at one part of the cell surface, so that this area expands, after which the bud's own surface tension rounds it into a roughly spherical form.
claims.quote: When a “bud” appears, whether with or without actual growth by osmosis or otherwise of the mass, it does so because at a certain part of the cell-surface the surface tension has more or less suddenly diminished, and the area of that portion expands accordingly
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Each new foraminiferal chamber is a surface-tension figure; the whole shell is not
claims.statement: In multichambered organisms such as the foraminifera Globigerina or Rotalia, and in desmids, each newly formed bud or chamber is a figure of equilibrium shaped by surface tension while still fluid, and is then solidified onto earlier chambers, so the whole organism is not itself a figure of minimal area.
claims.quote: The little organism as a whole is not a figure of equilibrium or of minimal area; but each new bud or separate chamber is such a figure, conditioned by the forces of surface tension, and superposed upon the complex aggregate of similar bubbles after these latter have become consolidated one by one into a rigid system.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Surface tension governs the forms of small organisms and cells, not large organisms
claims.statement: Surface tension governs form only where surface energy is a large fraction of total energy, so it determines the forms of minute organisms and of the small cells of larger organisms, while the general forms of large organisms are due to other, non-molecular forces.
claims.quote: in other words it will be small or minute organisms, or the small cellular elements of larger organisms, whose forms will be governed by surface-tension; while the general forms of the larger organisms will be due to other and non-molecular forces.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest unicellular forms
claims.statement: Of the six surfaces of revolution with constant mean curvature (plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid), spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest forms of small unicellular organisms and of cells in simple aggregates, and transitions between them are frequent during growth, reproduction and development.
claims.quote: That spheres, cylinders and unduloids are of the commonest occurrence among the forms of small unicellular organism, or of individual cells in the simpler aggregates, and that in the processes of growth, reproduction and development transitions are frequent from one of these forms to another, is obvious to the naturalist
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: A cylindrical cell's end cap has twice the cylinder's radius and height about 0.27R
claims.statement: Where a cylindrical cell of uniform wall tension is capped by part of a sphere, the sphere's radius is twice the cylinder's radius, the cap subtends a cone of 60°, and its height is about 0.27 of the cylinder radius (a little more than one-eighth of the diameter), proportions seen in the free end cells of Spirogyra.
claims.quote: the normal height of the spherical cap over the end of the cylindrical cell is just a very little more than one-eighth of the diameter of the cylinder, or of the radius of the sphere. And these are the proportions which we recognise, under normal circumstances, in such a case as the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra where its free end is capped by a portion of a sphere.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Viscid spider-thread coating breaks into beads at the cylinder stability limit
claims.statement: The sticky fluid coating of a spider's spiral thread, being a liquid cylinder, becomes unstable when its length exceeds its circumference and breaks up into equal, equally spaced beads (often with smaller beads between), the spacing being somewhat greater than theory owing to viscosity and drag on the core thread.
claims.quote: But this liquid cylinder has its limit of stability when its length equals its own circumference, and therefore just at the points so defined it tends to disrupt into separate segments
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Notched hydroid cups and annulated stems are both due to surface tension
claims.statement: The notching of the rim of hydroid calycles and the annular constrictions of their cylindrical stems are phenomena of the same order, both produced by surface tension acting on the structures while they are still fluid or semifluid films, as in the beaded rim of a splash.
claims.quote: In the case of the hydroid calycle (Fig. 72), we are led to the conclusion that the two common and conspicuous features of notching or indentation of the cup, and of constriction or annulation of the long cylindrical stem, are phenomena of the same order and are due to surface-tension in both cases alike.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Freely growing cylindrical cells owe their form to an anisotropic wall
claims.statement: A cylindrical cell such as Spirogyra that grows without external restraint takes its form because its developing membrane is anisotropic, extending more easily in one direction; a slight inequality of tension in two directions gives an ellipsoidal cell and a great inequality a cylindrical one.
claims.quote: I take it therefore, that the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra, or any other cylindrical cell which grows in freedom from any manifest external restraint, has assumed that particular form simply by reason of the molecular constitution of its developing surface-membrane; and that this molecular constitution was anisotropous, in such a way as to render extension easier in one direction than another.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Small organisms show a limited range of forms because molecular forces control them
claims.statement: Because protozoa, bacteria and other minute cells are of a size at which form is mainly controlled by molecular forces, they exhibit only a limited range of forms, which vary with physical conditions.
claims.quote: To the fact that these little organisms belong to an order of magnitude in which form is mainly, if not wholly, conditioned and controlled by molecular forces, is due the limited range of forms which they actually exhibit.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Bacterial form is too plastic to serve for species identification
claims.statement: Bacteria and micrococci change shape so much with life stage, circumstances and preparation that their specific identity can seldom be recognised by form, so they have a physiological rather than morphological specificity.
claims.quote: Whatever grounds we may have for attributing to these organisms a permanent or stable specific identity (after the fashion of the higher plants and animals), we can seldom safely do so on the ground of definite and always recognisable _form_
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Vorticella bells form a graded series of unduloids
claims.statement: The bells of the various species of Vorticella, like many other Infusoria, are unduloids or partial unduloids spanning every gradation from nearly cylindrical to nearly spherical, bounded by the stalk attachment and the ciliary ring as by two unequal supporting rings, and the species differ only in ratio or degree.
claims.quote: The cups of the various species of Vorticella (Fig. 75) are nothing in the world but a beautiful series of unduloids, or partial unduloids, in every gradation from a form that is all but cylindrical to one that is all but a perfect sphere.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Protozoan loricas form by adsorption into least-area surfaces, not for protection
claims.statement: The membranous cups (loricas) of Salpingoeca, Tintinnus and similar protozoa arise inevitably from substances adsorbed in the surface layer of the protoplasm, and molecular forces make the resulting pellicle a surface of least possible area under the circumstances, here an unduloid; this efficient cause, rather than a protective purpose, explains their form.
claims.quote: that this surface pellicle or membrane was inevitably bound, by molecular forces, to become a surface of the least possible area which the circumstances permitted
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Shared form in simple organisms need not imply common descent
claims.statement: The assumption that similar or identical forms indicate genealogical relationship is far less well founded for minute organisms with few, simple characters whose form is largely produced directly by a physical force, so identical forms of such organisms in different times or places need not indicate unbroken descent or common stock.
claims.quote: when we attempt to extend it to minute organisms whose specific characters are few and simple, whose simplicity becomes much more manifest when we regard it from the point of view of physical and mathematical description and analysis, and whose form is referable, or (to say the least of it) is very largely referable, to the direct and immediate action of a particular physical force.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: The unduloid Lagena shell is formed while hanging vertically in the sea
claims.statement: The flask-shaped (unduloid) shell of Lagena is formed while the organism hangs vertically, in a position of symmetry about its vertical axis, like a hanging drop; flattened or winged forms are those formed when this symmetry of position was absent and the shell lay horizontally.
claims.quote: but we may be pretty sure that it is suspended vertically in the sea, that is to say in a position of symmetry as regards its vertical axis, about which the unduloid surface of revolution is symmetrically formed.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Thin walls flute longitudinally; thick narrow necks pleat transversely
claims.statement: Small tension changes in a thin-walled elongated cell produce wrinkling in the plane of greatest curvature, hence longitudinal fluting, especially near the ends; where the wall is thick relative to diameter, as in the narrow neck of Lagena or tubular hydroid gonangia, bending stiffness makes folding transverse instead.
claims.quote: The manner in which our little Lagena-shell tends to fold or wrinkle, longitudinally in its wider part, and transversely or annularly in its narrow neck, is thus completely and easily explained.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Symmetrical surface-tension pull sets heliozoan filaments radially
claims.statement: Fluid surface protoplasm creeps up the stiff axial filaments of a heliozoan such as Actinophrys, and because this surface-tension pull is symmetrical around each filament the filaments are set normal to the cell surface, radiating from the centre; closely spaced filaments produce honeycomb-like depressions between them.
claims.quote: Since the attraction exercised by this surface tension is symmetrical around the filament, the latter will be pulled equally in all directions; in other words it will tend to be set normally to the surface of the sphere, that is to say radiating directly outwards from the centre.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: The trypanosome undulating membrane is a liquid film drawn up along a flagellum
claims.statement: The undulating membrane of trypanosomes and related flagellates forms when the flagellum lies near and parallel to the body and the fluid surface protoplasm is drawn up as a film along it, as a soap-film would be; the membrane is thus a liquid film of constant mean curvature whose undulations are produced by molecular tensions, not by its own active mobility.
claims.quote: It is a plausible assumption to suppose that, as the flagellum waves about, it comes to lie near and parallel to the body of the cell, and that the frill or undulating membrane is formed by the clear, fluid protoplasm of the surface layer springing up in a film to run up and along the flagellum, just as a soap-film would be formed in similar circumstances.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: The biconcave red blood corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure
claims.statement: The biconcave mammalian red blood corpuscle is not a surface of constant mean curvature and so cannot be a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone; some other force, possibly osmotic inequilibrium or fluid-crystal forces of its cholesterin-like constituents, must maintain its shape, which changes to a sphere in diluted blood.
claims.quote: Accordingly, from the point of view of surface tension alone, the blood-corpuscle is not a surface of equilibrium; or in other words, it is not a fluid drop suspended in another liquid.
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Decapod sperm-cell shape is an intermediate phase of osmotic shrinkage
claims.statement: The normal form of decapod crustacean sperm-cells is one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage from a spherical form, caused by osmotic withdrawal of fluid without a matching reduction of surface area, so that equivalent shapes are produced by salt solutions of equivalent (molecular-weight-proportional) concentration.
claims.quote: we see that what we call its normal appearance is just one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage, brought about by the abstraction of fluid from its interior as the result of an osmotic pressure greater outside than inside the cell
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Elastic fibrillae act as a microscopic skeleton shaping spiral cells
claims.statement: The spiral and other peculiar forms of decapod sperm-cells and of many Infusoria are produced by more or less elastic fibrillae in the cell, which restrain and modify the surface forces like the wire frames and coils in Plateau's experiments, acting as a microscopic skeleton.
claims.quote: In all probability we must in like manner attribute the peculiar spiral and other forms, for instance of many Infusoria, to the presence, among the multitudinous other differentiations of their protoplasmic substance, of such more or less elastic fibrillae, which play as it were the part of a microscopic skeleton
claims.chapter: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

claims.label: Cell-wall secretion is adsorption of constituents at the surface
claims.statement: The so-called secretion of a cell-wall or membrane is the adsorption of certain constituents of the cell, which lower surface tension, to its surface (as formulated by the Gibbs-Thomson law), where they also increase viscosity and rigidity; the formation of a cell membrane is thus a chemico-physical phenomenon.
claims.quote: The so-called “secretion” of this cell-wall is nothing more than a sort of exudation, or striving towards the surface, of certain constituent molecules or particles within the cell; and the Gibbs-Thomson law formulates, in part at least, the conditions under which they do so.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Spicules are deposited at interfaces between cells or vacuoles
claims.statement: Skeletal spicules, as in sponges and radiolaria, are characteristically deposited in the interfacial boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and their form is in many cases regulated by the arrangement of these boundaries.
claims.quote: it is highly characteristic of the whole process of spicule-formation for the deposits to be laid down just in the “interfacial” boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and that the form of the spicular structures tends in many cases to be regulated and determined by the arrangement of these boundaries.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Membranes and cysts form only after protoplasm rounds up with positive surface tension
claims.statement: Because adsorption requires a surface tension greater than zero, films or threads of creeping protoplasm do not form an encysting membrane, and an organism forms its cyst or cell-wall only when its protoplasm has developed a positive surface tension and gathered into a roughly spherical body.
claims.quote: It is for this reason that films or threads of creeping protoplasm shew little tendency, or none, to cover themselves with an encysting membrane; and that it is only when, in an altered phase, the protoplasm has developed a positive surface tension, and has accordingly gathered itself up into a more or less spherical body, that the tendency to form a membrane is manifested
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Winter encystment and winter-egg shells relate to temperature effects on adsorption
claims.statement: Since a rise of temperature reduces adsorbability (and surface tension), lower temperature favours adsorption and membrane formation, which probably accounts for the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter and the strong shells or capsules of winter eggs.
claims.quote: We may in all probability ascribe to this fact and to its converse, or at least associate with it, such phenomena as the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter, or the frequent formation of strong shells or membranous capsules in “winter-eggs.”
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Chondriosomes and similar fibrils are surface-tension clumps drawn along the cell axis
claims.statement: The mitochondria, chondriosomes and similar granules and fibrils of cells are not special entities with specific functions but clumps of heterogeneous cell contents gathered by surface tension and drawn out along the cell axis by osmotic currents arising from surface energy and adsorption, revealing a field of force and dynamical polarity in the cell.
claims.quote: while, from the physical point of view we are tempted to see but little mystery in the whole phenomenon, and to ascribe it, in all probability and in general terms, to the gathering or “clumping” together, under surface tension, of various constituents of the heterogeneous cell-content, and to the drawing out of these little clumps along the axis of the cell towards one or other of its extremities
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Potassium salts concentrate where cell-surface tension is weak
claims.statement: Potassium salts, like inorganic substances generally, raise surface tension and therefore concentrate at those parts of a cell surface where the tension is weak, so their localised accumulation (shown by Macallum's cobalt-nitrite method) indicates inequalities of surface tension.
claims.quote: and we may safely take it that our potassium salts, like inorganic substances in general, tend to _raise_ the surface tension, and will therefore be found concentrating at a portion of the surface whose tension is weak
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Conjugation outgrowths and root-hairs arise at sites of potassium concentration
claims.statement: The bulges that begin conjugation in algae such as Pleurocarpus and Mesocarpus, and the root-hair outgrowth of Equisetum spores, arise where surface tension is weakened, and these sites coincide with heavy concentrations of potassium salts, which disperse when the cell becomes symmetrical again.
claims.quote: This bulge is, in the first place, a sign of weakened surface tension on one side of the cell, which as a whole had hitherto been a symmetrical cylinder; in the second place, we see that the bulging area corresponds to the position of a great concentration of the potassic salt
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Potassium accumulates at the bases of cilia and flagella
claims.statement: Ciliate and flagellate cells show a characteristic accumulation of potassium at and near the base of their cilia, which accounts (through weakened surface tension) for the small protuberance where a flagellum arises and the ridge at the base of a row of cilia.
claims.quote: In the case of ciliate or flagellate cells, there is to be found a characteristic accumulation of potassium at and near the base of the cilia.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Unicellular forms and their asymmetries follow surface molecular forces
claims.statement: In unicellular organisms not only the general configuration but also the departures from symmetry can be correlated with molecular forces, especially local variations of surface tension, acting in their fluid or semifluid surfaces.
claims.quote: we have arrived at the conclusion, as regards unicellular organisms, that not only their general configuration but also _their departures from symmetry_ may be correlated with the molecular forces manifested in their fluid or semi-fluid surfaces.
claims.chapter: Ch. VI: A Note on Adsorption

claims.label: Forms of cell-aggregates are shaped chiefly by surface tension toward minimal areas
claims.statement: The forms of cells in contact with one another, and ultimately of tissues, are determined especially by surface tension, which shows itself in the production of surfaces of (relatively) minimal area.
claims.quote: we shall probably find, and we may at least begin by assuming, that the agency of surface tension is especially manifest and important. The effect of this surface tension will chiefly manifest itself in the production of surfaces _minimae areae_
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Right-angled cell walls arise because older walls solidify before new partitions form
claims.statement: Plant cell walls often meet at right angles (Sachs’s Rule) because an earlier wall has usually become solid and rigid before a later partition joins it, so the fluid partition sets itself at equal angles, i.e. perpendicular, to the rigid wall.
claims.quote: such validity as the rule possesses is due to the fact that among plant-tissues it very frequently happens that one cell-wall has become solid and rigid before another and later partition-wall is developed in connection with it.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Shape of paired cells depends on relative tensions at outer surface and partition
claims.statement: Whether two adjacent cells in a filament (as in Nostoc and its allies) are separated by flat partitions, are hemispherical, or are each more than a hemisphere depends on the relative magnitudes of the tension at the outer cell surface and at the boundary between the cells.
claims.quote: These various conditions depend, according to what we have already learned, upon the relative magnitudes of the tensions at the surface of the cells and at the boundary between them
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120°, regardless of cell size
claims.statement: In sections of tissues such as plant parenchyma, as in a froth of soap-bubbles, cell walls meet three at a time at angles of 120° whatever the sizes of the cells, while the relative sizes of neighbouring cells determine only the curvature of the walls.
claims.quote: in both cases we see the cell-walls everywhere meeting, by threes, at angles of 120°, irrespective of the size of the individual cells: whose relative size, on the other hand, determines the _curvature_ of the partition-walls.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Four cells of a segmenting egg never meet in a point; a polar furrow is always present
claims.statement: In the four-celled stage of a segmenting egg whose cells are in full fluid contact, the four cells cannot meet in a single point; a short intermediate partition (the polar furrow) must be present, and reports of four cells meeting in a simple cross are due to error or imperfect observation.
claims.quote: it is quite certain that no simple and homogeneous system of fluid films such as we are dealing with is in equilibrium without its presence.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Strong cell–cell tension relative to cell–medium tension makes cells round off
claims.statement: Where the tension at cell–cell contacts exceeds that at cell–medium surfaces, the external angle between neighbouring cells is less than 120°, and if the cell–cell tension equals or exceeds the sum of the other two the cells touch only at a point, which explains rounded-off blastomeres separated by spaces.
claims.quote: If the former be greater than either of the other two, the outside angle will be less than 120°; and if the tension along the surface _cc′_ be as much or more than the sum of the other two, then the drops will stand in contact only, save for the possible effect of external pressure, at a point.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: An epidermis’s physical characters follow simply from its lying on the outside
claims.statement: The fundamental character of an epidermis is that it lies on the outside of the cell mass, and its main physical features (flattened, rectangular cells meeting partitions at near right angles) follow from that position through unequal and consolidated tensions in its outer walls.
claims.quote: the fundamental character of an epidermis simply is that it lies on the outside, and that its main physical characteristics follow, as a matter of course, from the position which it occupies and from the various consequences which that situation entails.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Hexagons are regular only where cells are equal in size and forces uniform
claims.statement: Perfectly regular hexagonal cell patterns occur only where the cells are uniform in size and subject to uniform forces, as in the retinal pigment epithelium; where cell sizes vary (intestinal epithelium, parenchyma) or growth adds directional traction, the hexagons become irregular or elongated.
claims.quote: the cells, uniform in size, are flattened out to a uniform thickness by the fluid pressure acting radially; and their reaction on each other converts the flattened discs into regular hexagons.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Cylinders or spheres pressed into full surface contact form hexagons
claims.statement: Whenever cylinders or spheres of similar size are brought into complete surface contact by any uniform force (surface tension, growth pressure or external pressure), they tend to form a pattern of hexagons in section or surface view, each meeting six neighbours with 120° angles.
claims.quote: wherever we have a system of cylinders or spheres, associated together with sufficient mutual interaction to bring them into complete surface contact, there, in section or in surface view, we tend to get a pattern of hexagons.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Close-packed corallites of varying size are on average hexagonal
claims.statement: In colonial corals whose corallites are in close contact, the corallites are squeezed into hexagonal prisms; where their sizes vary irregularly they are hexagonal on average, some having fewer and some more than six sides, while loosely bundled corallites stay cylindrical.
claims.quote: where there is greater and more irregular variation in size, the cells will be _on the average_ hexagonal, but some will have fewer and some more sides than six
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: The bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism capped by rhombic-dodecahedral facets
claims.statement: The hive-bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism closed at one end by three rhombic facets of a rhombic dodecahedron meeting at about 109° 28′, the configuration that encloses a given volume with the least surface.
claims.quote: The bee’s cell, then, is this figure incompletely formed: it is a hexagonal prism with one open or unfinished end, and one trihedral apex of a rhombic dodecahedron.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Comb geometry arises from surface tension in semi-fluid wax, not bee design
claims.statement: The regular hexagonal and pyramidal geometry of the bee’s comb is produced automatically by surface tension acting on the cell walls while the wax (or the wasp’s paper pulp) is still semi-fluid, the insects merely building thin tubular cells packed closely together; it is not due to the bee seeking to economise wax.
claims.quote: It seems more likely that we have to do with a true surface-tension effect; in other words, that the walls assume their configuration when in a semi-fluid state, while the papery pulp is still liquid, or while the wax is warm under the high temperature of the crowded hive
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Parenchyma cells are generally rhombic dodecahedra, ideal froths tetrakaidecahedra
claims.statement: A perfectly fluid froth of equal cells is divided into Kelvin’s fourteen-sided tetrakaidecahedra, but in plant parenchyma, given restraint and imperfect fluidity, the cells generally take the rhombic dodecahedral form even under symmetrical conditions.
claims.quote: Accordingly, it is very probably the case that, in the parenchymatous tissue, under the actual conditions of restraint and of very imperfect fluidity, it is after all the rhombic dodecahedral configuration which, even under perfectly symmetrical conditions, is generally assumed.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Physical laws govern the whole configuration of later-stage segmenting eggs
claims.statement: The whole configuration of an egg in advanced stages of segmentation is determined by simple physical laws just as in the two- and four-celled stages, even though the mathematics becomes too difficult to follow.
claims.quote: We have little reason to doubt, and no just cause to disbelieve, that the whole configuration, for instance of an egg in the advanced stages of segmentation, is accurately determined by simple physical laws
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Polar-furrow arrangements follow relative cell sizes, not species identity
claims.statement: Small changes in the relative sizes of the four cells carry the median partition and its polar furrows through all their possible arrangements, which correspond to those observed in various embryos; these arrangements are physical phenomena distributed without relation to zoological classification, not species characters.
claims.quote: So, by slight and delicate modifications in the relative size of the cells, we may pass through all the possible arrangements of the median partition, and of the “furrows” which correspond to its upper and lower edges; and every one of these arrangements has been frequently observed in the four-celled stage of various embryos.
claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: No evidence that physical forces give way to unknown vital agencies in development
claims.statement: Although forces other than surface tension act in a growing embryo, there is no evidence at any stage that physical forces cease to govern its material form and are replaced by agencies unknown to physics.
claims.quote: But we have no evidence whatsoever that at this point, or that point, or at any, the dominion of the physical forces over the material system gives place to a new condition where agencies at present unknown to the physicist impose themselves on the living matter
