claims.chapter: Ch. VII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates

claims.label: Minimal bisecting walls cut the longest axis and alternate at right angles
claims.statement: For a rectangular cell to be divided equally by a partition of least area, the partition must cut across its longest axis, and in successive bisections each new partition must be at right angles to the one before.
claims.quote: From this we may draw the simple rule that, for a rectangular body or parallelopiped to be divided equally by means of a partition of minimal area, (1) the partition must cut across the longest axis of the figure; and (2) in the event of successive bisections, each partition must run at right angles to its immediate predecessor.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: A new cell wall has the least area that can enclose the given volume (Errera)
claims.statement: The fundamental rule of cell division is that the incipient partition of a dividing cell takes the least possible area that can divide the given volume; Sachs’s rule of successive divisions at right angles is a subordinate case of this principle.
claims.quote: a much more important and fundamental rule, due not to Sachs but to Errera; that (3) the incipient partition-wall of a dividing cell tends to be such that its area is the least possible by which the given space-content can be enclosed.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: A cell cutting off under ~3/10 of its volume uses a curved corner wall, not a plane
claims.statement: When a cubical or rectangular cell divides unequally and the smaller part is less than about three-tenths of the whole, the minimal partition is a quarter-cylinder cutting off one corner rather than a plane wall; below about 0.15 of the volume a spherical octant in a corner is smaller still.
claims.quote: that one portion by anything less than about three-tenths of the whole, or three-sevenths of the other portion, there will be a tendency for the cell to divide, not by means of a plane transverse partition, but by means of a curved, cylindrical wall cutting off one corner of the original cell
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: A quadrant-shaped flat cell divides by a curved anticlinal wall about 3:7 along its side
claims.statement: A flattened cell shaped like a quadrant of a circle divides into equal halves by a circular-arc anticlinal wall meeting the side and periphery at right angles, cutting off about 55° 22′ of the arc and starting about three-tenths of the radius from the centre, since this is the shortest bisecting wall.
claims.quote: Now we find that a flattened cell which is approximately a quadrant of a circle invariably divides after the manner of Fig. 145, C, that is to say, by an approximately circular, _anticlinal_ wall
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Sector cells divide anticlinally only between 62½° and 90°, otherwise periclinally
claims.statement: A sector-shaped (triangular) cell is likely to divide by an anticlinal wall only when its angle of arc lies between about 62½° and 90°; narrower, more tapering cells divide by a periclinal wall, which then has the smaller area.
claims.quote: We see from this, then, that what we have called an anticlinal partition, as _MP_, is only likely to occur in a triangular or prismatic cell whose angle of arc lies between 90° and 62½°. In all narrower or more tapering cells, the periclinal partition will be of less area, and will therefore be more and more likely to occur.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Uniform growth of a disc makes its daughter cells divide at different times
claims.statement: Uniform, symmetrical growth of a flattened disc does not imply uniform growth of its cells: after a quadrant divides into triangular and quadrilateral halves, the triangular cell gains area faster and reaches division size first (at about 1.345 times the radius, against about 1.517 for the quadrilateral).
claims.quote: For it shews us that a uniform and symmetrical growth of the organism (symmetrical, that is to say, under the limitations of a plane surface, or plane section) by no means involves a uniform or symmetrical growth of the individual cells, but may, under certain conditions, actually lead to inequality among these
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Successive minimal-area divisions leave quadrilateral cells forming an epidermis
claims.statement: Successive minimal-area divisions of a disc soon leave only quadrilateral cells at the periphery, which divide radially, producing a superficial layer of parallel-sided cells (an epidermis) contrasting with the irregular cells beneath.
claims.quote: we shall consequently have a superficial or peripheral layer of quadrilateral cells, with sides approximately parallel, that is to say what we are accustomed to call _an epidermis_.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: The arrangement of the first eight cells is not a constant character of a species
claims.statement: A particular arrangement of cell partitions at the eight-celled stage is not a specific or constant character of an organism; within a single species such as the frog, several essentially different arrangements occur.
claims.quote: is a particular arrangement of cell-partitions to be looked upon (as the published figures of the embryologist are apt to suggest) as a _specific character_, or at least a constant or normal character, of the particular organism? The answer to this question is a direct negative
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: All surface groupings of eight cells belong to one of thirteen types
claims.statement: Because n cells sharing a common outer boundary and meeting three at a time need n − 3 intermediate partitions, every possible grouping of eight cells all reaching the surface belongs to one of thirteen topological types, so all drawings of such eight-celled structures represent one of these types.
claims.quote: all possible groupings or arrangements whatsoever of eight cells (where all take part in the _surface_ of the group, none being submerged or wholly enveloped by the rest) are referable to some one or other of _thirteen_ types or forms.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Most stable cell groupings spread contacts evenly; unstable ones concentrate them
claims.statement: Among the possible arrangements of a small group of cells, the most stable (and therefore commonest) are those in which the cell-to-cell contacts are most evenly divided among the cells, and the least stable are those in which one cell has a predominant number of contacts.
claims.quote: But it would appear that the most stable arrangements are those in which the total number of contacts is most evenly divided, and the least stable are those in which some one cell has, as in type _f_, a predominant number of contacts.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Few partition patterns recur across organisms regardless of classification
claims.statement: Because a closed surface divided into a small number of faces admits only a small number of arrangements, the same few configurations of cells (and of parts and organs) recur in all kinds of plants and animals with no relation to biological classification.
claims.quote: This is the simple reason why we meet in such a case as we have been discussing (viz. the arrangement of a group or system of eight cells) with the same few types recurring again and again in all sorts of organisms, plants as well as animals, and with no relation to the lines of biological classification
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: A coral fossula reflects space-partitioning, not higher bilateral organisation
claims.statement: The asymmetrical chamber (fossula) of corals such as Heterophyllia and Zaphrentis arises as one of the possible arrangements of septa meeting three at a time, and gives no grounds for interpreting it as a sign of bilaterality or a higher grade of organisation.
claims.quote: Where a single fossula occurs, we are usually told that it is a symptom of “bilaterality”; and this is in turn interpreted as an indication of a higher grade of organisation than is implied in the purely “radial symmetry” of the commoner types of coral. The mathematical aspect of the case gives no warrant for this interpretation.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Stomata lie in rows on oblong-celled leaves and scattered on polygonal-celled ones
claims.statement: Because the stomatal mother cell is cut off by a minimal partition whose form depends on epidermal cell shape, stomata are arranged in regular rows where epidermal cells are oblong (as in hyacinth) and irregularly where they are polygonal (as in Sedum).
claims.quote: It is obvious that in the case of the oblong cells of the epidermis in the hyacinth the stomata will be found arranged in regular rows, while they will be irregularly distributed over the surface of the leaf in such a case as we have depicted in Sedum.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Pollen-grain shape depends on whether walls harden before the tetrad separates
claims.statement: Pollen grains and spores formed as tetrahedral tetrads keep the plane facets and sharp angles of the tetrad if their walls solidify before the grains separate, but become spherical if they separate while still soft.
claims.quote: the pollen-grains afterwards fall apart, and their individual form will depend upon whether or no their walls have solidified before this liberation takes place.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells
claims.statement: Because quadrangular cells subdivide by periclinal walls that strengthen the boundary while triangular cells divide by oblique anticlines, outward growth is greater over triangular cells, so buds and outgrowths tend to arise from triangular rather than quadrangular cells, as is widely seen in cryptogams.
claims.quote: As a direct and immediate consequence of this we might expect a tendency for special outgrowths, or “buds,” to arise from the triangular rather than from the quadrangular cells; and this turns out to be not merely a tendency towards which theoretical considerations point, but a widespread and important factor in the morphology of the cryptogams.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Division plane depends on the ratio of growth rate to division frequency
claims.statement: A growing cell divides according to the shape it has reached, set by the ratio of its growth rate to its division frequency: if markedly oblong it divides transversely, if a little more than a hemisphere obliquely, and if less than a hemisphere by a vertical wall along its axis.
claims.quote: the manner in which this latter cell divides will simply depend upon the form it has assumed before each successive act of division takes place, that is to say upon the ratio between its rate of growth and the frequency of its successive divisions.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Cell division pattern is the result, not the cause, of the form of the growing mass
claims.statement: The form of a growing organism regulates the form and number of the cells that compose it: the cell network is the result, not the cause, of the overall configuration, which is caused by whatever processes make growth faster in one direction than another.
claims.quote: The complex cell-network is not the cause but the result of the general configuration, which latter has its essential cause in whatsoever physical and chemical processes have led to a varying velocity of growth in one direction as compared with another.
claims.chapter: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

claims.label: Skeletal salts precipitate in dead or inactive matrix, not living protoplasm
claims.statement: Calcareous and other skeletal deposits are, as a rule, precipitated not within actively living protoplasm but in dead or inactive formed material, such as the intercellular matrix or the cell-wall, so their form is not directly shaped by the living cells.
claims.quote: for the actual _precipitation_ takes place, as a rule, not in actively living, but in dead or at least inactive tissue: that is to say in the “formed material” or matrix which (as for instance in cartilage) accumulates round the living cells
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Sea-urchin larvae reared without lime develop healthily but lack skeletal rods and arms
claims.statement: Sea-urchin eggs reared in lime-free sea-water develop into apparently healthy larvae that lack the calcareous skeletal rods, and the long larval arms normally supported by those rods are suppressed; the organism can live without the material of its skeleton.
claims.quote: the eggs of sea-urchins reared in lime-free water develop in apparent health, into larvae entirely destitute of the usual skeleton of calcareous rods, and in which, accordingly, the long arms of the Pluteus larva, which the rods support and distend, are entirely suppressed.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Biological molecular asymmetry may originate from circularly polarised sunlight
claims.statement: The one-handed molecular asymmetry of organic products need not be a prerogative of life; it may have started from a non-vital asymmetric force, such as sunlight circularly polarised by reflection from the sea, which acts unequally on right- and left-handed molecules.
claims.quote: an example limited but yet crucial (_if confirmed_), of an asymmetric force, non-vital in its origin, which might conceivably be the starting-point of that asymmetry which is characteristic of so many organic products.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Pearls and bony-fish otoliths share the structure of artificial calcospherites
claims.statement: The concentrically zoned, radiate structure of pearls and of the otoliths of molluscs and bony fishes is essentially the same as that of the calcospherites formed artificially when calcium carbonate is precipitated in albumin, implying the same physico-chemical mode of formation.
claims.quote: The typical structure of a calcospherite is no other than that of a pearl, nor does it differ essentially from that of the otolith of a mollusc or of a bony fish.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Concentric growth rings need not record periodic external conditions such as seasons
claims.statement: Because rhythmic Liesegang precipitation arises from diffusion within the system itself, concentric zones in fish scales, otoliths, bones and starch grains cannot be assumed to record periodic external conditions such as seasons or day and night.
claims.quote: it is at least obvious, with the Liesegang phenomenon in view, that we have no right to _assume_ that an appearance of rhythm and periodicity in structure and growth is necessarily bound up with, and indubitably brought about by, a periodic recurrence of particular _external_ conditions.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Calcium salts precipitate when the albumins holding them in solution break down
claims.statement: Albumin increases the solubility of calcium carbonate and phosphate, whereas its breakdown products dissolve them much less; hence skeletal calcium salts are thrown down when proteins are broken down in metabolism, not by direct action of carbonic acid on a more soluble salt.
claims.quote: The probability is, therefore, that the actual precipitation of the calcium salts is not due to the direct action of carbonic acid, etc. on a more soluble salt (as was at one time believed); but to catabolic changes in the proteids of the organism, which tend to throw down the salts already formed, which had remained hitherto in albuminous solution.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Cell-sized skeletal elements are shaped by molecular forces, large ones by mechanics
claims.statement: Skeletal elements comparable in size to a single cell (sponge spicules, radiolarian and foraminiferal skeletons) are shaped by molecular forces such as surface tension, whereas massive skeletons such as vertebrate bones are shaped by gravity, muscle action and mechanical loads, so scale produces essential differences in their controlling forces and forms.
claims.quote: The effect of _scale_, then, of which we had so much to say in our introductory chapter on Magnitude, is bound to be apparent in the study of skeletal fabrics, and to lead to essential differences between the big and the little, the massive and the minute, in regard to their controlling forces and their resultant forms.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: A straight-growing spicule confined to a cell surface grows along a geodetic
claims.statement: A spicule tending to grow in a straight line but confined within or against a cell wall grows along a geodetic of the cell surface, so in a spherical or ellipsoidal cell it becomes a circular arc, an elliptic arc or, most often, a portion of a spiral in space, as in C- and S-shaped sponge spicules.
claims.quote: let us suppose that it is confined either within a cell-wall or in adhesion thereto; it at once follows that its line of growth will be simply a geodetic to the surface of the cell.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Like spicules in silica and calcite show form is set by external forces, not chemistry
claims.statement: Holothurian spicules of calcium carbonate reproduce, often indistinguishably, the forms of siliceous sponge spicules, which shows that such spicule forms are determined by the external forces acting during growth (cell confinement), not by the chemical nature or molecular structure of the material.
claims.quote: the Holothurian spicules are composed of calcium carbonate while those which we have just described in the case of sponges are usually, if not always, siliceous: this being just another proof of the fact that in such cases the form of the spicule is not due to its chemical nature or molecular structure, but to the external forces
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Triradiate spicules form at three-cell junctions with rays at 120°, four-rayed at ~109°
claims.statement: Skeletal material deposited between cells or within their partitions takes the shape of the cell junctions: in a layer of equal cells, where partitions meet in threes at 120°, it forms triradiate spicules with rays at 120°, and in a solid aggregate of four cells it forms tetrahedral four-rayed spicules with rays at about 109°; unequal cells give unequal angles and curved rays.
claims.quote: It is plain, accordingly, that in any flattened or stratified assemblage of such cells, a solidified skeletal deposit which originates or accumulates either between the cells or within the thickness of their mutual partitions, will tend to take the form of triradiate bodies, whose rays (in a typical case) will be set at equal angles of 120°
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Six-rayed hexactinellid spicules reflect cubic, not closest, packing of vesicles
claims.statement: The six-rayed spicules of hexactinellid sponges form because the vesicles that mould them are arranged in linear series (cubic packing) rather than closest packing, so the spicules follow the angles and edges of a system of cubes instead of hexagons or dodecahedra.
claims.quote: the cells or vesicles by which they are conformed are not arranged in what is known as “closest packing,” but in linear series; so that in their arrangement, and by their mutual compression, we tend to get a pattern, not of hexagons, but of squares: or, looking to the solid, not of dodecahedra but of cubes or parallelopipeda.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Radiolarian species lack definite geographic ranges and many co-occur locally
claims.statement: Radiolarian species show vague distributions in space and time: many occur worldwide without specific geographic limits, families and genera appear unchanged since the Cambrian, and a small sample of sediment typically contains scores or hundreds of forms with no local predominance of one species.
claims.quote: the distribution of species in space is curious and vague; many species are found all over the world, or at least every here and there, with no evidence of specific limitations of geographical habitat
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Agglutinated protist shells form by surface energy, not choice or skill
claims.statement: The building of agglutinated shells from sand-grains, spicules or diatom frustules by rhizopods such as Difflugia is a purely physical consequence of foreign particles being trapped in the surface film by surface energy, with selectivity explained by specific surface-energies rather than volition.
claims.quote: The formation of an “agglutinated” shell is thus seen to be a purely physical phenomenon, and indeed a special case of a more general physical phenomenon which has many other important consequences in biology.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Hexagonal lattice shells form as silica collects in grooves between surface vesicles
claims.statement: When the outer surface of a radiolarian is covered by a layer of nearly equal froth-like vesicles, silica secreted or adsorbed at the surface collects in the grooves between them, producing a spherical shell of rods in a regular hexagonal network; less regular vesicles give less regular meshes, and repeated layers give concentric shells.
claims.quote: it will at once follow that they will show a tendency to aggregate in the grooves which separate the vesicles, and the result will be the development of a most delicate sphere composed of tiny rods arranged in a regular hexagonal network
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Lattice-shell form is independent of the material, being moulded on vesicles
claims.statement: Spherical hexagonal lattice shells are equally regular whether made of silica (oceanic Radiolaria), strontium sulphate (Acantharia) or an organic chitin-like substance (Clathrulina), showing that their form comes from moulding on an underlying vesicular structure, not from the material.
claims.quote: This is only another proof (if proof be needed) that the peculiar conformation of these little skeletons is not due to the material of which they are composed, but to the moulding of that material upon an underlying vesicular structure.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Callimitra's skeleton is formed on the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of four cells
claims.statement: The skeleton of the nassellarian Callimitra reproduces the interfacial film system of four soap-bubbles in tetrahedral contact (six plane interfaces meeting in threes at 120°, edges meeting near 109°), so it must have been formed at the interfaces of a tetrahedral group of cells.
claims.quote: It is obvious at a glance that this is such a skeleton as may have been formed (I think we may go so far as to say _must_ have been formed) at the interfaces of a little tetrahedral group of cells
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Regular dodecahedral radiolarian shells cannot arise by crystal-like space partitioning
claims.statement: Radiolaria show all five regular polyhedra, including the regular dodecahedron and icosahedron which cannot occur in crystals; therefore the regular radiolarian dodecahedron is not produced by the space-partitioning principles that govern crystallisation.
claims.quote: If we may safely judge from Haeckel’s figures, the pentagonal dodecahedron of the Radiolarian is perfectly regular, and we must presume, accordingly, that it is not brought about by principles of space-partitioning similar to those which manifest themselves in the phenomenon of crystallisation.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Twenty-spined Radiolaria have hexagonal symmetry, not Müller's arrangement
claims.statement: In twenty-spined Radiolaria the spines pass through the facets of a modified hexagonal prism, giving a true hexagonal symmetry of two polar spines, six equatorial spines and two whorls of six intermediate spines; Müller's law of five four-spined circles with no polar spine does not properly apply to any case.
claims.quote: The true symmetry of this figure, then, is hexagonal, with a polar axis, produced into two polar spicules; with six equatorial spicules, or rays; and with two sets of six spicular rays, interposed between the polar axis and the equatorial rays, and alternating in position with the latter.
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Radiolarian axial polarity arises in the central protoplasm, unexplained by mechanics
claims.statement: The polar symmetry of the radial spines in Radiolaria cannot be explained by any obvious mechanical forces of the peripheral froth; it arises in the central living protoplasm, and may reflect obscure but still physical directive forces analogous to Lehmann's 'Gestaltungskraft' in fluid crystals.
claims.quote: But there are no obvious mechanical forces by which we can so explain this peculiar polarity. This at least is evident, that it arises in the central mass of protoplasm, which is the essential living portion of the organism
claims.chapter: Ch. IX: On Concretions, Spicules, and Spicular Skeletons

claims.label: Annular, longitudinal and spiral wall thickenings of plant cells are cylinder geodetics
claims.statement: The three kinds of geodetic on a cylinder (parallel rings, straight longitudinal lines and helical spirals) are all realised in the local wall thickenings of cylindrical plant cells and vessels, and the helical geodetic in the spiral coils of insect tracheae and tracheids.
claims.quote: These three systems are all of frequent occurrence, and are all illustrated in the local thickenings of the wall of the cylindrical cells or vessels of plants.
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

claims.label: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex
claims.statement: On a right cone the spiral geodetic coils more and more closely as the cone narrows, and the sutural line and parallel striations of a turreted spiral shell such as Turritella are geodetics of this kind.
claims.quote: In a right cone, the spiral geodetic falls into closer and closer coils as the diameter of the cone narrows; and a very beautiful geodetic of this kind is exemplified in the sutural line of a spiral shell, such as Turritella
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

claims.label: Two crossing systems of geodetic spirals are a common source of reticulated patterns
claims.statement: In organic structures two opposite systems of geodetic spirals often coexist and interfere, forming a criss-cross arrangement, and this is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
claims.quote: and it is also common to find the two systems interfering with one another, and forming a criss-cross, or reticulated arrangement. This is a very common source of reticulated patterns.
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

claims.label: Muscle fibres on hollow organs arrange themselves along geodesic curves
claims.statement: A contractile fibre fixed at both ends on a curved surface first pulls itself into the shortest path on that surface before it can constrict the organ, so the muscle fibres of hollow organs such as the heart, stomach, arteries and intestine automatically lie along geodesics (annular and longitudinal in a simple tube).
claims.quote: Thus the muscular fibres, as they wind over the curved surface of an organ, arrange themselves automatically in geodesic curves: in precisely the same manner as we also automatically construct complex systems of geodesics whenever we wind a ball of wool or a spindle of tow
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

claims.label: Heart and stomach fibres stay geodetic after the twisting of the primitive tube
claims.statement: The heart and stomach develop from simple tubes by dilatation and twisting; their originally circular and longitudinal fibres remain geodetic on the distorted surface, new geodetic systems (such as the oblique stomach fibres) appear on new pouches, and the heart contracts effectively only because its fibres run the shortest course.
claims.quote: these systems of muscular fibres, geodetic to begin with, remain geodetic (in the sense in which we are using the word) after all the twisting to which the primitive cylindrical tube or tubes have been subjected.
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

claims.label: Small swimmers rotate about their axis, turning a constant swerve into a helical path
claims.statement: Small ciliated and flagellated organisms cannot steer, but by rotating about their long axis while swimming they convert a constant body-fixed swerve into a continually changing direction in space, so they travel along a helix around a nearly straight axis rather than in a circle.
claims.quote: And this axial rotation, just as in the case of a rifle-bullet, causes their natural swerve, which is always in the same direction as regards their own bodies, to be in a continually changing direction as regards space: in short, to make a spiral course around, and more or less approximate to, a straight axial line.
claims.chapter: Ch. X: A Parenthetic Note on Geodetics

claims.label: Horns, molluscan shells, foraminifera and sunflower florets follow the logarithmic spiral
claims.statement: The permanent spiral forms found in organisms, such as the horns of ruminants, molluscan and foraminiferal shells and the arrangement of florets in the sunflower, are all logarithmic spirals; the outline of a cordate leaf is the one spiral-like organic outline that is not.
claims.quote: Of the spiral forms which we have now mentioned, every one (with the single exception of the outline of the cordate leaf) is an example of the remarkable curve known as the Logarithmic Spiral.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: A spiral needs a deflecting force carried by the growing body, not an external one
claims.statement: A deflecting force of constant direction acting from outside, such as wind or gravity, can only bend a growing structure towards a limiting direction and never into a spiral; a spiral arises only when the deflecting force is intrinsic to the growing body and turns with the direction of growth, as the columellar muscle does in the snail-shell.
claims.quote: the growing curve will tend to wind round and round its point of origin. In the typical case of the snail-shell, such an intrinsic force is manifestly present in the action of the columellar muscle.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: A constant ratio of longitudinal to transverse growth rates yields a logarithmic spiral
claims.statement: In a tubular structure whose growth is unequal on its two sides, a constant ratio between the rates of growth in the longitudinal and transverse directions generally produces a logarithmic spiral, the value of the ratio fixing the spiral's constant angle, with the circle and the straight line as limiting cases.
claims.quote: In other words, in such a structure as we have presupposed, the existence or maintenance of a constant ratio between the rates of extension or growth in the vertical and transverse directions will lead, in general, to the development of a logarithmic spiral; the magnitude of that ratio will determine the character (that is to say, the constant angle) of the spiral;
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: The scorpioid cyme traces a true logarithmic spiral
claims.statement: In a scorpioid cyme, where each shoot arises from the last on the same side at an equal angle and successive shoots diminish in length in a constant ratio, the shoots are tangents to a true logarithmic spiral; in the helicoid cyme the same spiral is present but hidden by a superimposed twist.
claims.quote: The result is that the successive shoots, or successive increments of growth, are tangents to a curve, and this curve is a true logarithmic spiral.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: The shell grows in size without changing its shape
claims.statement: A spiral shell, like the animal within it, increases in size without changing its shape, even though it grows at one end only; this constant similarity of form under terminal growth is the defining property of the logarithmic spiral and of no other curve.
claims.quote: The shell, like the creature within it, grows in size _but does not change its shape_; and the existence of this constant relativity of growth, or constant similarity of form, is of the essence, and may be made the basis of a definition, of the logarithmic spiral.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Each increment of a spirally grown structure is a gnomon to the whole before it
claims.statement: In horns, shells and all other organic forms showing a logarithmic spiral, the existing structure is partly old and partly new, and each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the whole pre-existing structure, that is, an addition that leaves the enlarged whole similar to what it was before.
claims.quote: (2) it is characteristic of the growth of the horn, of the shell, and of all other organic forms in which a logarithmic spiral can be recognised, that _each successive increment of growth is a gnomon to the entire pre-existing structure_.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Logarithmic spirals occur in accreted hard parts, not in simultaneously formed soft parts
claims.statement: The logarithmic spiral should not be found in structures whose parts are produced simultaneously, such as the margin of a leaf or the contour of a fish, but in hard parts built of successive, permanently retained increments, such as shell, tusk, horn and claw, where it is usually accompanied by lines of growth.
claims.quote: For it follows as a simple corollary to this theorem of gnomons that we must not expect to find the logarithmic spiral manifested in a structure whose parts are simultaneously produced, as for instance in the margin of a leaf, or among the many curves that make the contour of a fish.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Whorl breadths of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod shells form a geometric progression
claims.statement: Careful measurement shows that the breadths of successive whorls along a radius of the Nautilus shell, and of spiral ammonitoid and gastropod shells generally, are in geometric progression, so that these shells are logarithmic spirals (for Nautilus each whorl is about three times as broad as the one before).
claims.quote: It was by observing, with the help of very careful measurement, this continued proportionality, that Moseley was enabled to verify his first assumption, based on the general appearance of the shell, that the shell of Nautilus was actually a logarithmic spiral, and this demonstration he was immediately afterwards in a position to generalise by extending it to all the spiral Ammonitoid and Gastropod mollusca
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: All differences of form between shells are differences of degree in a few growth ratios
claims.statement: The form of any turbinate shell is fixed by a small set of factors (shape of the generating curve, its rate of growth, its rate of rotation about the pole, its rate of translation along the axis, and its inclination), and all differences of form between one shell and another are differences of degree in the relative magnitudes of these factors.
claims.quote: In short it is obvious that _all_ the differences of form which we observe between one shell and another are referable to matters of _degree_, depending, one and all, upon the relative magnitudes of the various factors in the complex equation to the curve.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°
claims.statement: The constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is about 80° in Nautilus, where each whorl is about three times as broad as its predecessor, and in ordinary ammonitoid and typical spiral gastropod shells is seldom below 80° and usually between 80° and 85°.
claims.quote: the constant angle is in the neighbourhood of 80°; and hence also that, in all the ordinary Ammonitoid shells, and in all the typically spiral shells of the Gastropods, the constant angle is also a large one, being very seldom less than 80°, and usually between 80° and 85°.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Separation or overlap of whorls reflects the growth-rate ratio of outer to inner border
claims.statement: Whether the whorls of a spiral shell stand apart, just touch, or overlap (up to complete involution, as in Nautilus pompilius versus N. umbilicatus) depends only on the ratio of the rate of growth of the outer border of the tube to that of its inner border.
claims.quote: For the purposes of the morphologist, then, the main result of this last general investigation is to shew that all the various types of “open” and “closed” spirals, all the various degrees of separation or overlap of the successive whorls, are simply the outward expression of a varying ratio in the _rate of growth_ of the outer as compared with the inner border of the tubular shell.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Spiral constants of shells give no valid evidence of ancestry
claims.statement: The constant angle of a shell's spiral, like its size, is no evidence of which form is more primitive or ancestral, nor does an intermediate angle show that a shell is intermediate in time or descent; phylogenetic series built from straight, loosely coiled and closely coiled cephalopod shells are not supported by the mathematical study of shell form.
claims.quote: _To such phylogenetic hypotheses the mathematical or dynamical study of the forms of shells lends no valid support._ If we have two shells in which the constant angle of the spire be respectively 80° and 60°, that fact in itself does not at all justify an assertion that the one is more primitive, more ancient, or more “ancestral” than the other.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Mathematical morphology can reveal orthogenetic series and warn of convergence
claims.statement: Progressive change of growth ratios along a series of allied forms (orthogenesis) is real in some lineages, and the mathematical study of form can detect such series where they are not obvious, while also showing that strong resemblances of form may arise independently as numerical coincidences.
claims.quote: And to my mind, the mathematical (as distinguished from the purely physical) study of morphology bids fair to help us to recognise this phenomenon of orthogenesis in many cases where it is not at once patent to the eye; and also, on the other hand, to warn us, in many other cases, that even strong and apparently complex resemblances in form may be capable of arising independently,
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Ontogenetic change in spiral angle explains narrowing-whorled and uncoiling ammonites
claims.statement: In some ammonoids the spiral angle changes progressively during growth: where it increases the whorls become narrower (as in Oekotraustes), and where it diminishes towards zero the coil opens out into an almost straight curve (as in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites).
claims.quote: But let us suppose that the spiral angle increases somewhat rapidly; we shall then get a spiral with gradually narrowing whorls, and this condition is characteristic of Oekotraustes, a subgenus of Ammonites. If on the other hand, the angle α gradually diminishes, and even falls away to zero, we shall have the spiral curve opening out, as it does in Scaphites, Ancyloceras and Lituites,
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Dissimilar turbinate shells share similar spiral angles and differ mainly in apical angle
claims.statement: Shells as different in appearance as Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis differ very little in their spiral angle (the ratio of radial to tangential growth) and differ in form mainly in the apical angle of the enveloping cone, which is set by the rate of translation along the axis relative to growth.
claims.quote: We see from this that shells so different in appearance as Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis differ very little indeed in the magnitude of the spiral angle α, that is to say in the relative velocities of radial and tangential growth. It is upon the angle θ that the difference in their form mainly depends:
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Bivalve growth lines are coaxial curves set by direction-dependent growth rate
claims.statement: The lines of growth on bivalve shells are not concentric but coaxial curves through the umbo, and they arise because the rate of growth varies as a simple function of direction; in the simplest case the lines are coaxial circles (as in Anomia), and with more complex functions they are coaxial ellipses or other figures (as in Lima or Solen).
claims.quote: All that we are immediately concerned with is the simple fact that where a velocity, such as our rate of growth, varies with its direction,—varies that is to say as a function of the angular divergence from a certain axis,—then, in a certain simple case, we get lines of growth laid down as a system of coaxial circles,
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Incomplete moulting gives Estheria a mollusc-like spiral shell with growth lines
claims.statement: The bivalved carapace of the crustacean Estheria resembles a lamellibranch shell, with lines of growth and a logarithmic spiral of small angle, because its moult is incomplete: each old carapace is retained and the new one grows beneath it and projects beyond its edge.
claims.quote: But in Estheria (and one or two other small crustacea) the moult is incomplete: the old carapace is retained, and the new, growing up underneath it, adheres to it like a lining, and projects beyond its edge: so that in course of time the margins of successive old carapaces appear as “lines of growth” upon the surface of the shell.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Brachiopod spiral arm direction follows shell shape through spatial constraint
claims.statement: The form and direction of brachiopod spiral arms (brachidia) are determined by their initial curvature and the space and pressures within the shell, so that long outwardly directed spirals should go with transversely elongated shells such as Spirifer, inwardly directed spirals with rounded shells such as Atrypa, and discoid spirals with strongly flattened shells.
claims.quote: It is obvious that the incipient curvature of the arms, and consequently the form and direction of the spirals, will be influenced by the surrounding pressures, and these in turn by the general shape of the shell. We shall expect, accordingly, to find the long outwardly directed spirals associated with shells which are transversely elongated, as Spirifer is; while the more rounded Atrypas will tend to the opposite condition.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Ammonite shell and aptychus are two parts of a once united split cone
claims.statement: The shell and the aptychus of ammonites are probably the ventral and dorsal portions of a once united conical shell split by unequal growth, as in pteropods; other cephalopods retain only one of the two, the ventral one as the shell of Nautilus and the dorsal one as the shell of Sepia or Spirula.
claims.quote: In short, I think there is reason to believe, or at least to suspect, that we have in the shell and Aptychus of the Ammonites, two portions of a once united structure; of which other Cephalopods retain not both parts but only one or other, one as the ventrally situated shell of Nautilus, the other as the dorsally placed shell for example of Sepia or of Spirula.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Cephalopod septa take the form of minimal surfaces like soap films
claims.statement: Because a septum is first laid down as an elastic membrane under uniform pressure, it takes the shape of a soap film with the same boundary, a surface of minimal area: spherical in a straight cone with a perpendicular attachment, ellipsoidal with an oblique attachment, and saddle-shaped where the line of attachment is sinuous.
claims.quote: In all cases, provided only that the membrane be isotropic, the form assumed will be precisely that of a soap-bubble under similar conditions of attachment: that is to say, it will be (with the usual limitations or conditions) a surface of minimal area.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: The fine frilling of ammonite sutures is a surface-tension phenomenon
claims.statement: The minutely branched, arborescent outline superposed on the lobes and saddles of some ammonite sutures, with branches ending in rounded arcs, is a surface-tension phenomenon of the same kind as the patterns made by milk on a greasy plate or oil on an alkaline solution.
claims.quote: Superposed upon the usual sinuous outline, with its “lobes” and “saddles,” we have here a minutely ramified, or arborescent outline, in which all the branches terminate in wavy, more or less circular arcs,—looking just like the ‘landscape marble’ from the Bristol Rhaetic. We have no difficulty in recognising in this a surface-tension phenomenon.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: The same spiral shell forms recur across unrelated groups, all ages and all seas
claims.statement: Spiral shell forms appear with little relation to the kind of animal producing them, recurring in gastropods, cephalopods, foraminifera and tube worms, and mathematically identical forms recur in every geological period and are found mixed together regardless of climate or local conditions.
claims.quote: Again, we find the same forms, or forms which (save for external ornament) are mathematically identical, repeating themselves in all periods of the world’s geological history; and, irrespective of climate or local conditions, we see them mixed up, one with another, in the depths and on the shores of every sea.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Natural Selection plays no necessary part in producing spiral shell forms
claims.statement: Natural Selection, in any strictly biological sense, has no necessary share in producing the varied forms of spiral shells, which arise from differences in growth rates and ratios.
claims.quote: It is hard indeed (to my mind) to see where Natural Selection necessarily enters in, or to admit that it has had any share whatsoever in the production of these varied conformations.
claims.chapter: Ch. XI: The Logarithmic Spiral

claims.label: Single-chambered foraminiferal shells take the form of fluid drops under surface tension
claims.statement: The form of a single-chambered foraminiferal shell is explained by the laws of surface tension: the protoplasm behaves as a fluid drop whose equilibrium shape is fixed when it acquires its solid covering.
claims.quote: wherever the shell is but a single unit or single chamber, its form may be explained in general by the laws of surface tension: the assumption being that the little mass of protoplasm which makes the simple shell behaves as a _fluid drop_, the form of which is perpetuated when the protoplasm acquires its solid covering.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Foraminifera are spiral because they grow by permanent increments added outside
claims.statement: Foraminiferal shells tend towards a spiral form because they grow by successive increments added to the exterior, each of which becomes a permanent, rigid part of the structure.
claims.quote: That the shell in the Foraminifera should tend towards a spiral form need not surprise us; for we have learned that one of the fundamental conditions of the production of a concrete spiral is just precisely what we have here, namely the gradual development of a structure by means of successive increments superadded to its exterior, which then form part, successively, of a permanent and rigid structure.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Septa are convex outwards in Foraminifera and concave in Nautilus because of pressure side
claims.statement: Foraminiferal septa are convex outwards and those of Nautilus concave outwards because the pressure each membrane resisted when it set lay on opposite sides; in both cases the septum tends to a surface of minimal area.
claims.quote: The one septum is, speaking generally, the reverse of the other; the organism, so to speak, is outside the one and inside the other; and in both cases alike, the septum tends to assume the form of a surface of minimal area, as permitted, or as defined, by all the circumstances of the case.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, large shells similar to small ones
claims.statement: Spiral foraminiferal shells are logarithmic spirals, recognisable by continued similarity: the large many-chambered shell has the same shape as the smaller, younger shell.
claims.quote: The logarithmic spiral is easily recognisable in typical cases (and especially where the spire makes more than one visible revolution about the pole), by its fundamental property of continued similarity: that is to say, by reason of the fact that the big many-chambered shell is of just the same shape as the smaller and younger shell
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Fusulina whorls increase in ratio 1:1.5, a spiral of constant angle about 86°
claims.statement: In Fusulina the breadths of successive whorls stand in the nearly constant ratio 1 : 1.5, which corresponds to a logarithmic spiral with a constant angle of about 86°, like that of ammonites.
claims.quote: And this ratio of 1·5 between the breadths of successive whorls corresponds (as we see by our table on p. 534) to a constant angle of about 86°, or just such a spiral as we commonly meet with in the Ammonites
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Constant chamber-size ratio follows from growth proportional to existing mass
claims.statement: Each foraminiferal chamber bears a constant ratio of size to the next because the rate of increase at each instant is proportional to the whole existing mass of the homogeneous organism.
claims.quote: The law of increase by which each chamber bears a constant ratio of magnitude to the next may be looked upon as a simple consequence of the structural uniformity or homogeneity of the organism; we have merely to suppose (as this uniformity would naturally lead us to do) that the rate of increase is at each instant proportional to the whole existing mass.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Minimum potential energy plus proportional growth yields the logarithmic spiral
claims.statement: Each new protoplasmic drop settles in a position of minimum potential energy (including minimal area), which makes each chamber similar to the last; proportional growth of size then gives the series the form of a logarithmic spiral. Rhumbler's specific 'law of the constant angle' of contact is too narrow an explanation.
claims.quote: The physical law of minimum potential (including also the law of minimal area) is all that we need in order to explain, _in general terms_, the continued similarity of one chamber to another; and the physiological law of growth, by which a continued proportionality of size tends to run through the series of successive chambers, impresses upon this series of similar increments the form of a logarithmic spiral.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Attached Foraminifera form plane spirals with whorls flattened on the attached side
claims.statement: Most spiral Foraminifera are plane (discoid) spirals because some force keeps the chambers in a plane, especially in forms that live attached to rock or seaweed, whose whorls are flattened on the attached surface; freely floating forms such as Globigerina tend towards helicoid spirals.
claims.quote: The majority of spiral forms, on the other hand, are plane or discoid spirals, and we may take it that in these cases some force has exercised a controlling influence, so as to keep all the chambers in a plane. This is especially the case in forms like Rotalia or Discorbina (Fig. 316), where the organism lives attached to a rock or a frond of sea-weed
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Many foraminiferal species and genera may be temporary manifestations of variability
claims.statement: Because very slight changes in surface energies could turn one foraminiferal form into another, many forms distinguished as separate species and even genera may be no more than temporary manifestations of variability, as in Peneroplis.
claims.quote: but for all we know of the life-history of the Foraminifera, it may well be that a great number of the other forms which we distinguish as separate species and even genera are no more than temporary manifestations of the same variability
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Foraminiferal forms follow such simple laws that none is fitter than another to survive
claims.statement: Foraminiferal shells grow by laws so simple and so in harmony with their material and the forces acting on them that no form is better, fitter or less fit to survive than another, which accounts for the great diversity of types and their persistence since the Cretaceous.
claims.quote: It leads one to imagine that these shells have grown according to laws so simple, so much in harmony with their material, with their environment, and with all the forces internal and external to which they are exposed, that none is better than another and none fitter or less fit to survive.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Identical foraminiferal forms may have arisen independently again and again
claims.statement: The possible lines of variation in Foraminifera may be so narrow and determinate that identical forms have arisen independently many times.
claims.quote: It invites one also to contemplate the possibility of the lines of possible variation being here so narrow and determinate that identical forms may have come independently into being again and again.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Increased shell strength is not an advantage driving foraminiferal evolution
claims.statement: Against Rhumbler, niceties of shell form have little effect on survival: delicate foraminiferal shells survive unbroken in vast numbers, so breakage is not a constant danger and increased strength is not a selective advantage guiding their evolution.
claims.quote: And so I am not inclined to believe that niceties of form affect the case very much: nor in general that foraminiferal life involves a struggle for existence wherein breakage is a constant danger to be averted, and increased strength an advantage to be ensured.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Foraminifera are absent from coarse gravels because of hydraulic sorting by currents
claims.statement: Foraminiferal shells are absent from coarse sands and gravels not because they avoid concussion but because light shells are sorted by currents like any other graded sediment, settling where water is still.
claims.quote: The coarseness or fineness of the sediment on the sea-bottom is a measure of the current: where the current is strong the larger stones are washed clean, where there is perfect stillness the finest mud settles down; and the light, fragile shells of the Foraminifera find their appropriate place, like every other graded sediment, in this spontaneous order of lixiviation.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Forms set by physical forces undermine inference of kinship from similarity
claims.statement: Insofar as forms depend on physical forces and their variations on simple quantitative changes in those forces, similarity of form cannot safely be taken as evidence of consanguinity, and the link between classification and phylogeny must be revised.
claims.quote: But in so far as forms can be shewn to depend on the play of physical forces, and the variations of form to be directly due to simple quantitative variations in these, just so far are we thrown back on our guard before the biological conception of consanguinity, and compelled to revise the vague canons which connect classification with phylogeny.
claims.chapter: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

claims.label: Rhinoceros horn is a plane logarithmic spiral from constant front-to-back growth ratio
claims.statement: The rhinoceros horn grows faster anteriorly than posteriorly in a constant ratio, so it curves as a logarithmic spiral; lying in the median plane, it has no lateral twist and forms a plane spiral.
claims.quote: Its longitudinal growth proceeds with a maximum velocity anteriorly, and a minimum posteriorly; and the ratio of these velocities being constant, the horn curves into the form of a logarithmic spiral in the manner that we have already studied.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Paired horns of ruminants are conjugate, mirror-image spirals
claims.statement: The paired horns of hollow-horned ruminants are conjugate spirals, the left horn being the mirror image of the right.
claims.quote: But the two horns are in symmetry one with another; they form “conjugate” spirals, one being the “mirror-image” of the other.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Most horns are logarithmic spirals from constant unequal growth on opposite sides
claims.statement: In the great majority of horns the curve is a continuous logarithmic spiral, caused by unequal rates of growth parallel to the axis on opposite sides of the horn, the inequality keeping a constant ratio throughout growth.
claims.quote: But in the great majority of horns, we have no difficulty in recognising a continuous logarithmic spiral, nor in referring it, as before, to an unequal rate of growth (parallel to the axis) on two opposite sides of the horn, the inequality maintaining a constant ratio as long as growth proceeds.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Goat and sheep horns form a series of homologous spirals of increasing angle
claims.statement: Horns of wild goats and sheep form a series of homologous logarithmic spirals with increasing constant angle: under 40° in Oryx, under 70° in the Scinde wild goat, about 75° in Ovis ammon and a little more in the Highland ram.
claims.quote: we may easily arrange a series of forms, such for example as the Siberian ibex, the moufflon, _Ovis Ammon_, etc., and ending with the long-horned Highland ram: in which, as we pass from one to another, we recognise precisely homologous spirals, with an increasing angular constant, the spiral angle being, for instance, about 75° or rather less in _Ovis Ammon_, and in the Highland ram a very little more.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Argali horns share a spiral angle but differ in their shearing (helical) component
claims.statement: Among closely allied wild sheep (Argali) the constant angle of the horn's logarithmic spiral is nearly the same, and the species differ chiefly in the helical shearing component.
claims.quote: In all of these the constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is very much the same, but the shearing component differs greatly.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: A horn is a plane spiral only if fastest and slowest growth lie diametrically opposite
claims.statement: If the maximal and minimal growth rates around the basal growth zone of a horn lie diametrically opposite, the horn is a plane spiral; otherwise it is a spiral in space with a helical component, which is the usual case because the horn's field of force has no such plane of symmetry.
claims.quote: If the maximal and minimal velocities of growth be precisely at opposite sides of the zone of growth, the resultant spiral will be a plane spiral; but if they be not precisely or diametrically opposite, then the spiral will be a spiral in space, with a winding or helical component
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Uneven adhesion of the horn sheath to its bony core can itself produce the spiral
claims.statement: Unequal retardation of the growing horn sheath by its adhesion to the bony core can produce the same spiral as unequal growth, and is probably a very important and sometimes the chief factor in horn curvature.
claims.quote: had its elongation more retarded on one side than the other (prior to its complete solidification) by varying degrees of adhesion or membranous attachment to the bone core within, then the net result would be a spiral curve precisely such as would have arisen from initial inequalities in the rate of growth itself. It seems highly probable that this is a very important factor
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: The thicker the horn, the greater its spiral curvature
claims.statement: On the whole, thicker horns are more strongly spirally curved than slender ones, because a larger cross-section allows greater differences in growth or retardation between opposite sides.
claims.quote: I think it may be said that, on the whole, the thicker the horn, the greater is its spiral curvature.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Sinuous growth lines on non-cylindrical horns result from torsional strain
claims.statement: Horns that grow as curves of double curvature undergo torsional strain, because the sheath is attached to the core, and this strain warps the rings into the sinuous growth lines predicted by St Venant for a twisted non-circular prism; such lines are absent from cylindrical ox horns.
claims.quote: But there is yet another and a very remarkable phenomenon which we may discern in the growth of a horn, when it takes the form of a curve of double curvature, namely, an effect of torsional strain; and this it is which gives rise to the sinuous “lines of growth,” or sinuous boundaries of the separate horny rings, of which we have already spoken.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Twining of climbing stems results from unequal growth on different sides
claims.statement: The revolving nutation of twining plants, like the helicoid growth of an antelope horn, is caused by unequal rates of growth on different sides of the stem, the difference being that in the stem growth occurs along its whole length.
claims.quote: This tendency to revolution—“circumvolution,” as Darwin calls it, “revolving nutation,” as Sachs puts it—is very closely comparable to the process by which an antelope’s horn (such as the koodoo’s) grows into its spiral or rather helicoid form; and it is simply due, in like manner, to inequalities in the rate of growth on different sides of the growing stem.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Stem torsion on rough supports is a mechanical couple from adhesion, not an adaptation
claims.statement: Twining stems become twisted on rough supports but not on smooth ones because adhesion to the rough support sets up a mechanical couple, so Darwin's adaptive explanation (gaining rigidity) is unnecessary.
claims.quote: In the case of the roughened support, there is a temporary adhesion or “clinging” between it and the growing stem which twines around it; and a system of forces is thus set up, producing a “couple,” just as it was in the case of the ram’s or antelope’s horn through direct adhesion of the bony core to the surrounding sheath.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: A pair of antlers is confined to a single smooth spheroidal surface
claims.statement: The branches of a pair of deer antlers are confined to a single, more or less spheroidal or ellipsoidal curved surface, the two antlers forming one mirror-symmetric surface whose tine tips lie on a continuous curve; the antler is essentially a surface, whereas a horn is an axial rod.
claims.quote: The surface to which the branches of the antler tend to be confined is a more or less spheroidal, or occasionally an ellipsoidal one; and furthermore, when we inspect any well-developed pair of antlers, such as those of a red deer, a sambur or a wapiti, we have no difficulty in seeing that the two antlers make up between them _a single surface_
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Claws, beaks and teeth grown by unequal permanent accretion are logarithmic spirals
claims.statement: Wherever a structure grows by permanent increments with unequal longitudinal growth about its axis, as in nails, claws, beaks and teeth, it always tends to the form of a logarithmic spiral, which becomes conspicuous only when the structure is long.
claims.quote: The logarithmic spiral _always_ tends to manifest itself in such structures as these, though it usually only attracts our attention in elongated structures, where (that is to say) the radius vector has described a considerable angle.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Elephant and American mastodon tusks are the same spiral as the mammoth's, only shorter
claims.statement: The tusks of living elephants and American mastodons follow essentially the same logarithmic spiral as the mammoth's great spiral tusks and differ only in size, so that if they grew long enough they would become equally spiral.
claims.quote: but the American mastodons and the existing species of elephant have tusks which do not differ appreciably, except in size, from the great spiral tusks of the mammoth, though from their comparative shortness the spiral is little developed and only appears to the eye as a gentle curve.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

claims.label: Spirals of sunflower, thistle and cone are deformations of helices on a stem
claims.statement: The logarithmic spirals of flat or convex inflorescences and the helices on elongated stems are one phenomenon: the fir-cone, teasel, thistle and sunflower heads are successive geometric deformations of a long, nearly cylindrical stem, on which the same arrangement appears as helices.
claims.quote: the semi-ellipsoidal capitulum of the teasel, the more or less hemispherical one of the thistle, and the flattened but still convex one of the sunflower, are all beautiful and successive deformations of what is typically a long, conical, and all but cylindrical stem.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Sunflower spirals intersect isogonally, rarely orthogonally
claims.statement: Against Church, the spirals in a sunflower disc intersect isogonally (at a constant angle), and orthogonal intersection is only a particular and probably infrequent case.
claims.quote: The spirals intersect isogonally, but orthogonal intersection would be only one particular case, and in all probability a very infrequent one, in the intersection of logarithmic spirals developed about a common pole.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Phyllotactic spirals follow inevitably from similar parts produced at regular intervals
claims.statement: There is no subtle mystery in phyllotaxis: the steady production of similar parts, similarly placed, at similar successive intervals of time necessarily produces symmetrical patterns (helices on a cylinder, logarithmic spirals on a surface containing the pole), which are a secondary mathematical result rather than a primary phenomenon.
claims.quote: I, for my part, see no subtle mystery in the matter, other than what lies in the steady production of similar growing parts, similarly situated, at similar successive intervals of time.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Parastichy counts on fir-cones are nearly constant within a species
claims.statement: The numbers of conspicuous parastichies on fir-cones are on the whole very constant within a species, e.g. 5 and 3 in the Norway spruce and 8 and 5 in the common larch.
claims.quote: and among fir-cones, we can easily count these, and we find them to be on the whole very constant in number, according to the species.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Parastichy numbers change when the structure varies greatly in size
claims.statement: Phyllotactic parastichy numbers vary with the size of the whole structure, as in sunflower discs where one species may show 34/55, 55/89 or even 89/144 rows.
claims.quote: The arrangement, as we have seen, is apt to vary when the entire structure varies greatly in size, as in the disc of the sunflower.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Right- and left-handed parastichy directions occur about equally often
claims.statement: Within a species, cones with a given parastichy arrangement are nearly equally divided between right-handed and left-handed spiral directions (e.g. 224 versus 243 among 467 Norway spruce cones).
claims.quote: In each case they were nearly equally divided as regards direction; for instance of the 467 cones shewing the five-eight arrangement, the five-series ran in right-handed spirals in 224 cases, and in left-handed spirals in 243.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: One Fibonacci parastichy pair necessarily entails all the lower pairs
claims.statement: Following Tait, if a single genetic spiral exists and one pair of parastichy numbers from the series 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… is present, all the lower pairs of the series are necessarily present in the same system.
claims.quote: These are the very series which we have found to be common, or normal; and so far as our investigation has yet gone, it has proved to us that, if one of these exists, it entails, _ipso facto_, the presence of the rest.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Most phyllotaxis has between two and three leaves per turn of the genetic spiral
claims.statement: The prevalence of Fibonacci parastichy numbers arises because in the great majority of fir-cones and other phyllotactic systems there are more than two but fewer than three leaves in one turn of the genetic spiral (t = 2); other observed series correspond to t = 3, 4, 5.
claims.quote: And, determined in this manner, it is found in the great majority of cases, in fir-cones and a host of other examples of phyllotaxis, that _t_ = 2.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Which parastichies are conspicuous depends on leaf proportions, not on divergence
claims.statement: Which of the implicit spiral families is conspicuous does not depend on the angle of divergence but on the proportions of the leaves or scales, strictly on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboid circumscribing each leaf-area.
claims.quote: the conspicuousness of one set or another does not depend upon angular divergence. It depends on the relative proportions in length and breadth of the leaves themselves; or, more strictly speaking, on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboidal figure by which each leaf-area is circumscribed.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Convergence of phyllotactic ratios to the golden mean has no biological significance
claims.statement: That the phyllotactic fractions 1/2, 2/3, 3/5… converge to 0.618…, the golden mean, is a mathematical coincidence without biological significance; the precise divergence angle and orthostichies are likewise unimportant.
claims.quote: And lastly, the fact that the successional numbers, expressed as fractions, 1/2, 2/3, 3/5, represent a convergent series, whose final term is equal to 0·61803..., the _sectio aurea_ or “golden mean” of unity, is seen to be a mathematical coincidence, devoid of biological significance
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Close approximations to the golden mean are rare; poor ones like 2/3 are common
claims.statement: Against the 'ideal angle' theory, phyllotactic arrangements that closely approximate the golden mean (8/13, 13/21, 34/55 and higher) are comparatively rare, while poorer approximations such as 3/5, 2/3 and 1/2 are extremely common.
claims.quote: the arrangements by which a better approximation is got, such as 8/13, 13/21, and the very close approximations such as 34/55, 55/89, 89/144, etc., are comparatively rare, while the much less close approximations of 3/5 or 2/3, or even 1/2, are extremely common.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Leaf exposure is changed far more by internode length than by divergence angle
claims.statement: If leaves benefit from being spread apart for exposure to air, lengthening the axis to separate them vertically has a far greater effect than any adjustment of the divergence angle, so the azimuthal 'ideal angle' cannot be the plant's means of optimising exposure.
claims.quote: then it is surely manifest that the simple way to do so is to elongate the axis, and to set the leaves further apart, lengthways on the stem. This has at once a far more potent effect than any nice manipulation of the “angle of divergence.”
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: The Fibonacci series has no adaptive role introduced by natural selection
claims.statement: The Fibonacci series in phyllotaxis, its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis that natural selection introduced it into plant structure have no place in the study of botanical phenomena.
claims.quote: We come then, without more ado, to the conclusion that the “Fibonacci series,” and its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis of its introduction into plant-structure through natural selection, are all matters which deserve no place in the plain study of botanical phenomena.
claims.chapter: Ch. XIV: On Leaf-Arrangement, or Phyllotaxis

claims.label: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate
claims.statement: Hard-shelled eggs, while often pointed, are never flattened or discoidal: they are prolate, never oblate, solids of revolution.
claims.quote: It is an obvious but by no means negligible fact that the egg, while often pointed, is never flattened or discoidal; it is a prolate, but never an oblate, spheroid.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: The most pointed eggs are those largest relative to the parent bird
claims.statement: As a very common rule, the most asymmetrical, posteriorly tapered eggs are those that are large relative to the parent bird (guillemot, curlews, sandpipers, terns), because they are under the greatest pressure in the oviduct; relatively large but symmetrical eggs (apteryx) imply a relatively large oviduct.
claims.quote: It can be shown, at least as a very common rule, that those eggs which are most unsymmetrical, or most tapered off posteriorly, are also eggs of a large size relatively to the parent bird.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: A pullet's first eggs are smaller and rounder than its later ones
claims.statement: In the domestic fowl egg size and shape are directly related: a young pullet's first eggs are smaller and more nearly spherical than later ones, and breeds laying relatively smaller eggs lay rounder eggs.
claims.quote: In the case of the common fowl we can trace a direct relation between the size and shape of the egg, for the first eggs laid by a young pullet are usually smaller, and at the same time are much more nearly spherical than the later ones
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Peristaltic pressure behind the egg's middle makes the front blunt and rear pointed
claims.statement: Peristaltic contraction of the oviduct applies greatest pressure behind the middle of the forming egg, making the anterior end broader and the posterior narrower; the resulting tapered form also favours movement down the oviduct blunt end first.
claims.quote: from the nature and direction of motion of the peristaltic wave the pressure will be greatest somewhere behind the middle of the egg; in other words, the tube is converted for the time being into a more conical form, and the simple result follows that the anterior end of the egg becomes the broader and the posterior end the narrower.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Egg shape is caused by radial pressure of the oviduct before the shell hardens
