claims.statement: The essential cause of the form and variation of form of an egg is the regularly varying, largely radial pressure applied by successive rings of the oviduct before the shell solidifies, not adaptation to nesting circumstances.
claims.quote: this factor, the unknown but regularly varying, largely radial, pressure applied by successive annuli of the oviduct, is the essential cause of the form, and variations of form, of the egg.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Egg form obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P, the equation of all eggs
claims.statement: The shape of an egg, as an extensible membrane filled with incompressible fluid under external pressure, obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P (external normal pressure plus membrane tension times total curvature equals internal pressure), which Thompson calls the equation of all eggs.
claims.quote: In fact, in so far as the postulates correspond near enough to actualities, the above equation is the equation of _all eggs_ in the universe.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Membrane tension peaks at the small end, where abnormal eggs are irregular
claims.statement: In conical eggs with spherical ends, the tension of the envelope is greatest at and near the small end, so that is where eggs are most likely to be distorted or to burst and where abnormal eggs most often show irregularities.
claims.quote: further, that the tension _T_ is greatest at and near the small end of the egg. It is here, in short, that the egg is most likely to be irregularly distorted or even to burst, and it is here that we most commonly find irregularities of shape in abnormal eggs.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Lateral spine of Schistosoma eggs is moulded in the ootype, not a species mark
claims.statement: Following Looss, the lateral spine of some Schistosoma eggs is moulded mechanically in a funnel-shaped part of the uterus, so lateral- and terminal-spined eggs are mechanical variants of one thing and do not show the existence of a separate species, S. mansoni.
claims.quote: It ascribes to a mechanical cause a curious peculiarity of form; it shews, by reference to this mechanical principle, that two conditions which were very different to the systematic naturalist’s eye, were really only two simple mechanical modifications of the same thing; and it destroys the chief evidence for the existence of a supposed new species of worm
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Sea-urchin shell outlines match liquid drops flattened by gravity
claims.statement: The vertical outlines of regular sea-urchin shells are the forms of liquid drops depressed by gravity (with the pull of the tube-feet), their degree of flattening varying with the tension or strength of the shell: strong shells (Palaeechinus) stay nearly spherical, soft flexible ones (Phormosoma) are most flattened.
claims.quote: but we have no difficulty in seeing that the various forms represented in a series of sea-urchin shells are no other than those which we may easily and perfectly imitate in drops.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Vessel wall thickness tracks radius in large arteries but falls off in small ones
claims.statement: Under constant pressure the wall thickness of a blood-vessel should vary as its radius (P = T/R); because pressure falls with friction from large to small arteries, wall thickness is proportional to vessel size in larger vessels but becomes disproportionately thin in small arteries and capillaries.
claims.quote: and accordingly we find that while, for a time, the cross-sections of the larger and smaller vessels are symmetrical figures, with the wall-thickness proportional to the size of the tube, this proportion is gradually lost, and the walls of the small arteries, and still more of the capillaries, become exceedingly thin, and more so than in strict proportion to the narrowing of the tube.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Heart wall thickness varies inversely with the mean curvature of the chamber
claims.statement: Within each cavity of the heart, where pressure is uniform, wall thickness t varies inversely as the mean curvature, t(1/r + 1/r′) = C, so the highly curved apex of the left ventricle is thinnest.
claims.quote: that is to say, that the thickness (_t_) of the wall varies inversely as the mean curvature.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Left ventricle wall is 6–7 times right's, matching the pressure ratio
claims.statement: The left ventricle requires six to seven times the dilating pressure of the right, and its wall thickness is greater in the same proportion.
claims.quote: we find (1) that we have had to use a pressure in the left ventricle from six to seven times as great as in the right ventricle, and (2) that the thickness of the walls is just in the same proportion.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Blood-vessels are arranged for minimum effort and minimum wall-surface
claims.statement: The form and arrangement of blood-vessels are such that circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort and a minimum of wall-surface (and hence of friction).
claims.quote: The general principle is that the form and arrangement of the blood-vessels is such that the circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort, and with a minimum of wall-surface, the latter condition leading to a minimum of friction and being therefore included in the first.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Small arterial branches leave at large angles, large branches at small angles
claims.statement: Small arterial branches come off the main stem at large angles (about 70°–90° for the smallest) and large branches at small angles, with equal branches diverging at equal angles, as Roux's rules state.
claims.quote: In other words, it would seem that for small branches a large angle of bifurcation, and for large branches a small one, is always the better.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Optimal branching angle has cosine equal to ratio of energy loss in trunk and branch
claims.statement: The most favourable angle at which an arterial branch leaves its trunk is that whose cosine equals the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the main vessel to that in the branch (cos x = L/L′).
claims.quote: That is to say, the most favourable angle of branching will be such that the cosine of the angle is equal to the ratio of the loss of energy which the blood undergoes, per unit of length, in the main vessel, as compared with that which it undergoes in the branch.
claims.chapter: Ch. XV: On the Shapes of Eggs, and of Certain Other Hollow Structures

claims.label: Mechanical adaptations of form are demonstrable, unlike colour adaptations
claims.statement: Unlike explanations of colouration as cryptic, warning or mimetic, which cannot be demonstrated, the fitness of organic form for mechanical functions such as swimming or flight can be analysed and established in detail by statics and dynamics.
claims.quote: But of a very different order from all such “adaptations” as these, are those very perfect adaptations of form which, for instance, fit a fish for swimming or a bird for flight. Here we are far above the region of mere hypothesis, for we have to deal with questions of mechanical efficiency where statical and dynamical considerations can be applied and established in detail.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Bone is nearly as strong in tension as in compression
claims.statement: Fresh bone resists tearing almost as well as it resists crushing (tensile strength about 9–12 and crushing strength about 13–16 kg per sq. mm), which makes it an economical structural material that can serve equally as tie or strut.
claims.quote: At first sight, bone seems weak indeed; but it has the great and unusual advantage that it is very nearly as good for a tie as for a strut, nearly as strong to withstand rupture, or tearing asunder, as to resist crushing.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Structures that must resist bending are built as hollow tubes
claims.statement: Where stiffness against bending in all directions is required, organisms use a hollow cylindrical construction with little or no material in the core, as in the thin-walled, almost empty wing bones of long-winged birds such as the albatross, quills, and hollow stems of reeds and straw.
claims.quote: it is appropriate in every case where _stiffness_ is required, where bending has to be resisted. The long bone of a bird’s wing has little or no weight to carry, but it has to withstand powerful bending moments; and in the arm-bone of a long-winged bird, such as an albatross, we see the tubular construction manifested in its perfection
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Femoral wall thickness follows the bending-moment distribution along the shaft
claims.statement: Because bending strain is greatest at mid-length of a bent column, the walls of a long bone such as the femur are thickest in the middle of the shaft and thin gradually towards the ends, so that wall thickness forms a graph of the bending moments along the bone.
claims.quote: Hence, if our cylindrical column be exposed to strong bending stresses, it will be prudent and economical to make its walls thickest in the middle and thinning off gradually towards the ends; and if we look at a longitudinal section of a thigh-bone, we shall see that this is just what nature has done.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Trabeculae of cancellous bone follow the lines of compressive and tensile stress
claims.statement: The trabeculae of cancellous bone, as in the head of the femur, are arranged along the principal lines of compressive and tensile stress of the loaded bone, crossing one another at right angles, exactly as in the engineer's stress diagram of a comparable structure such as a crane-head.
claims.quote: and we have no difficulty in seeing that the anatomical arrangement of the trabeculae follows precisely the mechanical distribution of compressive and tensile stress or, in other words, accords perfectly with the theoretical stress-diagram of the crane.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Shear removes obliquely laid trabeculae, leaving those aligned with stress lines
claims.statement: Trabecular alignment arises because a trabecula laid down along a pressure or tension line is undisturbed, since there is no shear along those lines, whereas one lying obliquely is acted on by shearing force and displaced until it comes into line with the stress.
claims.quote: If it lie in the direction of one of the pressure-lines, for instance, it will be in a position of comparative equilibrium, or minimal disturbance; but if it be inclined obliquely to the pressure-lines, the shearing force will at once tend to act upon it and move it away.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Trabecular architecture remodels to new force patterns after malunited fracture
claims.statement: Trabecular arrangement is produced by the forces acting on the bone, not by heredity: when a fracture heals with the parts displaced so that the stress lines are redistributed, the trabecular system is entirely remodelled within weeks to align with the new forces, even at a distance from the injury.
claims.quote: If a bone be broken and so repaired that its parts lie somewhat out of their former place, so that the pressure-and tension-lines have now a new distribution, before many weeks are over the trabecular system will be found to have been entirely remodelled, so as to fall into line with the new system of forces.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Mechanical strain directly stimulates growth
claims.statement: A state of strain produced by stress is a direct stimulus to growth, so that tissues under increased load grow stronger or thicker, as when the fibula of a puppy whose tibia was excised grew as thick as or thicker than the normal tibia.
claims.quote: a condition of _strain_, the result of a _stress_, is a direct stimulus to growth itself. This indeed is no less than one of the cardinal facts of theoretical biology.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: The quadruped backbone is a double-armed cantilever girder, not an arch
claims.statement: Because the jointed legs cannot resist the horizontal thrust of an arch and there is no tie between its ends, the backbone of a standing quadruped is not an arch, tied arch or bowstring girder but is mechanically comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.
claims.quote: The structure is not an arch, nor a tied arch, nor a bowstring girder: but it is strictly and beautifully comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Height of vertebral spines is proportional to the local bending moment
claims.statement: In the vertebral girder, ligaments form the upper tension member, vertebral bodies the lower compression member and the spines the web, and the height of the vertebral spines at each point along the back is proportional to the bending moment at that point.
claims.quote: secondly we observe that the depth of the web, or distance apart of the principal members,—that is to say the height of the vertebral spines,—must be proportional to the bending-moment at each point along the length of the girder.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Quadrupeds carry more of their weight on the fore-legs than on the hind-legs
claims.statement: In large quadrupeds the fore-legs carry considerably more of the body weight than the hind-legs (about 55–58% in horses and elephants and about two-thirds in camels and llamas).
claims.quote: It will be observed that in all these animals the load upon the fore-feet preponderates considerably over that upon the hind, the preponderance being rather greater in the elephant than in the horse, and markedly greater in the camel and the llama than in the other two.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Heavy heads give tall withers spines; heavy tails give tall lumbar-sacral spines
claims.statement: Animals whose head and neck form a large fraction of body weight have large bending moments over the fore-legs and correspondingly tall spines over the withers, whereas animals with light heads and heavy tails (anteaters, Diplodocus) or that are bipedal (kangaroo, Iguanodon) have their tallest spines over the loins and haunches.
claims.quote: Wherever we have a heavily loaded anterior cantilever arm, that is to say whenever the head and neck represent a considerable fraction of the whole weight of the body, we tend to have large bending-moments over the fore-legs, and correspondingly high spines over the vertebrae of the withers.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Aquatic mammals lack the tall withers and haunch spines of land quadrupeds
claims.statement: Because buoyancy neutralises gravity so that there are no piers or cantilevers, all aquatic mammals (whales, seals, sea-cows) have lost the high arched vertebral spines over the withers and haunches, and aquatic birds have a weak, straight pelvis compared with terrestrial birds.
claims.quote: For here the effect of gravity is neutralised; we have neither piers nor cantilevers; and we find accordingly in all aquatic mammals of whatsoever group—whales, seals or sea-cows—that the high arched vertebral spines over the withers, or corresponding structures over the hind-limbs, have both entirely disappeared.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Fish vertebral processes are set at about 120° to one another for uniform stiffness
claims.statement: In ordinary fishes such as cod and haddock (and partly in whales), the backbone is stiffened by three series of ligament-connected processes, dorsal and two transverse, arranged at nearly equal angles of 120°, which gives the greatest and most uniform strength possible for such a system.
claims.quote: And here we see (as we see partly also among the whales), that these three series of processes, or struts, tend to be arranged well-nigh at equal angles, of 120°, with one another, giving the greatest and most uniform strength of which such a system is capable.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Backbone girders are shallower than engineers would build because flexibility is needed
claims.statement: The vertebral girder of large animals such as Diplodocus or Stegosaurus is shallower than an engineer's cantilever of comparable load, because a deeper girder would increase rigidity, and an animal's backbone must combine strength with flexibility.
claims.quote: If we adopt a much greater depth (or ratio of depth to length) as in the modern cantilever, we shall greatly increase the _strength_ of the structure; but at the same time we should greatly increase its _rigidity_, and this is precisely what, in the circumstances of the case, it would seem that nature is bound to avoid.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Skeletal form is largely a diagram of mechanical stress
claims.statement: Skeletal form, as produced by growth, is to a very large extent determined by mechanical stress: material is laid down along the lines of stress so as to avoid shear, from the trabeculae within each bone to the arrangement of the bones in the whole skeleton.
claims.quote: Let us not press either argument or hypothesis too far: but be content to see that skeletal form, as brought about by growth, is to a very large extent determined by mechanical considerations, and tends to manifest itself as a diagram, or reflected image, of mechanical stress.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Mechanically shaped single bones are unreliable guides to phylogenetic affinity
claims.statement: Because the form of bones such as the scapula or vertebrae reflects the mechanical stresses of an animal's mode of life, resemblance or difference in a single such bone is no reliable evidence for or against blood-relationship, as in comparing Zeuglodon with whales.
claims.quote: That the Zeuglodon has a scapula like that of a whale is to my mind no necessary argument that he is akin by blood-relationship to a whale: that his dorsal vertebrae are very different from a whale’s is no conclusive argument that such blood-relationship is lacking.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: New mechanical forces modify many correlated parts together, not isolated bones
claims.statement: When altered environment and habits introduce new forces, the resulting modifications of form appear not as isolated changes in single parts but as slow, general, graded modifications spread over many correlated parts or the whole body.
claims.quote: And if this be really so, it will further imply that modifications of form will tend to manifest themselves, not so much in small and _isolated_ phenomena, in this part of the fabric or in that, in a scapula for instance or a humerus: but rather in some slow, _general_, and more or less uniform or graded modification, spread over a number of correlated parts
claims.chapter: Ch. XVI: On Form and Mechanical Efficiency

claims.label: Organic forms depart from mathematical ideals only as inanimate forms do
claims.statement: There is no essential difference between organic and inorganic form: living forms depart from ideal mathematical figures only because secondary forces act alongside the main one, just as no chain hangs as a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere.
claims.quote: There is no such essential difference between these phenomena of organic form and those which are manifested in portions of inanimate matter. No chain hangs in a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere: and this for the simple reason that forces and resistances other than the main one are inevitably at work.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Specific differences in form are mainly differences of relative magnitude
claims.statement: The essential differences in form between species of the same group are differences of proportion or relative magnitude (Aristotle's 'excess and defect'), and these are the main cause of specific differences.
claims.quote: It is precisely this difference of relative magnitudes, this Aristotelian “excess and defect” in the case of form, which our co-ordinate method is especially adapted to analyse, and to reveal and demonstrate as the main cause of what (again in the Aristotelian sense) we term “specific” differences.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Evolution varies the whole body in correlation, not character by character
claims.statement: Because dissimilar related fishes can be referred as wholes to the same figure in different coordinate systems, variation has proceeded on definite and orderly lines under a comprehensive law of growth affecting the whole structure, rather than by independent variation of separate parts as the usual conception of natural selection assumes.
claims.quote: But if, on the other hand, diverse and dissimilar fishes can be referred as a whole to identical functions of very different co-ordinate systems, this fact will of itself constitute a proof that variation has proceeded on definite and orderly lines, that a comprehensive “law of growth” has pervaded the whole structure in its integrity
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Related organisms differ by simple, symmetrical Cartesian transformations
claims.statement: The forms of related organisms can, as a general rule, be mapped onto one another by a simple and symmetrical deformation of a Cartesian coordinate grid, such as would result from a slight and simple change in the system of forces acting on the growing organism.
claims.quote: We are dealing in this chapter with the forms of related organisms, in order to shew that the differences between them are as a general rule simple and symmetrical, and just such as might have been brought about by a slight and simple change in the system of forces to which the living and growing organism was exposed.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Shear-deformed fossils are often mistaken for distinct species
claims.statement: Fossils in folded and inclined strata are often symmetrically deformed, usually by simple shear, so that they have been described as distinct species and occasionally even as new genera.
claims.quote: the contained fossils are apt to be so curiously and yet so symmetrically deformed (usually by a simple shear) that they may easily be interpreted as so many distinct and separate “species.”
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Cannon-bones of ox, sheep and giraffe differ by a simple one-axis stretch
claims.statement: The cannon-bones of the ox, sheep and giraffe differ essentially only in relative length and breadth: at equal length, the sheep's bone is about two-thirds and the giraffe's about one-third as broad as the ox's.
claims.quote: In other words, the main (and perhaps the only) difference between the two bones is simply that that of the sheep is elongated, along the vertical axis, as compared with that of the ox in the relation of 3/2.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Ratio of radial to tangential growth about a node yields lanceolate, ovate, cordate leaves
claims.statement: Dicotyledon leaf shapes arise from growth radial to and transverse to radii about a node of no growth at the leaf base; increasing the ratio of tangential to radial growth carries the outline successively from lanceolate to ovate to cordate.
claims.quote: If we now alter the ratio between the radial and tangential velocities of growth—in other words, if we increase the angles between corresponding radii—we pass successively through the various configurations which the botanist describes as the lanceolate, the ovate, and finally the cordate leaf.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: The lopsided begonia leaf reflects unequal, not asymmetrical, growth
claims.statement: The two halves of a begonia leaf, one ovate and the other cordate, are mathematically similar figures produced by unequal growth on either side of the midrib, so that angles to equal radii on the two sides are in constant proportion.
claims.quote: the so-called unsymmetrical leaf of a begonia, in which one side of the leaf may be merely ovate while the other has a cordate outline, is seen to be really a case of _unequal_, and not truly asymmetrical, growth on either side of the midrib.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Organisms grow along stream lines definable by a mathematical transformation
claims.statement: The law of growth implied by representing related forms as orthogonal coordinate transformations is that the organism grows along stream lines definable by a suitable mathematical transformation; departures from orthogonality reflect the organism not being homogeneous and isotropic.
claims.quote: the “law of growth” which our biological analysis by means of orthogonal co-ordinate systems presupposes, or at least foreshadows, is one according to which the organism grows or develops along _stream lines_, which may be defined by a suitable mathematical transformation.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Many organic forms arise from uniform expansive growth limited by local constraints
claims.statement: Many developmental changes of form are produced by local trammels or lines of constraint acting on otherwise uniform and symmetrical expansive growth, as a ligature turns a gourd into two globes or a muscular band makes the stomach a lopsided bubble.
claims.quote: It is clear, I think, that we may account for many ordinary biological processes of development or transformation of form by the existence of trammels or lines of constraint, which limit and determine the action of the expansive forces of growth that would otherwise be uniform and symmetrical.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: One transformation accounts for the differences between porcupine-fish and sunfish
claims.statement: Deforming the coordinate grid of Diodon (concentric circles and approximately hyperbolic curves) yields the outline of the sunfish Orthagoriscus, so that a single integral transformation accounts for all their apparently separate external differences while leaving the head region nearly unchanged.
claims.quote: And as such it accounts, by one single integral transformation, for all the apparently separate and distinct external differences between the two fishes.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: One harmonious deformation accounts for all skull differences among crocodilians
claims.statement: Across most crocodilian genera, the skull contours and even the shapes and sizes of individual bones and vacuities can be derived from one another by a single simple coordinate transformation, so that the skull of Notosuchus can be reconstructed bone for bone from that of Crocodilus.
claims.quote: To all intents and purposes, then, this not very complex system, representing one harmonious “deformation,” accounts for _all_ the differences between the two figures, and is sufficient to enable one at any time to reconstruct a detailed drawing, bone for bone, of the skull of _Notosuchus_ from the model furnished by the common crocodile.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Perissodactyls are more closely related to hares and rabbits than to other ungulates
claims.statement: Since the rabbit's skull is derived from that of a primitive rhinoceros by a simple uniform downward flexure, the Perissodactyla are more closely related to the Leporidae than to other ungulates, and the Leporidae more closely to Perissodactyla than to other rodents.
claims.quote: For my part, I would go further; for I think there is strong reason to believe that the Perissodactyles are more closely related to the Leporidae than the former are to the other Ungulates, or than the Leporidae are to the rest of the Rodentia.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Fossil horse skulls match interpolated stages between Hyracotherium and Equus
claims.statement: Skulls interpolated by coordinate transformation between Hyracotherium (Eohippus) and Equus coincide closely with actual fossil skulls of Mesohippus and Protohippus, which therefore lie on the transformation series from Eohippus to the horse.
claims.quote: it will be seen that the actual fossil skull coincides in the most perfect fashion with one of the hypothetical forms or stages which our method shews to be implicitly involved in the transition from _Hyracotherium_ to _Equus_.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Parahippus is a divergent offshoot, not on the direct line to Equus
claims.statement: Because the skull of Parahippus fits the interpolated transformation series from Eohippus to Equus poorly, Parahippus is not in the direct line of descent but represents a divergent branch of the Equidae.
claims.quote: In short, though some writers have placed _Parahippus_ in the direct line of descent between _Equus_ and _Eohippus_, we see at once that there is no place for it there, and that it must, accordingly, represent a somewhat divergent branch or offshoot of the Equidae.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Ape and human skull differences form one continuous, roughly logarithmic transformation
claims.statement: The differences between the human skull and the skulls of the chimpanzee and baboon form one continuous integral deformation in which corresponding areas of the grid increase approximately logarithmically downwards and forwards, rather than separate modifications of jaws, braincase and face.
claims.quote: In both dimensions, as we pass from above downwards and from behind forwards, the corresponding areas of the network are seen to increase in a gradual and approximately logarithmic order in the lower as compared with the higher type of skull; and, in short, it becomes at once manifest that the modifications of jaws, braincase, and the regions between are all portions of one continuous and integral process.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Human and anthropoid skulls show divergent rather than linear evolutionary change
claims.statement: No continuous transformation series passes through known fossil and living human and anthropoid skulls (Mesopithecus, Pithecanthropus, Neanderthal, modern man), indicating that there is no single straight line of descent and that their variation has been divergent.
claims.quote: The failure is not the fault of our method. It merely indicates that no one straight line of descent, or of consecutive transformation, exists; but on the contrary, that among human and anthropoid types, recent and extinct, we have to do with a complex problem of divergent, rather than of continuous, variation.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: Depth expansion and lateral compression vary inversely, conserving fish volume
claims.statement: In related fishes, expansion in one transverse dimension tends to be compensated by compression in the other, so that volume at a given length changes less than linear dimensions; the plaice is about twice as deep and half as thick as the haddock and has almost the same length-weight coefficient k = W/L^3.
claims.quote: the very fact that the two dimensions tend to vary _inversely_ already assures us that, in the general process of deformation, the _volume_ is less affected than are the _linear dimensions_.
claims.chapter: Ch. XVII: On the Theory of Transformations, or the Comparison of Related Forms

claims.label: A mathematical approach is essential to the study of organic form
claims.statement: A mathematical aspect of morphology, largely neglected by morphologists, is interwoven with their problems, complementary to description, and essential to the proper understanding of form.
claims.quote: My task is finished if I have been able to shew that a certain mathematical aspect of morphology, to which as yet the morphologist gives little heed, is interwoven with his problems, complementary to his descriptive task, and helpful, nay essential, to his proper study and comprehension of Form.
claims.chapter: Ch. Epilogue: Epilogue

claims.label: Mathematical regularity and usefulness coincide in living forms
claims.statement: What is most beautiful and regular in natural form, as in the bee's cell, is also found to be most useful and excellent.
claims.quote: Moreover the perfection of mathematical beauty is such (as Maclaurin learned of the bee), that whatsoever is most beautiful and regular is also found to be most useful and excellent.
claims.chapter: Ch. Epilogue: Epilogue

claims.label: Living and non-living things are bound alike by physical and mathematical law
claims.statement: Living and non-living things alike are governed by the same physical and mathematical laws.
claims.quote: The living and the dead, things animate and inanimate, we dwellers in the world and this world wherein we dwell,—πάντα γα μὰν τὰ γιγνωσκόμενα,—are bound alike by physical and mathematical law.
claims.chapter: Ch. Epilogue: Epilogue

claims.label: Rules governing nature need not be those of traditional mathematics
claims.statement: Although theoretical science requires that the systems it studies follow definite rules, those rules need not be the equation-based rules of traditional mathematics; the more general rules embodied in simple computer programs are equally candidates for describing the natural world.
claims.quote: the crucial realization that led me to develop the new kind of science in this book is that there is in fact no reason to think that systems like those we see in nature should follow only such traditional mathematical rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Programs with very simple rules often behave in complex ways
claims.statement: When simple computer programs are enumerated and run systematically, their behavior is often far from simple, and some of the very simplest programs produce behavior as complex as any known.
claims.quote: despite the simplicity of their rules, the behavior of the programs was often far from simple. Indeed, even some of the very simplest programs that I looked at had behavior that was as complex as anything I had ever seen.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Natural complexity arises because natural systems behave like typical programs
claims.statement: The great complexity seen across physical, biological and other natural systems is explained by those systems operating like typical simple programs, which commonly produce complex behavior, rather than by any special or supernatural source of complexity.
claims.quote: For all it takes is that systems in nature operate like typical programs and then it follows that their behavior will often be complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Equation-based descriptions work for simple behavior but fail for complex behavior
claims.statement: Describing behavior with mathematical equations succeeds for fairly simple behavior such as planetary motion but almost inevitably fails when behavior is more complex, and descriptions based on natural selection share this limitation; thinking in terms of programs allows meaningful statements about highly complex behavior.
claims.quote: while their basic idea of describing behavior in terms of mathematical equations works well in cases like planetary motion where the behavior is fairly simple, it almost inevitably fails whenever the behavior is more complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: The same basic forms of behavior recur in simple programs regardless of details
claims.statement: Across the world of simple programs the same basic forms of behavior occur repeatedly almost independently of the underlying details of the rules, suggesting universal principles of overall behavior that should also apply to systems throughout nature.
claims.quote: in the world of simple programs I have discovered that the same basic forms of behavior occur over and over again almost independent of underlying details.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Simple programs yield a straightforward explanation of thermodynamic behavior
claims.statement: The long-standing difficulty in understanding how thermodynamic behavior, including the Second Law of Thermodynamics, arises in physics can be resolved by a straightforward explanation drawn from the behavior of simple programs.
claims.quote: For more than a century, for example, there has been confusion about how thermodynamic behavior arises in physics. Yet from my discoveries about simple programs I have developed a quite straightforward explanation.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Universal computation is possible in systems with one-sentence rules
claims.statement: Contrary to the assumption that computational universality requires elaborate systems like electronic computers, there exist systems whose rules can be stated in a single sentence that are nevertheless universal, able to perform any possible computation.
claims.quote: there are systems whose rules are simple enough to describe in just one sentence that are nevertheless universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Most systems with non-simple behavior are computationally irreducible
claims.statement: Predicting a system's outcome by a mathematical shortcut is normally possible only for special systems with simple behavior; other systems are computationally irreducible, so their behavior can be found only by tracing each step with roughly as much computational effort as the system itself expends.
claims.quote: such systems are computationally irreducible—so that in effect the only way to find their behavior is to trace each of their steps, spending about as much computational effort as the systems themselves.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Computational irreducibility explains free will despite deterministic rules
claims.statement: Computational irreducibility provides an explanation of how humans, even if they follow definite underlying rules, can meaningfully be said to have free will.
claims.quote: it leads to an explanation of how we as humans—even though we may follow definite underlying rules—can still in a meaningful way show free will.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Complexity of simple abstract systems imposes fundamental limits on proof
claims.statement: The complexity found in simple abstract systems leads to fundamental limitations on mathematical proof, of the kind hinted at by Gödel's Theorem, and these limitations are relevant well beyond the narrow scope of current mathematics.
claims.quote: one of the consequences of this complexity is that it leads to fundamental limitations on the idea of proof that has been central to traditional mathematics.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Simple programs capture how genetic programs generate biological forms
claims.statement: Simple programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms and appear to capture essential mechanisms by which genetic programs generate observed biological forms, enabling new models and general abstract theories in biology.
claims.quote: such programs can reproduce many features of biological organisms—and for example seem to capture some of the essential mechanisms through which genetic programs manage to generate the actual biological forms we see.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Sophisticated tasks need only extremely simple underlying rules
claims.statement: Contrary to engineering experience, performing sophisticated tasks does not require correspondingly complicated basic rules; extremely simple underlying rules, potentially implementable directly at the atomic scale, are often sufficient.
claims.quote: extremely simple underlying rules—that might for example potentially be implemented directly at the level of atoms—are often all that is needed.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: Natural selection tends to oppose rather than generate complexity
claims.statement: Darwinian natural selection does not clearly imply the generation of complexity and in many respects tends to oppose it; a different mechanism, the intrinsic complexity of simple programs, is responsible for most great complexity in biology.
claims.quote: I will argue in this book that in many respects it tends to oppose complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 1: The Foundations for a New Kind of Science

claims.label: A rule-90-type cellular automaton produces a nested self-similar pattern
claims.statement: A one-dimensional cellular automaton in which each cell becomes black when exactly one of its two neighbors was black (rule 90), started from a single black cell, produces an intricate but regular nested pattern made of triangular pieces that are smaller copies of the whole.
claims.quote: it actually consists of many nested triangular pieces that all have exactly the same form.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Rule 30 from a single black cell produces an irregular, complex pattern
claims.statement: The elementary cellular automaton rule 30, started from a single black cell, produces a highly irregular and complex pattern with almost no overall regularity, rather than a uniform, repetitive or nested one.
claims.quote: Rather than getting a simple regular pattern as we might expect, the cellular automaton instead produces a pattern that seems extremely irregular and complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Simple rules with simple initial conditions can yield highly complex behavior
claims.statement: As a general phenomenon, a system with simple underlying rules started from simple initial conditions can nevertheless show highly complex behavior.
claims.quote: even though the underlying rules for a system are simple, and even though the system is started from simple initial conditions, the behavior that the system shows can nevertheless be highly complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Complexity from simple rules accounts for most complexity in nature
claims.statement: The generation of complex behavior from simple rules and simple initial conditions is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity seen in nature.
claims.quote: I will argue that it is this basic phenomenon that is ultimately responsible for most of the complexity that we see in nature.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Rule 30's center column shows no deviation from randomness over a million steps
claims.statement: The sequence of cell colors directly below the initial black cell in rule 30 does not repeat in its first million steps, and statistical tests show no meaningful deviation from perfect randomness.
claims.quote: in the first million steps in this sequence, for example, it never repeats, and indeed none of the tests I have ever done on it show any meaningful deviation at all from perfect randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Some cellular automata make even average properties hard to predict
claims.statement: Some simple cellular automata, such as rule 110, are more complex than random-looking ones like rule 30: they mix regular regions with interacting localized structures, so that even average properties of their behavior become very difficult to predict.
claims.quote: there are cellular automata whose behavior is in effect still more complex—and in which even such averages become very difficult to predict.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Rule 110's fate can be determined only by running it
claims.statement: Whether the localized structures in rule 110 eventually annihilate into a regular pattern or proliferate into randomness apparently cannot be determined in advance; the only reliable method is to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as needed.
claims.quote: The only sure way to answer these questions, it seems, is just to run the cellular automaton for as many steps as are needed
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Rule 110 from one black cell becomes periodic with period 240 after about 2780 steps
claims.statement: Rule 110 started from a single black cell resolves after about 2780 steps: one localized structure survives and interacts with periodic stripes from the left to give behavior that repeats every 240 steps.
claims.quote: the outcome is finally clear after about 2780 steps: one structure survives, and that structure interacts with the periodic stripes coming from the left to produce behavior that repeats every 240 steps.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Identical cell rules yield diverse behaviors through different configurations
claims.statement: Even though every cell of a cellular automaton follows the same rule, different configurations of cell colors can collectively produce many different kinds of behavior, such as regular backgrounds and distinct localized structures.
claims.quote: even though individual cells follow the same rule, different configurations of cells with different sequences of colors can together produce all sorts of different kinds of behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Intuition that complex results need complex plans comes from engineering
claims.statement: The intuition that complex objects require complex construction plans fails because it derives from engineering, where designers restrict themselves to systems whose behavior they can understand and predict, a constraint nature does not share.
claims.quote: Yet to do this reliably, we have to restrict ourselves to systems whose behavior we can readily understand and predict—for unless we can foresee how a system will behave, we cannot be sure that the system will do what we want.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Systems with simple rules and complex behavior are very common in nature
claims.statement: Because nature is not constrained to predictable designs, systems whose simple rules produce complex behavior, like rule 30 and rule 110, are very common in nature.
claims.quote: one of the important conclusions of this book is that such systems are actually very common in nature.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Complex cellular-automaton-like patterns are absent from historical ornament
claims.statement: Historical ornamental art contains many repetitive patterns and some nested ones, but the more complicated patterns produced by simple cellular automata such as rule 30 never appear to have been used.
claims.quote: Repetitive patterns are common and some nested patterns are seen, but the more complicated kinds of patterns discussed in this chapter do not ever appear to have been used.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Computers enable discoveries beyond working out mathematical equations
claims.statement: Computers are not limited to computing the consequences of mathematical equations; directly studying the behavior of even the simplest computer programs yields fundamental scientific discoveries.
claims.quote: computers are not just limited to working out consequences of mathematical equations. And indeed, what we have seen in this chapter is that there are fundamental discoveries that can be made if one just studies directly the behavior of even some of the very simplest computer programs.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Unknown phenomena are found only by systematic, preconception-free experiments
claims.statement: Phenomena not already known to exist can be found only by very systematic and general experiments whose results are examined with as few preconceptions as possible.
claims.quote: the only way to find phenomena that one does not already know exist is to do very systematic and general experiments, and then to look at the results with as few preconceptions as possible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Lack of adequate computers delayed discovery of complexity from simple rules
claims.statement: A main reason that complexity from simple programs was not discovered before the 1980s is that computer technology powerful enough for the required large-scale exploratory experiments did not yet exist, together with a lack of intuition drawn from practical computing.
claims.quote: one of the main reasons that the discoveries I describe in this chapter were not made before the 1980s is just that computer technology did not yet exist powerful enough to do the kinds of exploratory experiments that were needed.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: It is usually very hard to foresee what even a simple program will do
claims.statement: Practical computing shows that it is usually very difficult to foresee the behavior of even a simple program, which is why software bugs are so common; the simple structure of cellular automaton rules likewise does not make their behavior easy to predict.
claims.quote: from experience in practical computing one knows that it is usually very difficult to foresee what even a simple program will do.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Primes follow simple generating rules yet are distributed seemingly randomly
claims.statement: The prime numbers, though generated by simple rules, have a distribution that seems in many respects random, an early instance of complexity from simple rules that mathematics largely neglected in favor of proving regularities.
claims.quote: The rules for generating primes are simple, yet their distribution seems in many respects random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Complexity from simple programs was never discovered before despite many hints
claims.statement: Although there were many hints over several centuries, including primes, digits of pi, iterated maps and the Game of Life, the basic phenomenon of simple programs producing complex behavior was never identified before Wolfram's work.
claims.quote: despite many hints over the course of several centuries, the basic phenomenon that I have described in this chapter was never discovered before.
claims.chapter: Ch. 2: The Crucial Experiment

claims.label: Overall behavior types are similar across all kinds of simple programs
claims.statement: Whatever kind of underlying rules a simple program uses (cellular automata, mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, register machines, symbolic systems), the overall behavior that emerges falls into the same few basic types first seen in elementary cellular automata.
claims.quote: whatever kind of underlying rules one uses, the behavior that emerges turns out to be remarkably similar to the basic examples that we have already seen in cellular automata.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Most elementary cellular automata give fixed-size patterns from a single black cell
claims.statement: Among the 256 elementary (two-color, nearest-neighbor) cellular automata started from a single black cell, about two-thirds produce patterns that stay of fixed size and about one-third produce patterns that grow forever, with about 14% yielding patterns more complicated than repetition.
claims.quote: In about two-thirds of all the cellular automata shown on the last few pages [54, 55, 56], the patterns produced remain of a fixed size. But in about one-third of cases, the patterns instead grow forever.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Ten of the 256 elementary cellular automata produce apparent randomness
claims.statement: Of the 256 elementary cellular automata started from a single black cell, 10 produce patterns that seem in many respects random, falling into three basic forms, while 24 produce nested patterns falling into only three fundamentally different forms.
claims.quote: And out of the 256 rules discussed here, it turns out that 10 yield such apparent randomness. There are three basic forms, as illustrated on the facing page.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Beyond a threshold, more complex rules do not give more complex behavior
claims.statement: At least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules of a system does not lead to more complex overall behavior; in cellular automata, all the ingredients for the most complex behavior already exist in the elementary two-color rules.
claims.quote: at least beyond a certain point, adding complexity to the underlying rules for a system does not ultimately lead to more complex overall behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: About 85% of three-color totalistic cellular automata behave regularly
claims.statement: About 85% of the 2187 three-color nearest-neighbor totalistic cellular automata produce behavior that is ultimately quite regular, while the remainder include rules with seemingly random behavior and rules with interacting localized structures like rule 110.
claims.quote: About 85% of all three-color totalistic cellular automata produce behavior that is ultimately quite regular.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: No basic mobile automaton shows behavior beyond repetition or nesting
claims.statement: None of the 65,536 two-color mobile automata whose rule updates only the active cell shows behavior more complex than repetition or nesting; complex behavior appears only when the rule can also update the active cell's neighbors, and even then it is rare.
claims.quote: Of the 65,536 possible mobile automata with rules of the kind discussed so far it turns out that not a single one shows more complex behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Complex behavior correlates with many cells being active at once
claims.statement: In generalized mobile automata, complex behavior almost never occurs unless many cells are active simultaneously, and this correlation between overall activity and complexity helps explain why complexity is much more common in cellular automata than in mobile automata.
claims.quote: complex behavior almost never occurs except when large numbers of cells are active at the same time.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Two- and three-state two-color Turing machines give only repetition or nesting
claims.statement: All 4096 two-state, two-color Turing machines, and all of the roughly three million three-state, two-color Turing machines started on a blank tape, ultimately produce only repetitive or nested patterns.
claims.quote: all ultimately turn out to yield just repetitive or nested patterns—at least if they are started with all cells white.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Four head states suffice for random-looking Turing machine behavior
claims.statement: Two-color Turing machines with four head states can produce seemingly random behavior (about five in every million such rules), and allowing more than four states makes apparent randomness only slightly more common without changing the kinds of behavior seen.
claims.quote: With four states, however, more complicated behavior immediately becomes possible. Indeed, in about five out of every million rules of this kind, one gets patterns with features that seem in many respects random
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only produce nested patterns
claims.statement: Substitution systems in which each element is replaced according to its own color alone always produce nested patterns, so obtaining behavior more complicated than nesting requires rules that depend on at least one neighboring element.
claims.quote: To get behavior that is more complicated than simple nesting, it follows therefore that one must consider substitution systems whose rules depend not only on the color of a single element, but also on the color of at least one of its neighbors.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Substitution systems with deletion need three or more colors for complexity
claims.statement: Among two-color substitution systems that allow elements to be destroyed, those with slow growth produce only simple repetitive patterns, but allowing three or four colors immediately makes patterns as random-looking as those of cellular automata possible.
claims.quote: allowing elements to have three or four colors rather than just two immediately makes much more complicated behavior possible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Text-editor-like search-and-replace rules can generate great complexity
claims.statement: Sequential substitution systems, which repeatedly apply the first matching search-and-replace rule like a text editor, give only simple behavior with two replacements and two elements, but with three replacements about one in 10,000 random rules produces seemingly random behavior.
claims.quote: just by using the simple operations available even in a very basic text editor, it is still ultimately possible to produce behavior of great complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: One-element-deletion tag systems reduce to neighbor-independent substitution
claims.statement: A tag system that removes only one element per step always acts as a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system and so produces only repetitive or nested patterns, whereas removing two elements per step can yield very complicated behavior.
claims.quote: if only one element is removed at each step, then a tag system always effectively acts just like a slow version of a neighbor-independent substitution system of the kind we discussed on page 83.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Simple cyclic tag systems show random fluctuations in sequence growth
claims.statement: Some cyclic tag systems with two alternating blocks, started from a single black element, produce sequences whose average growth is steady but whose fluctuations about that growth are in many respects random.
claims.quote: if one looks at the fluctuations in this growth, as in the plots on the next page, then one finds that these fluctuations are in many respects random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Register machines need eight instructions to show complex behavior
claims.statement: Among two-register machines with increment and decrement-jump instructions, all programs of up to four instructions behave repetitively, only two five-instruction programs give nesting, none up to seven instructions is substantially more complicated, and 126 of the 11,019,960,576 eight-instruction programs show complex behavior.
claims.quote: But with eight instructions, 126 out of the 11,019,960,576 possible programs finally do show more complicated behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Short programs in ordinary low-level languages can behave randomly
claims.statement: Because register machines idealize programs in low-level languages such as C, Basic, Java or assembler, searching many millions of short programs in such languages typically yields at least a few with complex, seemingly random behavior.
claims.quote: searching through many millions of short programs typically yields at least a few that exhibit complex and seemingly random behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Combinator-like symbolic rewriting systems can behave randomly
claims.statement: Symbolic systems that repeatedly apply a single rewrite rule of the form e[x_][y_] → (expression in x and y) to nested expressions can, like other simple programs, produce behavior that is complex and seemingly random rather than stabilizing.
claims.quote: But often—just as in so many other kinds of systems—the behavior is instead complex and seemingly quite random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Complexity does not depend on the special features of cellular automata
claims.statement: Removing the special features of cellular automata, such as a rigid array of cells and parallel updating, does not prevent complex behavior from simple rules, so the phenomenon of complexity is universal and independent of the details of particular systems.
claims.quote: So this suggests that in fact the phenomenon of complexity is quite universal—and quite independent of the details of particular systems.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: The rule-complexity threshold for complex behavior is very low
claims.statement: Systems with sufficiently simple rules show only repetition, slightly more complicated rules often add nesting, and complex behavior requires crossing a threshold in rule complexity, but in every kind of system studied this threshold is extremely low.
claims.quote: The remarkable discovery that we have made, however, is that this threshold is typically extremely low.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures dominate everywhere
claims.statement: The four themes of repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures are the dominant types of behavior across a vast range of systems, and these overall behavior types are almost independent of the details of the underlying rules.
claims.quote: the basic themes of repetition, nesting, randomness and localized structures that we already saw in specific cellular automata in the previous chapter are actually very general, and in fact represent the dominant themes in the behavior of a vast range of different systems.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Overall behavior of natural systems can be inferred without knowing their details
claims.statement: Because the typical types of behavior are independent of rule details, one can make fundamental statements about the overall behavior of a natural system without knowing its internal details, and its important features will usually be ones already seen in very simple programs.
claims.quote: even if we do not know all the details of what is inside some specific system in nature, we can still potentially make fundamental statements about its overall behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Computer experiments let one discover phenomena not anticipated in advance
claims.statement: A methodology based on computer experiments, in which one runs precisely specified programs and observes their behavior, can discover genuinely unexpected phenomena that a traditional approach of constructing examples of predefined behavior would miss, while giving results as precise as mathematical statements.
claims.quote: And the great advantage of such an experimental approach is that it does not require one to know in advance exactly what kinds of behavior can occur.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: One can never start a computer experiment with too simple a system
claims.statement: Computer experiments should study the simplest possible systems with the simplest possible procedures, because simple systems already show complex behavior, and the most common mistake is studying systems far more complicated than necessary.
claims.quote: in my experience the single most common mistake in doing computer experiments is to look at systems that are vastly more complicated than is necessary.
claims.chapter: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

claims.label: Number systems fully solvable by analysis show only simple behavior
claims.statement: Systems based on numbers that traditional mathematics (e.g. calculus) can analyze completely end up showing only fairly simple behavior; textbook systems are selected for analyzability and therefore are simple.
claims.quote: Inevitably, however, when such complete analysis is possible, the final behavior that is found is fairly simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Simple arithmetic systems can produce highly complex behavior
claims.statement: When systems based on numbers are studied by computer experiment rather than by mathematical analysis, even very simple ones turn out to produce highly complex behavior.
claims.quote: if one ignores the need for analysis and instead just looks at the results of computer experiments, then one quickly finds that even rather simple systems based on numbers can lead to highly complex behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Base-2 digits of powers of 3 look random beyond small-scale structure
claims.statement: Successive powers of 3 written in base 2 form a pattern that, apart from some small-scale structure, appears random for all practical purposes, even though it comes from repeated multiplication by 3.
claims.quote: Some small-scale structure is visible, but on a larger scale the pattern seems for all practical purposes random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Fractional parts of powers of 3/2 are complex and apparently random
claims.statement: The fractional parts of successive powers of 3/2, a base-independent measure of size, show the same complexity and apparent randomness that appears in their digit sequences.
claims.quote: they too exhibit the kind of complexity and apparent randomness that is evident at the level of digits.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Simple whole-number rules can yield complex sizes, not just complex digits
claims.statement: Simple rules acting only on whole numbers (such as multiplying by 5/2 when even and adding 1 then halving when odd) can produce sequences whose overall sizes fluctuate in a complex, apparently random way with no sign of repetition, so complexity is not just an artifact of looking at digits.
claims.quote: So even if one just looks at overall sizes of whole numbers it is still possible to get great complexity in systems based on numbers.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Non-local arithmetic rules still behave like local cellular automata
claims.statement: Although arithmetic operations are non-local in digits (carries can propagate arbitrarily far) while cellular automaton rules are local, the overall behavior of number-based systems is very similar to that of cellular automata, so the details of underlying rules do not crucially affect the kinds of behavior that occur.
claims.quote: But despite fundamental differences like this in underlying rules, the overall behavior produced by systems based on numbers is still very similar to what one sees for example in cellular automata.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Reverse-and-add in base 2 shows localized structures and never repeats
claims.statement: The base-2 reverse-and-add process (add a number to its digit-reversal) started from 512 produces localized structures like those in cellular automata, and its overall pattern never appears to become simply repetitive.
claims.quote: Localized structures are visible, but the overall pattern never seems to take on any kind of simple repetitive form.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Recursive sequences using only addition and subtraction can be complex
claims.statement: Recursive integer sequences whose rule refers back a variable distance (e.g. f[n - f[n - 1]]) and uses only addition and subtraction can produce fluctuations that are complex and in many respects random.
claims.quote: even though the rules ultimately involve only addition and subtraction, they nevertheless correspond to programs that are capable of producing behavior of great complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: The sequence of primes is in many respects random
claims.statement: Even though the primes are generated by a simple sieving rule, the sequence of primes appears in many respects remarkably random.
claims.quote: the actual sequence of primes that is obtained seems in many respects remarkably random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Complexity in number-theoretic sequences arises from their generating rules
claims.statement: Sequences defined by simple properties of numbers (primes, divisor sums, representations as sums of squares or primes) show complexity that persists despite centuries of number theory, and this complexity arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules generating them, just as in other simple programs.
claims.quote: such sequences of numbers exhibit complexity that somehow arises as a fundamental consequence of the rules by which the sequences are generated.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes
claims.statement: Despite pi's simple definition, its digit sequence shows no significant regularity in all computed digits and appears for practical purposes completely random.
claims.quote: Despite the simplicity of its definition, the digit sequence of π seems for practical purposes completely random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Square roots of non-square integers have random-looking digits
claims.statement: As far as can be determined, the square root of every whole number that is not a perfect square has a digit sequence that appears completely random.
claims.quote: so far as one can tell, all whole numbers other than perfect squares have square roots whose digit sequences appear completely random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Cube roots, logarithms and exponentials also have random-looking digits
claims.statement: Beyond square roots, almost all cube roots, fourth roots, logarithms and exponentials of simple numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
claims.quote: And so far as one can tell, almost all these kinds of numbers also have apparently random digit sequences.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences
claims.statement: Every rational number p/q has a digit sequence that eventually repeats (with period at most q - 1), and rational numbers are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences.
claims.quote: In fact, rational numbers turn out to be the only kinds of numbers that have repetitive digit sequences.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Roots never have nested digit sequences
claims.statement: Nested digit sequences, such as those produced by substitution systems, never correspond to numbers obtainable by taking roots (square roots, cube roots, and so on).
claims.quote: such a digit sequence never corresponds to a number that can be obtained by the mathematical operation of taking roots.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Continued fractions of pi and higher roots look random
claims.statement: In continued fraction representation, square roots are purely repetitive and e shows definite regularity, but pi, cube roots, fourth roots and similar numbers have continued fraction terms that seem essentially random.
claims.quote: But for π, as well as for cube roots, fourth roots, and so on, the continued fraction representations one gets seem essentially random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Numbers from simple operations are intrinsically complex in any representation
claims.statement: For any representation of numbers in which recovering the value takes comparable effort for all numbers, some numbers look simple but others produced by simple mathematical operations look random, so such numbers are often intrinsically complex independent of representation.
claims.quote: numbers generated by simple mathematical operations are often in some intrinsic sense complex, independent of the particular representation that one uses to look at them.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Axis crossings of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] follow a continued-fraction substitution system
claims.statement: For a sum of two sine functions Sin[x] + Sin[a x], the arrangement of axis crossings is generated by a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from successive continued fraction terms of (a - 1)/(a + 1), giving nested patterns when a is a quadratic irrational.
claims.quote: for any curve like Sin[x] + Sin[α x] the relative arrangements of these crossing points turn out to be related to the output of a generalized substitution system in which the rule at each step is obtained from a term in the continued fraction representation of (α - 1)/(α + 1).
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: The shift map only transcribes randomness from its initial condition
claims.statement: The shift map (doubling modulo 1) generates no randomness of its own: it just moves digits of the initial number leftward, so its output is random only if the initial number's digit sequence was already random.
claims.quote: in no real sense is any randomness actually being generated by the evolution of this system. Instead, it is just that randomness that was inserted in the digit sequence of the original number shows up in the results one gets.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Some simple iterated maps generate randomness intrinsically from simple seeds
claims.statement: Some simple iterated maps, such as taking the fractional part of 3x/2, produce behavior that looks random even when started from very simple initial numbers like 1/2, so they intrinsically generate randomness rather than transcribing it from initial conditions.
claims.quote: a crucial discovery in this book is that systems like (a) and (b) on pages 150 and 151 can show behavior that seems in many respects random even when their initial conditions show no sign of randomness and are in fact extremely simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions does not itself produce randomness
claims.statement: Sensitive dependence on initial conditions (the chaos phenomenon) only amplifies differences already present in initial conditions, so on its own it contributes nothing to the ultimate production of randomness, even in systems that also show intrinsic randomness.
claims.quote: this phenomenon on its own can make no contribution at all to what we can reasonably consider the ultimate production of randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Continuous cellular automata show the same complexity as discrete ones
claims.statement: Cellular automata whose cells take a continuous range of gray levels, updated by simple maps of the neighborhood average, show the same kind of complexity as ordinary discrete cellular automata, and can even show localized structures.
claims.quote: despite the presence of continuous gray levels, the behavior that is produced exhibits the same kind of complexity that we have seen in many ordinary cellular automata and other systems with discrete underlying elements.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Nature does not fundamentally follow continuous differential equations
claims.statement: Although almost all traditional models in physics (Maxwell, Einstein, Schrödinger equations) are partial differential equations, nature does not fundamentally follow these continuous mathematical abstractions.
claims.quote: it is certainly not that nature fundamentally follows these abstractions.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Partial differential equations predominate largely by historical accident
claims.statement: The dominance of partial differential equations as models in science is in many respects a historical accident of their being solvable by explicit formulas before computers; had computers come earlier, scientific modeling would probably be very different.
claims.quote: I suspect that in fact the current predominance of partial differential equations is in many respects a historical accident—and that had computer technology been developed earlier in the history of mathematics, the situation would probably now be very different.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Simple partial differential equations can show complex behavior
claims.statement: Complex behavior of the kind seen in simple programs is not restricted to discrete systems: some fairly simple partial differential equations, found by searching, produce highly complex patterns, even with apparently discrete patches.
claims.quote: we now know that the same kind of behavior can also occur in completely continuous systems such as partial differential equations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Complexity is not rarer in continuous systems, only harder to detect
