claims.statement: Complexity is probably not fundamentally rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones; it was much easier to discover in discrete systems because they can be studied directly by computer experiment without approximation artifacts.
claims.quote: Probably complexity is not in any fundamental sense rarer in continuous systems than in discrete ones. But the point is that discrete systems can typically be investigated in a much more direct way than continuous ones.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Phenomena seen in discrete simple programs also occur in simple continuous systems
claims.statement: Essentially all of the phenomena observed in discrete simple programs can also be found in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
claims.quote: I suspect that essentially all of the various phenomena that we have observed in discrete systems in the past several chapters can in fact also be found even in continuous systems with fairly simple rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 4: Systems Based on Numbers

claims.label: Adding dimensions does not fundamentally change the occurrence of complexity
claims.statement: Contrary to what traditional science suggests, going from one to two or more dimensions produces some specific new effects but does not fundamentally change the overall behavior or the occurrence of complexity in simple programs.
claims.quote: adding more dimensions does not ultimately seem to have much effect on the occurrence of behavior of any significant complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Slices of 2D cellular automata resemble 1D cellular automata
claims.statement: The complexity inside patterns generated by two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata is very similar to that of one-dimensional cellular automata: a one-dimensional slice through the 2D pattern evolves much like an ordinary 1D cellular automaton.
claims.quote: if one looks at the evolution of a one-dimensional slice through each two-dimensional pattern the results one gets are strikingly similar to what we have seen in ordinary one-dimensional cellular automata.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles
claims.statement: Some simple two-dimensional cellular automata on a square grid grow patterns whose overall shape closely approximates a perfect circle, despite the grid's square symmetry.
claims.quote: it is even possible to find cellular automata that yield overall shapes that closely approximate perfect circles.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors
claims.statement: A simple 2D cellular automaton (a cell turns black when exactly three of its eight neighbors are black, otherwise unchanged) can grow patterns whose overall shapes keep changing with no simple form, so complexity can appear in a pattern's overall shape as well as in its interior.
claims.quote: there can be great complexity not only in the detailed arrangement of black and white cells in a two-dimensional cellular automaton pattern, but also in the overall shape of the pattern.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Three-dimensional cellular automata show the same basic kinds of behavior
claims.statement: Three-dimensional cellular automata show some new specific phenomena but the same basic kinds of behavior as one- and two-dimensional ones, so the phenomenon of complexity does not depend crucially on dimensionality.
claims.quote: But overall it seems that the basic kinds of behavior produced are just the same as in one and two dimensions.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Complex behavior in 2D Turing machines is as rare as in 1D
claims.statement: Two-dimensional Turing machines behave much like one-dimensional ones: with two or three head states only repetitive and nested behavior normally occurs, and with four states complex behavior is possible but rare (a few rules per million).
claims.quote: For Turing machines with two or three possible states, only repetitive and nested behavior normally seem to occur. With four states, more complex behavior is possible, but it is still rather rare.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Neighbor-independent geometric replacement rules always give nested fractals
claims.statement: Substitution systems and geometric replacement rules in which each element is replaced independently of other elements, including those of traditional fractal geometry, inevitably produce purely nested patterns.
claims.quote: with this kind of setup, it is ultimately inevitable that all the patterns produced must have a completely regular nested structure.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Fractal geometry misses complexity by excluding interactions between elements
claims.statement: Traditional fractal geometry does not consider interactions between elements, which is why all patterns it produces are purely nested; allowing replacements to depend on neighbors on a grid readily yields complicated, non-nested patterns.
claims.quote: in traditional fractal geometry the idea of interaction between elements is not considered—so that all patterns that are produced have a purely nested form.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Networks of identical two-connection nodes can form arrays of any dimension
claims.statement: Networks in which every node is identical and has exactly two outgoing connections can, purely by the pattern of connections, form structures equivalent to arrays of any number of dimensions, as well as trees and nested structures.
claims.quote: using the same principles an array with any number of dimensions can easily be obtained.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Network rules depending on distance-two neighborhoods can give random growth
claims.statement: Network systems whose rewiring rules depend only on whether a node's two connections lead to the same node always grow in an essentially repetitive way, but when rules depend on nodes up to two connections away, even the number of nodes can vary in an apparently random way (in about one in 10,000 rules).
claims.quote: even the total number of nodes at each step can vary in a way that seems in many respects completely random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Network systems may underlie the structure of space and spacetime
claims.statement: Some network systems will likely turn out to be closely related to the basic structure of space and spacetime in our universe.
claims.quote: I suspect that some of these systems will in the end turn out to be closely related to the basic structure of space and spacetime in our universe.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Most multiway systems grow exponentially or not at all
claims.statement: Most multiway systems (which keep all sequences produced by all possible replacements at each step) either grow exponentially fast or do not grow at all; slow growth is rare.
claims.quote: most either grow exponentially quickly, or not at all; slow growth of the kind seen on the facing page is rather rare.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Slowly growing multiway systems eventually become repetitive
claims.statement: Even when slowly growing multiway systems show early apparent randomness in their state counts, they typically end up showing some form of repetition (sometimes with long periods, such as 1071 steps).
claims.quote: even when such growth leads to a certain amount of apparent randomness it typically in the end seems to exhibit some form of repetition.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Multiway systems build their own network of connections in time
claims.statement: Because each sequence in a multiway system always leads to the same successors, the evolution can be represented as a network of which state leads to which, so multiway systems build up their own, often complicated, pattern of connections in time.
claims.quote: multiway systems can in effect build up their own pattern of connections in time—and this pattern can often be quite complicated.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern
claims.statement: In one dimension, any set of local constraints on cell colors that can be satisfied at all can be satisfied by a simple, purely repetitive arrangement, so simple 1D constraints cannot force complex patterns.
claims.quote: in one dimension it is possible to prove that any local set of constraints that can be satisfied at all can always be satisfied by some simple and purely repetitive arrangement of colors.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: All satisfiable 2D nearest-neighbor template constraints allow repetitive patterns
claims.statement: Of all 4,294,967,296 two-dimensional constraints defined by allowed templates of a cell and its four neighbors, 766,979,044 cannot be satisfied, and every one of the rest can be satisfied by a repetitive pattern, with 171 repetitive patterns sufficing for all.
claims.quote: among the 3,527,988,252 that remain, it turns out that every single one can be satisfied by a simple repetitive pattern.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Constraint systems require going outside the system to find their patterns
claims.statement: Unlike rule-based systems, which can be run directly, systems defined by constraints offer no direct procedure for finding the patterns they allow; one must search from outside the system, which can take enormous computational effort.
claims.quote: But in a system that is based on constraints, there is no such direct procedure, and instead one must in effect always go outside of the system to work out what patterns can occur.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: The simplest constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern forces a nested one
claims.statement: Among 2D template constraints that also require one template to appear somewhere, systematic search over more than 18 million constraints finds that the first constraint forcing a non-repetitive pattern (number 18762389) forces a unique nested pattern.
claims.quote: after examining more than 18 million of them, one finally discovers the system shown on the facing page. And in this system, unlike all others before it, no repetitive pattern is possible; the only pattern that satisfies the constraint is the non-repetitive nested pattern shown in the picture.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: No tested simple template constraint forces more than nested behavior
claims.statement: Of the 137,438,953,472 template constraints with a required-template condition, none of the millions tested forces anything more complicated than nested behavior.
claims.quote: of the millions of these that I have tested, none have forced anything more complicated than the kind of nested behavior seen on the previous page.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: 3x3 template constraints can force a rule 30–like random pattern
claims.statement: Constraints on 3×3 blocks of cells can be constructed to force complex patterns: a set of 56 allowed templates forces a unique, largely random pattern equivalent to the evolution of the rule 30 cellular automaton.
claims.quote: a system with 56 allowed templates in which the only pattern satisfying the constraint is a complex and largely random one, derived from the rule 30 cellular automaton.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Simple constraints rarely force complex behavior, unlike simple rules
claims.statement: Unlike simple evolution rules, almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns; complex behavior forced by constraints is rare.
claims.quote: it seems that almost all simple constraints lead only to fairly simple patterns.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Constraint-like equations helped hide complexity from traditional science
claims.statement: Because describing complex behavior with constraints requires fairly complicated constraints, the traditional focus of science and mathematics on equations that act like constraints is another reason they failed to identify the phenomenon of complexity.
claims.quote: the fact that traditional science and mathematics tends to concentrate on equations that operate like constraints provides yet another reason for their failure to identify the fundamental phenomenon of complexity that I discuss in this book.
claims.chapter: Ch. 5: Two Dimensions and Beyond

claims.label: Simple systems self-organize from random initial conditions
claims.statement: Many simple-rule systems such as cellular automata, when started from completely random initial conditions, spontaneously organize themselves and produce behavior with many distinctly non-random features.
claims.quote: many systems spontaneously tend to organize themselves, so that even with completely random initial conditions they end up producing behavior that has many features that are not at all random.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Cellular automaton behavior falls into four basic classes
claims.statement: Despite differing in detail for almost every rule, the patterns produced by cellular automata of all kinds from random initial conditions can almost always be easily assigned to one of just four classes: uniform final state (class 1), simple stable or periodic structures (class 2), apparently random behavior (class 3), and interacting localized structures (class 4).
claims.quote: among all kinds of cellular automata, it seems that the patterns which arise can almost always be assigned quite easily to one of just four basic classes illustrated below.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Class 4 consists of simple localized structures interacting in complex ways
claims.statement: Class 4 cellular automata mix order and randomness: they produce localized structures that are individually fairly simple, but which move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.
claims.quote: class 4 involves a mixture of order and randomness: localized structures are produced which on their own are fairly simple, but these structures move around and interact with each other in very complicated ways.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Detailed cellular automaton properties correlate with the four classes
claims.statement: Most detailed properties of cellular automata correlate closely with the four visually defined classes, so that knowing a cellular automaton's class is often enough to predict its detailed properties.
claims.quote: most of these properties were closely correlated with the classes that I had already identified. Indeed, in trying to predict detailed properties of a particular cellular automaton, it was often enough just to know what class the cellular automaton was in.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: A cellular automaton's class usually cannot be read off its rule
claims.statement: For most cellular automata there is no easy way to determine from the underlying rule which class of behavior it will produce; one generally has to run it and see, though some rule forms can be shown to give only class 1 or 2 behavior.
claims.quote: In most cases there is no easy way to do this, and in fact there is little choice but just to run the cellular automaton and see what it does.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Class 4 lies between class 2 and class 3 in activity
claims.statement: Although class 4 is the most complex in appearance, in terms of overall activity it is intermediate between class 2 and class 3, and in sequences of rules it commonly appears at the transition between class 2 and class 3 rules.
claims.quote: Class 4 systems are then in the middle: for the activity that they show neither dies out completely, as in class 2, nor remains at the high level seen in class 3.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Continuous cellular automata show the same four classes
claims.statement: Cellular automata whose cells take continuous gray-level values show essentially the same four classes of behavior as discrete cellular automata, with class 4 behavior and its discrete localized structures typically appearing at transitions as the rule parameter is varied.
claims.quote: But it seems that this behavior falls into essentially the same four classes that we have already seen in ordinary cellular automata.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Two-dimensional cellular automata show the same four classes
claims.statement: Two-dimensional cellular automata exhibit the same four classes of behavior as one-dimensional ones, which becomes evident when one-dimensional slices through their evolution are examined; class 4 behavior, as in the Game of Life, occurs even on a white background with slightly more complicated rules.
claims.quote: Indeed, by looking at such slices one can readily identify the very same four classes of behavior as in one-dimensional cellular automata.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: The four classes respond differently to small changes in initial conditions
claims.statement: Changing one cell of the initial condition has characteristically different effects by class: in class 1 the change dies out, in class 2 it stays localized, in class 3 it spreads at a uniform rate to affect the whole system, and in class 4 it spreads only sporadically.
claims.quote: In class 1, changes always die out, and in fact exactly the same final state is reached regardless of what initial conditions were used. In class 2, changes may persist, but they always remain localized in a small region of the system.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Natural systems can be understood by how they handle information
claims.statement: Some of the most important features of natural systems can often be understood just by identifying which cellular automaton class their handling of information (forgetting, localized retention, long-range communication) corresponds to.
claims.quote: it is often possible to understand some of the most important features of systems that occur in nature just by looking at how their handling of information corresponds to what we have seen in the basic classes of systems that we have identified here.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Class 2 repetitiveness stems from lack of long-range communication
claims.statement: Class 2 cellular automata are always eventually repetitive because their lack of long-range communication makes each part behave as an independent system of limited size, typically only a few cells across, and hence with short repetition periods.
claims.quote: the absence of long-range communication effectively forces each part of a class 2 system to behave as if it were a system of limited size.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat
claims.statement: Any system of limited size made of discrete elements and following definite rules must eventually exhibit repetitive behavior, with repetition period at most equal to its total number of possible states.
claims.quote: it is then a general result that any system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules must always eventually exhibit repetitive behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Repetition periods of class 3 rules grow rapidly with system size
claims.statement: In cellular automata on a finite cyclic lattice, a rapid increase of repetition period with lattice size is characteristic of class 3 behavior, with large fluctuations as size changes; among elementary rules only rule 45 appears to give periods always near the maximum possible.
claims.quote: In general, a rapid increase with size is characteristic of class 3 behavior. Of the elementary rules, however, only rule 45 seems to yield periods that always stay close to the maximum of 2^n.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions
claims.statement: The randomness of class 3 systems is not merely inherited from random initial conditions: random behavior can be generated even when the initial conditions contain no randomness at all.
claims.quote: the crucial point that I discovered only some time later is that random behavior can also occur even when there is no randomness in initial conditions.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Additive rule 90 only transmits randomness from its initial conditions
claims.statement: Because rule 90 is additive, its patterns are superpositions of the single-cell nested pattern, so it cannot generate randomness intrinsically; any randomness it shows comes from the initial conditions, and deviations such as a low initial density persist forever, unlike in rule 22.
claims.quote: In rule 22 the low initial density has no long-term effect. But in rule 90 its effect continues forever.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Intrinsic randomness generation makes large-scale behavior stable
claims.statement: Systems that intrinsically generate randomness, like rule 22 or rule 30, produce the same overall random behavior with the same large-scale properties whatever their initial conditions, giving them a fundamental stability that he says underlies the apparent stability of many systems in nature.
claims.quote: By intrinsically generating randomness such systems in a sense have a certain fundamental stability: for whatever is done to their initial conditions, they still give the same overall random behavior, with the same large-scale properties.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Spatially periodic initial conditions always give repetitive behavior
claims.statement: In any cellular automaton, an initial condition consisting of a fixed block of n cells repeated forever leads to repetitive behavior with period at most 2^n, since each block evolves like a finite cyclic system.
claims.quote: in any cellular automaton it is inevitable that initial conditions which consist just of a fixed block of cells repeated forever will lead to simple repetitive behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Special initial conditions often make one cellular automaton emulate another
claims.statement: It is common for a cellular automaton to have special initial conditions under which it behaves exactly like some other cellular automaton; for example rule 126 behaves like rule 90 when started from paired-cell blocks, and class 3 rules can thereby act like class 2 rules.
claims.quote: it turns out to be quite common for there to exist special initial conditions for one cellular automaton that make it behave just like some other cellular automaton.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Nested patterns arise from rules that emulate themselves
claims.statement: A cellular automaton whose blocks of cells evolve by the same rule as individual cells must produce patterns that are either essentially uniform or nested; this self-emulation is why rule 90 and rules that emulate it produce nested patterns.
claims.quote: And this can be achieved in only two ways: either the pattern must be essentially uniform, or it must have a nested structure—just like we see in rule 90.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Additive rules self-emulate; rules 90 and 150 are the only elementary ones
claims.statement: Every additive cellular automaton rule can emulate itself and therefore yields nested patterns, and among two-color nearest-neighbor rules the only fundamentally different additive rules are rules 90 and 150; self-emulation is otherwise rare, though non-additive examples such as rule 184 exist.
claims.quote: one can show that any rule that is additive will be able to emulate itself and will thus yield nested patterns. But there are rather few additive rules, and indeed with two colors and nearest neighbors the only fundamentally different ones are precisely rules 90 and 150.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Allowed-sequence networks grow fast for class 3 and 4, slowly for 1 and 2
claims.statement: As cellular automata evolve, the set of cell sequences that can occur generally becomes progressively restricted; the finite networks describing these sets stay simple (about t^2 nodes after t steps) for class 1 and 2 rules but grow at least exponentially for most class 3 and 4 rules, apart from surjective rules started from all possible sequences.
claims.quote: Indeed, this kind of rapid increase in network complexity is a general characteristic of most class 3 and 4 rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Class 4 systems always have structures that persist forever
claims.statement: A crucial feature of any class 4 cellular automaton is that, although most structures that form eventually die out, there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.
claims.quote: Most of these structures eventually die out, sometimes in rather complicated ways. But a crucial feature of any class 4 systems is that there must always be certain structures that can persist forever in it.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Complicated persistent structures imply moving structures exist
claims.statement: In class 4 cellular automata, whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found; moving structures are what allow information to travel and complex class 4 behavior to occur.
claims.quote: My experience with many different rules is that whenever sufficiently complicated persistent structures occur, structures that move can eventually be found.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Class 4 automata can mimic many other systems
claims.statement: Class 4 cellular automata can, with appropriate initial conditions, mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems, including producing unbounded growth of either complex or very simple form.
claims.quote: it is a general feature of class 4 cellular automata that with appropriate initial conditions they can mimic the behavior of all sorts of other systems.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Interactions among simple structures in rule 110 give immense complexity
claims.statement: Although individual persistent structures in class 4 systems such as rule 110 behave fairly repetitively, collisions between them can produce cascades of new structures and outcomes that take very many steps to resolve, yielding behavior of immense complexity from an extremely simple rule.
claims.quote: So even though the individual structures in class 4 systems like rule 110 may behave in fairly repetitive ways, interactions between these structures can lead to behavior of immense complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 6: Starting from Randomness

claims.label: Universal behavior types span simple programs and natural systems
claims.statement: The same kinds of overall behavior arise regardless of the details of underlying rules, and this universality holds not only among simple programs but also between simple programs and systems in nature, so idealized cell models and real molecular systems should show the same universal features.
claims.quote: And the crucial point is that I believe that this universality extends not only across simple programs, but also to systems in nature.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Just three basic mechanisms account for randomness
claims.statement: Apparent randomness in any system arises from one of just three basic mechanisms: continual random input from the environment, randomness transcribed from initial conditions, or intrinsic generation of randomness by the system's own rules with no random input.
claims.quote: But from my investigations of simple programs I have come to the conclusion that one can in fact identify just three basic mechanisms for randomness, as illustrated in the pictures below.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Intrinsic randomness generation explains most randomness in nature
claims.statement: The mechanism in which a system's own deterministic rules generate randomness without any random input is ultimately responsible for a large fraction, and perhaps essentially all, of the randomness seen in the natural world.
claims.quote: I believe that this mechanism is in fact ultimately responsible for a large fraction, if not essentially all, of the randomness that we see in the natural world.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Hardware noise-based random generators deviate from perfect randomness
claims.statement: Devices that generate randomness by amplifying microscopic environmental noise (spark gaps, vacuum tubes, semiconductor diodes) have consistently been found to produce output with significant deviations from perfect randomness, because the sampling device relaxes only gradually and because the environment itself has correlations.
claims.quote: But despite such sensitivity to microscopic effects, what has consistently been found in practice is that the output from such devices has significant deviations from perfect randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Randomness from initial conditions lasts only a limited number of steps
claims.statement: In physical chaotic systems such as kneading, mirror arrangements or pegboards, randomness can be attributed purely to initial conditions only for a small number of steps (around ten collisions for a pegboard), because amplification quickly reaches atomic scales and environmental perturbations take over; the limit is set by the separation between observed large-scale and uncontrollable small-scale features.
claims.quote: So the idea that randomness comes purely from initial conditions can be realistic only for a fairly small number of steps; randomness which is seen after that must therefore typically be attributed to other mechanisms.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Solar system motion should show sensitive dependence over millions of years
claims.statement: Although planetary motion looks regular on human timescales, sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur in the solar system, producing significant randomness over a few million years that may explain some present-day features of the solar system.
claims.quote: But calculations imply that sensitive dependence on initial conditions should ultimately occur even in our solar system.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Maximal-period linear congruential generators still show strong nonrandomness
claims.statement: Linear congruential random number generators designed to have maximal repetition period have repeatedly turned out to deviate substantially from perfect randomness (for example, successive outputs plotted as points fall on regular stripes), because the mathematical tractability that guarantees their period also implies regularity.
claims.quote: But in practice over the years, one after another linear congruential generator that has been constructed to have maximal repetition period has turned out to exhibit very substantial deviations from perfect randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Amenability to mathematical analysis implies deviations from randomness
claims.statement: The very possibility of detailed mathematical analysis of a system tends to imply that its output has at least some deviations from perfect randomness, whereas simple rules not constrained by the need for such analysis can generate highly random behavior.
claims.quote: the very possibility of any detailed mathematical analysis tends to imply the presence of at least some deviations from perfect randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Rapid production of much randomness indicates intrinsic generation
claims.statement: Whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be responsible, because it uses every component of a system to produce new randomness and has no length limit, whereas environmental amplification is slow and initial-condition randomness is short-lived.
claims.quote: The basic answer, I believe, is that whenever a large amount of randomness is produced in a short time, intrinsic randomness generation is overwhelmingly likely to be the mechanism responsible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Intrinsically generated randomness is repeatable across experimental runs
claims.statement: If randomness in an experiment comes from intrinsic generation, then even the precise details of the random-looking behavior should be repeatable from one run to the next, because such behavior is robust to perturbations below a critical size, whereas randomness from the environment or from initial conditions should show little or no repeatability.
claims.quote: But what is remarkable is that if intrinsic randomness generation is the mechanism at work, then the precise details of the behavior can also be repeatable.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Detailed visual similarities in organisms imply intrinsic randomness
claims.statement: Detailed visual similarities between members of the same species, and between the two symmetric sides of a system, in features that look complex and random cannot be attributed to environmental or initial-condition randomness and must come from intrinsic randomness generation.
claims.quote: And instead, there is no choice but to conclude that the randomness must in fact come from the mechanism of intrinsic randomness generation that I have discovered in simple programs, and discussed in this section.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Randomness lets discrete components produce continuous behavior
claims.statement: Systems made of discrete components appear smooth and continuous on large scales mainly because microscopic randomness averages out the discreteness, and it does not matter whether that randomness comes from outside or from intrinsic generation, as shown by random walks, aggregation models and deterministic cellular automata that grow circular shapes.
claims.quote: But it turns out that all that really seems to matter is that randomness is present: the mechanism through which it arises appears to be largely irrelevant.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Continuity requires slow features relative to small-scale random changes
claims.statement: Continuous large-scale behavior can arise in a system with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes; for growth, the random small-scale changes must occur much faster than the overall growth.
claims.quote: In general the point is that continuous behavior can arise in systems with discrete components only when there are features that evolve slowly relative to the rate of small-scale random changes.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Density-driven discrete transitions are rare in 1D CAs, common in higher dimensions
claims.statement: Cellular automata in which a continuous change in initial density of black cells produces a discrete switch in long-time behavior, with whichever color was initially more common taking over the whole system, are fairly rare in one dimension, where domain boundaries often get stuck, but become increasingly common in two and more dimensions.
claims.quote: And so long as the boundaries of the regions do not get stuck—as happens in many one-dimensional cellular automata—the result is that whichever color was initially more common eventually takes over the whole system.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Continuous rules can yield discrete behavior, so discrete models often fit
claims.statement: Even systems governed by continuous equations, such as certain chemical reaction kinetics, commonly have a limited number of stable states with discrete transitions between them, and because discrete overall behavior is often a system's most obvious feature, discrete models like cellular automata are often the most appropriate.
claims.quote: And in fact it is quite common for such behavior to be one of the most obvious features of a system—which is why discrete systems like cellular automata end up often being the most appropriate models.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Complex natural behavior is almost never best explained by constraints
claims.statement: Almost none of the complex behavior seen in nature is best explained as the satisfaction of constraints, because finding a pattern that satisfies a constraint is usually far too difficult a computation to happen routinely in nature; explicit processes of evolution are the more plausible explanation.
claims.quote: But despite this, my strong suspicion is that of all the examples of complex behavior that we see in nature almost none can in the end best be explained in terms of constraints.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Local-improvement procedures get stuck when satisfying discrete constraints
claims.statement: For discrete constraint systems the landscape of constraint violations is almost always jagged, so iterative procedures that only move downhill almost invariably get stuck far from a solution, random modifications help only slowly, and no speed-up techniques work well across broad classes of systems; hence natural systems are unlikely to come close to satisfying such constraints.
claims.quote: So what this suggests is that even if in some idealized sense a system in nature might be expected to satisfy certain constraints, it is likely that in practice the system will actually not have a way to come even close to doing this.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Pushed or jiggled spheres do not reach densest packing
claims.statement: Unlike identical coins in two dimensions, which readily form the densest hexagonal packing when pushed together, balls in three dimensions pushed together or jiggled almost always get stuck and essentially never reach the densest repetitive packing, which seems obtainable only by careful one-by-one placement.
claims.quote: But if one just tries pushing balls together they almost always get stuck, and never take on anything like the arrangement shown.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Complex biological forms come from growth rules, not selection-driven constraints
claims.statement: Natural selection can produce forms determined by constraint satisfaction only when those forms are rather simple; complex biological forms are associated instead with explicit evolution rules, mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.
claims.quote: when more complex forms are seen they once again tend to be associated not with constraints but rather with the effects of explicit evolution rules—mostly those governing the growth of an individual organism.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Rule complexity does not determine behavioral complexity
claims.statement: There is no direct correspondence between the complexity of a system's underlying rules and the complexity of its behavior: some of the simplest rules yield highly complex behavior, fairly complicated rules often yield simple behavior, and rules differing at a single position can behave very differently.
claims.quote: Traditional intuition might have made one assume that there must be a direct correspondence between the complexity of observed behavior and the complexity of underlying rules. But one of the central discoveries of this book is that in fact there is not.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Nesting in nature mostly arises from building up, not splitting down
claims.statement: Nested patterns can arise either from elements splitting or branching into smaller ones or from larger elements being built up from smaller ones (as in additive cellular automata), and the building-up route is probably the more common origin of nesting in nature.
claims.quote: it can also arise when larger elements are built up from smaller ones—and indeed I suspect that this is its more common origin in nature.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Merging of independently growing domains generically produces nesting
claims.statement: Nesting can arise from random initial conditions through progressive annihilation of randomly placed elements: in essentially any system where domains grow fairly independently and then progressively merge, an overall nested pattern resembling a river-tributary tree forms, even when domain boundaries move as random walks.
claims.quote: And indeed in essentially any system where there are domains that grow fairly independently and then progressively merge the same basic overall nesting will be seen.
claims.chapter: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

claims.label: Models of complex systems should first be judged by comparing overall pictures
claims.statement: For systems with complex behavior, a model cannot be adequately assessed by matching a few extracted numbers; the best first test is a visual comparison of the model's overall behavior with that of the real system.
claims.quote: by far the best first step in assessing a model is not to look at numbers or other details, but rather just to use one's eyes, and to compare overall pictures of a system with pictures from the model.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Snowflake shapes arise from growth inhibition captured by a hexagonal cellular automaton
claims.statement: The main features of snowflake shapes are reproduced by a hexagonal cellular automaton in which a cell becomes ice only if exactly one neighbor is ice, which represents the inhibition of nearby growth by released latent heat.
claims.quote: One can capture this basic effect by having a cellular automaton with rules in which cells become black if they have exactly one black neighbor, but stay white whenever they have more than one black neighbor.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Growing snowflakes should alternate between tree-like and faceted shapes
claims.statement: During the growth of an individual snowflake its shape should alternate between tree-like and faceted forms, as new branches grow and then collide with one another.
claims.quote: one expects that during the growth of a particular snowflake there should be alternation between tree-like and faceted shapes, as new branches grow but then collide with each other.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Randomness in crystal shapes is often intrinsically generated by simple growth rules
claims.statement: Apparent randomness in the shapes of crystalline materials often arises intrinsically from simple deterministic growth rules, rather than from randomness in the seed or the growth environment.
claims.quote: And contrary to what has always been assumed, I suspect that this is actually how the apparent randomness that one sometimes sees in shapes formed by crystalline materials often comes about.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Randomness of fracture surfaces comes from a material-independent intrinsic mechanism
claims.statement: The roughness and randomness of fracture paths does not come from random irregularities in a material but from a general mechanism in which deterministic interactions of element displacements around a moving crack intrinsically generate randomness, as in a simple cellular automaton model.
claims.quote: I nevertheless suspect that even when much more realistic models for specific materials are used, the fundamental mechanisms responsible for randomness will still be very much the same as in the extremely simple model shown here.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Conservation plus microscopic randomness yields universal fluid behavior
claims.statement: Any system of particles that conserves quantities such as particle number and momentum and has sufficient microscopic randomness will show the same large-scale fluid behavior, so a discrete cellular automaton particle model can reproduce the flow of real fluids.
claims.quote: so long as certain physical quantities such as particle number and momentum are conserved, then whenever there is sufficient microscopic randomness, it is almost inevitable that the same overall fluid behavior will be obtained.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Large-scale fluid flow shows little sensitive dependence on initial conditions
claims.statement: In almost all cases, large-scale fluid behavior does not depend discernibly on the detailed initial conditions; small perturbations are damped out by viscosity, so sensitive dependence (chaos) is the exception rather than the rule.
claims.quote: when it comes to large-scale fluid behavior, it seems to be true that in almost all cases there is no discernible difference between what happens with different detailed initial conditions.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Turbulent randomness is intrinsically generated at the level of large-scale fluid motion
claims.statement: The randomness seen in turbulent fluids is mostly neither inserted from outside nor inherited from molecular randomness, but is intrinsically generated by the dynamics of the large-scale fluid motion itself.
claims.quote: Instead, what seems to be happening is that intrinsic randomness generation occurs directly at the level of large-scale fluid motion.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Random-looking yet repeatable fluid flows should be producible
claims.statement: Because turbulent randomness is generated intrinsically by large-scale motion, carefully prepared experiments should produce fluid flows that look random yet are essentially the same on every repeated run.
claims.quote: with sufficiently careful preparation it should be possible to produce patterns of flow that seem quite random but that are nevertheless effectively repeatable—so that they look essentially the same on every successive run of an experiment.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Evolution cannot have found optimal solutions to complex fitness constraints
claims.statement: Since iterative random search converges only for simple constraints, the roughly trillion generations of life on Earth are insufficient to find optimal solutions to complex constraints, so most features of organisms are merely good-enough solutions rather than optima.
claims.quote: it is still completely implausible that the trillion or so generations of organisms since the beginning of life on Earth would be sufficient to allow optimal solutions to be found to constraints of any significant complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Most biological complexity comes from randomly chosen programs, not natural selection
claims.statement: Most of the complexity seen in biological organisms originates from the abstract fact that many randomly chosen programs produce complex behavior, rather than from adaptation or careful optimization by natural selection.
claims.quote: the vast majority of the complexity we see in biological systems actually has its origin in the purely abstract fact that among randomly chosen programs many give rise to complex behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Complexity of individual organism parts has been roughly constant for eons
claims.statement: The complexity of individual parts of organisms, such as textures and other morphological features, was already present in early fossils and has not changed much in at least several hundred million years.
claims.quote: there is every indication that the level of complexity of individual parts of organisms has not changed much in at least several hundred million years.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Genetic programs for complex pigment patterns are short
claims.statement: The genetic programs that generate patterns such as those on mollusc shells are short, as indicated by the large variety of patterns within species, and molecular biology should be able to isolate them and confirm their brevity.
claims.quote: Modern molecular biology should soon be able to isolate the specific programs responsible, say, for the patterns on mollusc shells, and see explicitly how long they are. But there are already indications that these programs are quite short.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Natural selection works meaningfully only on simple behavior
claims.statement: The power of natural selection is limited: it can systematically optimize only systems or parts of systems whose behavior is simple, and achieves very little when behavior is complex.
claims.quote: what I suspect is that in the end natural selection can only operate in a meaningful way on systems or parts of systems whose behavior is in some sense quite simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Natural selection makes organisms simpler and more engineering-like
claims.statement: Rather than generating complexity, the main effect of natural selection is to make biological systems avoid complexity, favoring simple, somewhat independent components with smoothly adjustable properties, as in engineered systems.
claims.quote: my strong suspicion is that in fact the main effect of natural selection is almost exactly the opposite: it tends to make biological systems avoid complexity, and be more like systems in engineering.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Features that change fastest between species are the most complex
claims.statement: Among related species, the features that differ most rapidly (such as pigmentation and texture patterns) are the ones that show the most obvious complexity, while features under natural selection stay nearly constant.
claims.quote: it is almost always those features which change most rapidly between species that show the most obvious signs of complexity.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Convergent structures recur because they are common among programs, not optimal
claims.statement: When similar complex structures arise independently in very different organisms, this is because those structures are common outputs of programs of certain kinds, not because they are optimal.
claims.quote: the reason certain structures appear repeatedly is just that they are somehow common among programs of certain kinds
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Natural selection does not inherently drive organisms toward more elaborate structure
claims.statement: Natural selection does not inevitably produce progressively more elaborate organisms; increases in complexity in the fossil record come from random mutations that add features without fatal flaws, while selection's systematic effect is to simplify.
claims.quote: It is certainly not the case—as is often assumed—that natural selection somehow inevitably leads to organisms with progressively more elaborate structures and progressively larger numbers of parts.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Plant branching patterns come from simple substitution-system growth rules
claims.statement: The overall branching patterns of plants, from algae to ferns to trees and flowering plants, are produced by simple growth rules in which each stem tip repeatedly splits into smaller copies of itself at fixed relative lengths and angles.
claims.quote: And no doubt it is from such simple rules of growth that most such overall branching patterns come.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Leaf shapes arise from the same simple branching process as whole plants
claims.statement: The shapes of leaves, from smooth to prickly to irregular, are produced by the same simple branching growth process that governs overall plant forms, and small changes in its parameters can change leaf shape greatly.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that in fact the very same simple process of branching is ultimately responsible both for the overall forms of plants, and for the shapes of their leaves.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: The 137.5° phyllotaxis angle results from a simple inhibition growth process
claims.statement: The near-universal 137.5° (golden-ratio) angle between successive plant organs is not an optimization found by natural selection but the inevitable result of a simple process where each new element forms where a chemical concentration is highest and depletes it nearby.
claims.quote: And instead what I strongly suspect is that the patterns are just inevitable consequences of a rather simple process of growth not unlike one that was already discussed, at least in general terms, nearly a century ago.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Simple growth-rate models generate essentially all mollusc shell shapes
claims.statement: Mollusc shell shapes result from secreting material at different rates around the shell opening, and essentially every form produced by a simple growth model with a few parameters is found in some real mollusc.
claims.quote: The remarkable fact illustrated on the next page is that essentially all of them are found in some kind of mollusc or another.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Animal embryos develop hierarchically because of a fixed length scale
claims.statement: Because regions of tissue a few tenths of a millimeter across subdivide into regions using different sections of the genetic program (controlled by chemical gradients and homeobox genes), embryos necessarily develop hierarchically, e.g. a leg region before a foot region.
claims.quote: The existence of a fixed length scale at which such processes occur then almost inevitably implies that an embryo must develop in a somewhat hierarchical fashion.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Shape differences between related animals come from differing growth rates
claims.statement: Differences in shape among related animals are largely due to different patterns of relative growth rates of their parts, so their shapes are related by simple smooth geometric transformations.
claims.quote: differences between the shapes and forms of animals may often be due in large part merely to different patterns in the rates of growth for their different parts.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Diversity of plant and animal forms comes from different simple rules
claims.statement: Most of the diversity and complexity in the forms of plants and animals arises because slightly different, essentially randomly picked simple growth rules lead to very different and often complex behavior.
claims.quote: it is this basic phenomenon that I suspect is responsible for most of the diversity and complexity that we see in the forms of plants and animals.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Mollusc shell pigment patterns are generated like one-dimensional cellular automata
claims.statement: Pigmentation patterns on mollusc shells are produced line by line by pigment-secreting elements whose new states depend on neighbors' previous states, so the range of shell patterns closely matches the patterns of the simplest symmetric one-dimensional cellular automata.
claims.quote: comparing the patterns in these pictures with patterns on actual mollusc shells, one notices the remarkable fact that the range of patterns that occur in the two cases is extremely similar.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Mollusc shell pattern rules are effectively random, not optimized
claims.statement: The rules generating mollusc shell patterns are effectively chosen at random from the simplest possibilities rather than optimized against predators or for mates, as shown by many species whose patterns are hidden by opaque skin throughout life.
claims.quote: these patterns are instead generated by rules that are in effect chosen at random from among a collection of the simplest possibilities.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Animal coat patterns arise from local activation and longer-range inhibition rules
claims.statement: The few recurring kinds of animal pigmentation patterns (spots, labyrinths, stripes) are produced by a simple rule in which each element tends to match the average color of nearby elements and oppose that of elements further away, as in a two-dimensional cellular automaton.
claims.quote: The idea is that when a pattern forms, the color of each element will tend to be the same as the average color of nearby elements, and opposite to the average color of elements further away.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Short-timescale market randomness comes from internal market dynamics
claims.statement: Much of the apparent randomness in financial prices, especially on timescales of minutes or seconds, is generated by the internal dynamics of trading entities interacting with one another, not by external news or changes in the value of the asset.
claims.quote: particularly on short timescales much of the randomness that one sees is purely a consequence of internal dynamics in the market, and has little if anything to do with the nature or value of what is being traded.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: Simple cellular automaton markets generate random-looking price series
claims.statement: In a market modelled as a one-dimensional cellular automaton of buy/sell agents reacting to neighbors, any rule that lets information eventually propagate to all agents makes the running buy-minus-sell total show significant randomness.
claims.quote: as soon as the underlying rule for the cellular automaton is such that information will eventually propagate from one entity to all others—in effect a minimal version of an efficient market hypothesis—it is essentially inevitable that running totals of numbers of cells will exhibit significant randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 8: Implications for Everyday Systems

claims.label: A very simple program may underlie all of physics
claims.statement: Underneath the known laws of physics there may be a single very simple program from which all known laws, and all the complexity of the universe, emerge.
claims.quote: Underneath the laws of physics as we know them today it could be that there lies a very simple program from which all the known laws—and ultimately all the complexity we see in the universe—emerges.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Reversible rules are rare among cellular automata
claims.statement: Reversibility is rare among simple cellular automaton rules: only 6 of the 256 elementary two-color nearest-neighbor rules are reversible, and only 1800 of the 7,625,597,484,987 three-color nearest-neighbor rules are.
claims.quote: There are a total of 7,625,597,484,987 cellular automata with three colors and nearest-neighbor rules, and searching through these one finds just 1800 that are reversible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Reversible systems can behave as complexly as any other
claims.statement: Although only a tiny fraction of possible rules are reversible, reversible cellular automata can still produce behavior, including apparent randomness and localized structures, as complex as that of non-reversible systems.
claims.quote: So in the end it seems that even though only a very small fraction of possible systems have the property of being reversible, such systems can still exhibit behavior just as complex as one sees anywhere else.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Second Law holds because experiments cannot prepare randomness-decreasing states
claims.statement: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is observed to hold because practical experiments can only set up initial conditions that are simple to describe and construct, and finding initial conditions of a reversible system that would lead to decreasing randomness requires computation as great as the system's own evolution.
claims.quote: The consequence of this is that no reasonable experiment can ever involve setting up the kind of initial conditions that will lead to decreases in randomness, and that therefore all practical experiments will tend to show only increases in randomness.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Reversible rule 37R does not obey the Second Law
claims.statement: The reversible cellular automaton rule 37R, even as a closed system, shows neither a systematic trend toward increasing randomness nor simple predictable behavior, but fluctuates indefinitely between more and less ordered states, so it does not obey the Second Law for practical purposes.
claims.quote: There is, I believe, no choice but to conclude that for practical purposes rule 37R simply does not obey the Second Law.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Biological order arises from partitioning into separated compartments
claims.statement: Biological systems can show increasing order despite the Second Law mainly because they partition into parts (cells, organisms) separated by membrane-like boundaries, within which organized behavior can occur while the boundary survives.
claims.quote: This basic mechanism may well be the main one at work in many biological systems: each cell or each organism becomes separated from others, and while it survives, it can exhibit organized behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: The Second Law is general but not universally valid
claims.statement: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is an important and general principle but is not universally valid; many systems in nature behave like rule 37R and do not show a uniform trend toward increasing randomness.
claims.quote: And indeed I strongly suspect that there are many systems in nature which behave in more or less the same way. The Second Law is an important and quite general principle—but it is not universally valid.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Continuum behavior emerges from discrete randomizing conserving rules
claims.statement: Smooth continuum behavior, such as diffusion of density, emerges from discrete systems whenever small-scale apparent randomness washes out individual details and conserved quantities constrain overall features, as shown by block cellular automata whose average density follows the diffusion equation.
claims.quote: And much as in physical systems like fluids, what ultimately leads to this is the presence of small-scale apparent randomness that washes out details of individual cells or molecules—as well as of conserved quantities that force certain overall features not to change too quickly.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: The fundamental rule cannot be found by working backwards from known laws
claims.statement: If the ultimate rule for the universe is simple, it cannot realistically be found by engineering it from observed features; the only practical method is to choose a straightforward representation and systematically search through large numbers of candidate rules.
claims.quote: my guess is that the only realistic way to find the rule in the first place will be to start from some very straightforward representation, and then just to search through large numbers of possible rules in this representation.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Space, gravity and quantum features are generic across many candidate rules
claims.statement: Features such as seemingly continuous space and certain aspects of gravitation and quantum mechanics will emerge from many different underlying rules for the universe, whereas properties like the spectrum of particle masses, and perhaps the dimensionality of space, will be specific to particular rules.
claims.quote: so also I suspect that properties such as the existence of seemingly continuous space, as well as certain features of gravitation and quantum mechanics, will emerge with many different possible underlying rules for the universe.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Most known physical laws are emergent, not fundamental
claims.statement: Most physical laws discovered so far are not fundamental but are emergent large-scale features of an underlying rule, so their simplicity says little about the simplicity of that rule.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that the vast majority of physical laws discovered so far are not truly fundamental, but are instead merely emergent features of the large-scale behavior of some ultimate underlying rule.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Space is discrete below the scales probed by experiment
claims.statement: Space, though experimentally continuous down to about 10^-20 meters, is very likely made of discrete elements at still smaller scales, just as fluids and other seemingly continuous things have turned out to be.
claims.quote: Particle physics experiments have shown that space acts as a continuum down to distances of around 10^(-20) meters—or a hundred thousandth the radius of a proton. But there is absolutely no reason to think that discrete elements will not be found at still smaller distances.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Space and matter should be made of the same stuff
claims.statement: In the simplest ultimate model of the universe there is no distinction between space and its contents: matter and everything else are made of the same underlying structure as space, unlike in a cellular automaton.
claims.quote: But if the ultimate model for the universe is to be as simple as possible, then it seems much more plausible that both space and its contents should somehow be made of the same stuff—so that in a sense space becomes the only thing in the universe.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: At the lowest level space is a network of nodes
claims.statement: At the lowest level, space is most likely a giant network of nodes defined only by their connections (and it suffices to consider nodes with exactly three connections), with ordinary space emerging as a large-scale limit.
claims.quote: And with this in mind I believe that what is by far the most likely is that at the lowest level space is in effect a giant network of nodes.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Network dimension is set by growth of node counts with distance
claims.statement: A network corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space exactly when the number of nodes within graph distance r of a node grows in a limiting sense like r^d; tree-like or randomly connected networks correspond to no finite dimension.
claims.quote: in general the condition for a network to correspond to ordinary d-dimensional space is precisely that the total number of nodes that appear in it out to distance r grows in some limiting sense like r^d
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Observers perceive time only through the causal network of events
claims.statement: An observer embedded in a system such as a mobile automaton cannot see its individual update steps; all the observer can perceive is the network of causal relationships between updating events, so perceived time and spacetime derive purely from that causal network, and sequential updating can appear as synchronized parallel evolution.
claims.quote: The most they will be able to tell is that a certain network of causal relationships exists—and their perception of time must therefore derive purely from the properties of this network.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Non-overlapping replacement rules give update-order-independent causal networks
claims.statement: A substitution system whose rules replace only blocks that can never overlap themselves or each other always yields the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are applied (the property Wolfram calls causal invariance).
claims.quote: And any substitution system whose rules specify replacements only for blocks such as these is guaranteed to yield the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are performed.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: The universe's rules likely yield a unique causal network
claims.statement: Although the universe has no global clock and its rules may be applicable in arbitrary order, its actual rules most likely have the property of always yielding the same causal network, and so a unique perceived history.
claims.quote: it still tends to be my suspicion that there is not—and that in fact the particular rules followed by the universe do in the end have the property that they always yield the same causal network.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Small-scale randomness in the network makes space robustly 3D
claims.statement: The ultimate rules for the universe will produce networks that look largely random at small scales, and this randomness is what allows a definite and robust dimensionality of 3 to emerge for space.
claims.quote: my expectation is that they will give rise to networks that on a small scale look largely random. But this very randomness will most likely be what for example allows a definite and robust value of 3 to emerge for the dimensionality of space
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Elementary length and time are tiny and their ratio is light speed
claims.statement: Each connection in the causal network of the universe corresponds to an identical elementary distance (perhaps about 10^-35 meters) and elementary time (perhaps about 10^-43 seconds), whose ratio is a fixed speed identified with the speed of light.
claims.quote: One may guess that this elementary distance is around 10^(-35) meters, and that the elementary time interval is around 10^(-43) seconds. But whatever these values are, a crucial point is that their ratio must be a fixed speed, and we can identify this with the speed of light.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Causal invariance yields special relativity
claims.statement: If the underlying rules of the universe are causal invariant, then slices through the causal network at different angles, corresponding to different uniform velocities, are all governed by the same rules, so physics is the same regardless of uniform motion and the standard phenomena of special relativity such as time dilation follow.
claims.quote: And the crucial point is that whenever the underlying system is causal invariant the exact same underlying rules will account for what one sees in slices at different angles. And what this means is that in effect the same rules will apply regardless of how fast one is going.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Elementary particles are persistent localized structures in the network
claims.statement: Elementary particles are analogs of the localized structures seen in class 4 cellular automata: persistent structures (such as tangles or non-planar cores) in the network of space, so that the fundamental rules need make no reference to particular particles.
claims.quote: An immediate possibility that I suspect is actually not too far from the mark is that such particles are analogs of the localized structures that we saw earlier in this book in systems like the class 4 cellular automata shown below.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Fundamental particle masses may still have simple ratios
claims.statement: Although observed elementary particle masses are not in simple ratios (unlike electric charges), truly fundamental particle masses may still have simple relations, because observed masses include varying amounts of interaction energy.
claims.quote: But despite such results, it is still conceivable that there could in the end be simple relations between truly fundamental particle masses—since it turns out that the masses that have actually been observed in effect also include varying amounts of interaction energy.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Network curvature appears in node counts via the Ricci scalar
claims.statement: In a large network approximating d-dimensional space, the leading correction to the number of nodes reached within distance r is proportional to the Ricci scalar curvature times r^(d+1), so curvature can be determined purely from network connectivity.
claims.quote: But in fact the leading correction to the number of nodes reached is always quite simple: it is just proportional to what is called the Ricci scalar curvature, multiplied by r^(d + 1).
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Causal invariant dimension-preserving network rules give Einstein equations
claims.statement: Network replacement rules that are causal invariant and maintain a fixed number of dimensions will almost inevitably produce large-scale behavior close to the vacuum Einstein equations of general relativity, analogous to how Navier–Stokes behavior emerges from cellular automaton fluids.
claims.quote: But I suspect that if one has replacement rules that are causal invariant and that in effect successfully maintain a fixed number of dimensions they will almost inevitably lead to behavior that follows something close to the Einstein equations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Network-based programs will reproduce the key features of quantum theory
claims.statement: Discrete network models of the universe with causal invariance will ultimately turn out to exhibit many if not all of the key features of quantum theory, even though they are not set up in terms of its standard formalism.
claims.quote: And in fact it is my strong suspicion that the kinds of programs that I have discussed in the past few sections will actually in the end turn out to show many if not all the key features of quantum theory.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Network threads let deterministic models produce quantum correlations
claims.statement: The quantum correlations between distant particles usually taken to rule out definite underlying processes can arise in a deterministic network model, because particles created together stay linked by threads of connections that bypass ordinary three-dimensional space.
claims.quote: And the basic reason for this is that if the universe is a network then it can in a sense easily contain threads that continue to connect particles even when the particles get far apart in terms of ordinary space.
claims.chapter: Ch. 9: Fundamental Physics

claims.label: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs
claims.statement: The basic mechanisms underlying human perception and scientific analysis, like the mechanisms behind many natural processes, can be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
claims.quote: the evidence we have suggests that the basic mechanisms at work can once again successfully be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard
claims.statement: Although inferring the generating procedure from observed behavior is fairly easy for the rules of traditional mathematics, for general simple programs it is often extremely difficult, because their complex output shows no obvious trace of its simple origin.
claims.quote: But for the more general rules that I discuss in this book it appears to often be extremely difficult. For even though the rules may be simple, the behavior they produce is often highly complex, and shows absolutely no obvious trace of its simple origins.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions
claims.statement: Defining something as random only when no short description of it exists at all is too restrictive and uncomputable (it would mean deterministic rules can never generate randomness), so any useful definition of randomness must refer to how short descriptions are to be found.
claims.quote: Indeed, what I suspect is that ultimately no useful definition of randomness can be based solely on the issue of what short descriptions of something may in principle exist.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Something is random if essentially no simple program detects regularities in it
claims.statement: Since essentially all standard methods of perception and analysis are based on simple programs, something should be considered random whenever essentially no simple program succeeds in detecting regularities in it.
claims.quote: something should be considered to be random whenever there is essentially no simple program that can succeed in detecting regularities in it.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do
claims.statement: Once a few simple programs corresponding to standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities in some data, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed, so the everyday judgment of randomness is in practice fairly unambiguous.
claims.quote: For once a few simple programs corresponding to a few standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed in detecting them.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis
