claims.label: Complexity means our perception and analysis fail to find a short description
claims.statement: To call something complex is to say that our methods of perception and analysis have failed to find a short description of the features of it that we are interested in; complexity therefore depends on which features one chooses to capture.
claims.quote: when we say that something seems complex, what we are effectively saying is that our powers of perception and analysis have failed on it.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features
claims.statement: People tend to lose interest in images with no simple features (such as perfectly random ones), and the images that hold attention and seem most aesthetically pleasing are those in which some features are simple to describe while others have no short description findable by human visual perception.
claims.quote: the images that draw us in the most—and typically that we find the most aesthetically pleasing—are those for which some features are simple for us to describe, but others have no short description that can be found by any of our standard processes of visual perception.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else
claims.statement: Structurally different lossless data compression methods (run-length, block/Huffman, pointer-based and two-dimensional schemes) have remarkably similar capabilities: they compress uniform regions, repetitive behavior and to some extent nested behavior, but achieve no substantial compression of more complex behavior even when it is generated by very short programs.
claims.quote: Essentially every method, for example, will successfully compress large regions of uniform color. And most methods manage to compress behavior that is repetitive, and at least to some extent behavior that is nested—exactly the two kinds of simple behavior that we have noted many times in this book.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression
claims.statement: Under lossy compression by keeping only some basic forms (as in JPEG-like schemes), the relevant features of both simple and completely random images remain recognizable at high compression, whereas images normally considered complex need much lower compression, and reordering the basic forms does not change this substantially.
claims.quote: But images that one would normally consider complex tend to have features that cannot be recognized except at significantly lower levels of compression.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features
claims.statement: Human perception generally works by cells responding to specific fixed features and ignoring others; in vision, cortical cells act as templates for small local patterns, and textures are distinguished by the densities of such local features, much as colors are distinguished by densities of red, green and blue.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that it is density differences such as these that allow our visual system to distinguish textures.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting
claims.statement: Humans can readily see by eye that a two-dimensional pattern is purely repetitive, but generally cannot tell that a pattern is nested (unless it is dominated by large uniform areas), even though a simple two-dimensional pointer-based encoding recognizes the nesting.
claims.quote: it is remarkably difficult for us to tell that the patterns are nested. And this can be viewed as a clear example of a limitation in our powers of visual perception.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else
claims.statement: For sounds generated from sequences with fairly uniform properties, the human auditory system recognizes only exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies; nested or other non-repetitive structure, beyond a few large spectral peaks, is heard as random noise.
claims.quote: we readily recognize exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies, and essentially nothing else.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Best-fit probabilistic models of deterministic data look more random than the data
claims.statement: When probabilistic models such as block-frequency, Markov or probabilistic cellular automaton models are fitted to data generated by deterministic cellular automata, they reproduce the statistics used in fitting but their typical behavior is considerably more random and misses most detailed features of the data.
claims.quote: In most cases, the typical behavior produced by the model looks considerably more random than the data.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Equal block frequencies of all lengths is not a universal randomness test
claims.statement: Checking that all blocks of all lengths occur with equal frequency does not guarantee absence of regularity: sequences such as linear feedback shift register output or concatenated binary digits of successive integers have accurate block frequencies yet are non-random, as revealed for instance by an abnormally small spread of those frequencies.
claims.quote: it has sometimes been thought that if one could just compute frequencies of blocks of all lengths one would have a kind of universal test for randomness. But sequences like (e) and (f) on the facing page make it clear that this is not the case.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Rule 30 center column and digits of pi pass statistical tests for randomness
claims.statement: The center column of the rule 30 cellular automaton and the base 2 digits of pi show no detectable deviation from randomness under block-frequency statistics or under analysis by simple cellular automata, even though both are generated by simple rules.
claims.quote: statistical analysis, even with some generalization, cannot readily recognize that sequences like (g) and (h) are anything but completely random—even though at an underlying level these sequences were generated by quite simple rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Rule 30 can serve as a cryptographic stream cipher as secure as any known
claims.statement: Simple rules with complex behavior, such as the rule 30 cellular automaton sampled sparsely to give an encrypting sequence, can be used to build stream ciphers at least as secure against cryptanalysis as any known system, unlike additive cellular automata or linear feedback shift registers, whose keys are easily recovered.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that they can, and that in fact they allow one to construct systems that are at least as secure to cryptanalysis as any that are known.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Every nested pattern likely has a formula in generalized hypergeometric functions
claims.statement: Although most nested patterns have no obvious relation to ordinary mathematical functions, a formula for the color of each cell of any nested pattern can probably be found in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions or similar generalizations of traditional functions.
claims.quote: it is my guess that in the end it will in fact turn out to be possible to get a formula for any nested pattern in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: No simple formula describes many steps of rule 30 evolution
claims.statement: Minimal Boolean formulas (in disjunctive normal form or in Nand operations) for the outcome of rule 30 grow rapidly with the number of steps, unlike those for simple rules such as 90 and 254, indicating that no simple formula describes rule 30 evolution and that, in most cases, cellular automaton patterns have no simple mathematical formula.
claims.quote: So even if one allows rather general structure, the evidence is that in the end there is no way to set up any simple formula that will describe the outcome of evolution for a system like rule 30.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Human memory works like similarity-preserving hashing by layers of neurons
claims.statement: Human memory likely retrieves data by a simple hashing-like mechanism in which successive layers of nerve cells, each responding to patterns in fixed random sets of inputs, produce representations that are the same for inputs differing by small changes, allowing retrieval by similarity.
claims.quote: this basic mechanism provides a simple way to get a representation—and thus a hash code—that will tend to be the same for pieces of data that somehow have enough features that are similar.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Memory retrieval, not logic, underlies almost all of human thinking
claims.statement: Retrieval from memory on the basis of similarity underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking, including generalization, analogy and intuition, and logical reasoning is not fundamental but is itself carried out by retrieving learned patterns of argument from memory.
claims.quote: My strong suspicion is that the use of memory is what in fact underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules
claims.statement: Despite the complicated construction of the brain, there is a core to human thinking that is largely independent of neural details and is based on rather simple rules, with nothing fundamentally special about the processes involved.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that there is a definite core to the phenomenon of human thinking that is largely independent of such details—and that will in the end turn out to be based on rules that are rather simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: General human-like thinking is easier to reproduce than task-specific versions
claims.statement: Because complex behavior from simple rules is hard to direct to specific tasks, it will likely be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than a special version of human-like thinking restricted to specific tasks; a recognizably human-like system would also need a human-like base of experience.
claims.quote: most likely it will at some level be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than to set up some special version of human-like thinking only for specific tasks.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: No method of perception or analysis can recognize all possible regularities
claims.statement: No method of perception and analysis, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize all possible regularities and thus tell immediately whether a piece of data can be generated from some simple description, although higher methods could recognize some regularities current methods miss.
claims.quote: My strong belief—as I will argue in Chapter 12—is that at least in complete generality this will never be possible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Practical perception and analysis methods recognize only repetition and nesting
claims.statement: Essentially all methods of perception and analysis in practical use have similar capabilities, recognizing repetition and sometimes nesting but almost nothing more complex, possibly because only such regularities are both common and quickly recognizable, or because humans choose methods matching their built-in perception.
claims.quote: Most of them, for example, recognize repetition, and some also recognize nesting. But almost none recognize anything more complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Extraterrestrial signals taken for noise could be meaningful messages
claims.statement: Some extraterrestrial radio and other signals that are detected and assumed to be random noise could be meaningful messages encoded in a way recognizable only by higher forms of perception and analysis than those applied so far.
claims.quote: it seems far from inconceivable that some of the extraterrestrial radio and other signals that we pick up and assume to be random noise could in fact be meaningful messages
claims.chapter: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

claims.label: Computation is the central organizing idea of the new science
claims.statement: The most important idea underlying Wolfram's new kind of science is computation: systems such as cellular automata should be viewed as computations, with initial conditions as input and later states as output, so that systems with entirely different rules can be discussed in a unified, abstract way.
claims.quote: And in many respects the single most important idea that underlies this new science is the notion of computation.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Any system can be viewed as performing a computation
claims.statement: Any system whatsoever, not just a cellular automaton, can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.
claims.quote: At some level, any cellular automaton—or for that matter, any system whatsoever—can be viewed as performing a computation that determines what its future behavior will be.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Universality is crucial for understanding complexity in natural systems
claims.statement: Although universality has never before been seriously considered in natural science, it is crucial for finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity seen in natural systems.
claims.quote: But what I will show in this chapter and the next is that in fact universality is for example quite crucial in finding general ways to characterize and understand the complexity we see in natural systems.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: A universal system can produce arbitrarily complex behavior
claims.statement: Because a universal system can emulate any other system, it can produce behavior as complex as that of any other system, so knowing a system is universal implies it can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.
claims.quote: So knowing that a particular system is universal thus immediately implies that the system can produce behavior that is in a sense arbitrarily complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Universality is widespread and occurs in many systems in nature
claims.statement: Contrary to the assumption that universality is rare and found only in systems specifically constructed to have it, universality is a widespread phenomenon that also occurs in a wide range of important systems found in nature.
claims.quote: But one of the results of this chapter is that in fact universality is a much more widespread phenomenon. And in the next chapter I will argue that for example it also occurs in a wide range of important systems that we see in nature.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: A fixed universal cellular automaton can emulate any cellular automaton
claims.statement: A single cellular automaton with fixed rules (Wolfram's 19-color, next-nearest-neighbor construction) can, given suitable initial conditions, emulate any cellular automaton whatsoever, regardless of how many colors or neighbors its rules involve, including rules more complicated than its own.
claims.quote: And the conclusion is therefore that the universal cellular automaton can ultimately emulate a cellular automaton with absolutely any set of rules, regardless of how many neighbors and how many colors they may involve.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Cellular automata can emulate nearly all other system types, even computers
claims.statement: Cellular automata can be set up to emulate almost every type of system considered in the book—mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, sequential substitution and tag systems, register machines, arithmetic systems, logic circuits and random-access memory—and in principle a practical computer in its entirety.
claims.quote: But what I will show in this section is that in fact this is not the case, and that in the end cellular automata can actually be made to emulate almost every single type of system that we have discussed in this book.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step
claims.statement: Unlike mobile automata or Turing machines, substitution systems cannot in general be emulated one step per cellular automaton step, because the number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor each step while a cellular automaton pattern can grow only by a fixed amount per step; progressively more cellular automaton steps are needed per substitution step.
claims.quote: That this must ultimately be the case one can see from the fact that the total number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor from one step to the next, while in a cellular automaton the size of a pattern can only ever increase by a fixed amount at each step.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata
claims.statement: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only generate repetitive or nested patterns, so they cannot emulate cellular automata such as rule 30, whereas neighbor-dependent substitution systems can emulate cellular automata straightforwardly.
claims.quote: For as we discussed on page 83, neighbor-independent substitution systems can generate only patterns that are either repetitive or nested—so they can never yield the more complicated patterns that are, for example, needed to emulate rule 30.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Any system type that can emulate every cellular automaton has universal members
claims.statement: Since a universal cellular automaton exists, any type of system shown capable of emulating any cellular automaton—including mobile automata, Turing machines, neighbor-dependent and sequential substitution systems, tag systems, cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines—must contain universal examples.
claims.quote: And as soon as one knows that any particular type of system is capable of emulating any cellular automaton, it immediately follows that there must be examples of that type of system that are universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal
claims.statement: A system that repeatedly takes a whole number, computes its remainder modulo a constant and applies an arithmetic operation chosen by that remainder can emulate a register machine, and is therefore universal; given how widespread universality is, arithmetic supporting it is unsurprising.
claims.quote: The picture below shows that such a system can be set up to emulate a register machine. And from the fact that register machines are universal it follows that so too are such arithmetic systems.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Structurally different systems are computationally equivalent
claims.statement: Because essentially all the kinds of systems studied (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, register machines and others) can emulate each other, a wide variety of systems with very different underlying structures are fundamentally equivalent in the computations they can perform, so computation can be studied abstractly with results applying across systems.
claims.quote: In a sense its most important consequence is that it implies that from a computational point of view a very wide variety of systems, with very different underlying structures, are at some level fundamentally equivalent.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Past the threshold of universality, more complex rules add no capability
claims.statement: As systems of a given type are given progressively greater computational capabilities they eventually pass a threshold of universality, after which the set of computations they can perform is always the same, so more sophisticated rules gain nothing further and a universal system's capabilities are independent of the details of its construction.
claims.quote: But the phenomenon of universality implies that this is not the case, and that as soon as one has passed the threshold of universality, nothing more can in a sense ever be gained.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Elementary cellular automaton rule 110 is universal
claims.statement: Rule 110, a two-color nearest-neighbor elementary cellular automaton, is universal: by arranging its naturally occurring localized structures as components, it can be made to emulate any cyclic tag system, and hence any Turing machine.
claims.quote: And indeed in the case of rule 110 it took several years of work to develop the necessary ideas and tools. But finally it has turned out to be possible to show that the rule 110 cellular automaton is in fact universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Universality should be common, including among very simple rules
claims.statement: The universality of rule 110, one of the simplest possible cellular automaton rules, implies that universality is far more common than previously thought and should occur in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.
claims.quote: But knowing that a system like rule 110 is universal, the whole picture changes, and now it seems likely that instead universality should actually be seen in a very wide range of systems, including many with rather simple rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Complexity of behavior saturates soon after the simplest rules
claims.statement: As rules become progressively more complicated, overall behavior grows more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached, and since that threshold is very low, behavior beyond the very simplest rules of any kind should quickly become as complex as it will ever be—consistent with the Chapter 3 survey.
claims.quote: So what this means is that if one looks at a sequence of systems with progressively more complicated rules, one should expect that the overall behavior they produce will become more complex only until the threshold of universality is reached.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: All class 4 cellular automata are expected to be universal
claims.statement: Any cellular automaton showing class 4 behavior (localized structures moving and interacting in complicated ways) will, like rule 110, turn out to be universal, because such rules eventually yield localized structures rich enough to support universality.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that it is true in general that any cellular automaton which shows overall class 4 behavior will turn out—like rule 110—to be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Rule 110 and its reflections are the only clear elementary class 4 rules
claims.statement: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata, the only clear immediate example of class 4 behavior is rule 110 together with its left-right and black-white equivalents (rules 124, 137 and 193), while class 4 behavior is common once more colors or neighbors are allowed, even for totalistic rules.
claims.quote: Among the 256 so-called elementary cellular automata that allow only two possible colors for each cell and depend only on nearest neighbors, the only clear immediate example is rule 110—together with rules 124, 137 and 193 obtained by trivially reversing left and right or black and white.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal
claims.statement: Cellular automata that produce only uniform or repetitive patterns (class 1 and class 2) can never be universal, because they transmit information only over limited distances and so support only processes involving a limited number of cells.
claims.quote: In a sense the fundamental reason for this—as we discussed on page 252—is that such class 1 and class 2 cellular automata never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Nested-pattern and additive cellular automata cannot be universal
claims.statement: Cellular automata whose information transmission is highly constrained so that patterns are essentially nested, and additive rules such as rules 90 and 150 whose states after a power-of-two number of steps are simple superpositions of shifted copies of the initial condition, cannot be universal.
claims.quote: And since there are many kinds of behavior that do not return to such predictable forms after any limited number of steps, one must conclude that additive rules cannot be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Rule 54 shows only repetitive or nested forms in 100 million initial conditions
claims.statement: Rule 54, a possible class 4 elementary cellular automaton, shows only repetitive or nested behavior in its first hundred million initial conditions, leaving it uncertain whether rule 54 is universal.
claims.quote: And as one continues one sees various other repetitive and nested forms. But at least up to the hundred millionth initial condition one sees nothing that is fundamentally any more complicated.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Any non-repetitive, non-nested system is expected to be universal
claims.statement: More or less any system whose behavior is not fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal, so there is a close connection between universality and the appearance of complex behavior, though proving it will be far easier for some systems (such as rule 110) than others.
claims.quote: As I will discuss in the next chapter, my general expectation is that more or less any system whose behavior is not somehow fundamentally repetitive or nested will in the end turn out to be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Uncontrolled information flow in class 3 rules hinders universality proofs
claims.statement: Universality proofs proceed by building components from localized structures, which requires controlled transmission of information; in class 3 systems a change to a single cell eventually spreads to all cells, making it very hard to identify definite components and hence to prove universality.
claims.quote: And this kind of uncontrolled transmission of information makes it very difficult to identify pieces that could be used as definite components in a construction.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Rules 30 and 45 are expected to be universal
claims.statement: Although the localized structures found in rules 30 and 45 on repetitive backgrounds all move at the same speed and so cannot interact, preventing a rule 110-style proof, rules 30 and 45 will nevertheless turn out to be universal.
claims.quote: So although this means that the particular type of approach we used to demonstrate the universality of rule 110 cannot immediately be used for rule 30 or rule 45, it certainly does not mean that these rules are not in the end universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Complex elementary rules can emulate one step of every elementary rule
claims.statement: Using block encodings, elementary rules with complex behavior such as rules 22, 30 and 110 can be made to emulate a single step of all 256 elementary cellular automata, whereas rules with simple behavior such as 90 and 184 can emulate only a few; this supports the idea that complex-looking cellular automata can do arbitrarily sophisticated computations.
claims.quote: But for underlying rules that have more complex behavior—like rules 22, 30, or 110—it turns out that in the end it is always possible to emulate all 256 elementary rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal
claims.statement: Since elementary cellular automata whose behavior looks complex can do computations as sophisticated as desired, they are expected to be universal, so perhaps as many as 27 of the 256 elementary rules are universal.
claims.quote: And this suggests that such cellular automata will in the end turn out to be universal—with the result that out of the 256 elementary rules one expects that perhaps as many as 27 will in fact be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: A 2-state 5-color Turing machine is universal via rule 110
claims.statement: A Turing machine with just 2 states and 5 colors, far simpler than the 7-state 4-color machine that had long been the simplest known, is universal because it emulates rule 110 by sweeping back and forth and updating all cells by one rule 110 step per sweep.
claims.quote: And in fact, by using the universality of rule 110 it turns out to be possible to come up with the vastly simpler universal Turing machine shown below—with just 2 states and 5 possible colors.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: No 2-state 2-color Turing machine can be universal
claims.statement: All 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors have behavior too simple to support universality.
claims.quote: If one looks at the 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors it is fairly easy to see that their behavior is in all cases too simple to support universality.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Complex behavior is rare but present in small Turing machine spaces
claims.statement: Starting from a blank tape, roughly one in 50,000 2-state 4-color Turing machines and one in 200,000 4-state 2-color machines show complex behavior, and 14 essentially equivalent machines among the 2,985,984 with 2 states and 3 colors do so.
claims.quote: Among such 2-state 4-color Turing machines perhaps one in 50,000 shows complex behavior when started from a blank tape.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: A complex 2-state 3-color Turing machine is likely the simplest universal one
claims.statement: The 2-state 3-color Turing machine numbered 596,440, which yields complicated behavior from a blank tape, is likely universal, and if so would by most measures be the simplest universal Turing machine.
claims.quote: And although it will no doubt be very difficult to prove, it seems likely that this Turing machine will in the end turn out to be universal. And if so, then presumably it will by most measures be the very simplest Turing machine that is universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: All 3-state 2-color Turing machines behave simply from blank tape
claims.statement: With blank initial conditions all 2,985,984 Turing machines with 3 states and 2 colors quickly produce simple repetitive or nested behavior, and even with more complicated initial conditions their behavior eventually seems to resolve into a simple form.
claims.quote: With 3 states and 2 colors it turns out that with blank initial conditions all of the 2,985,984 possible Turing machines of this type quickly evolve to produce simple repetitive or nested behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Combinators show highly complex behavior despite simple rules
claims.statement: Combinators, symbolic systems long known to be universal, show highly complex behavior despite simple rules—for example a length-8 initial expression grows exponentially with seemingly random internal structure—and they can emulate rule 110, suggesting their universality is just associated with general complex behavior.
claims.quote: But from pictures like the ones on the facing page it is rather clear that despite their fairly simple underlying rules, the behavior of combinators can be highly complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 11: The Notion of Computation

claims.label: Every process, natural or artificial, can be viewed as a computation
claims.statement: Any process that follows definite rules, including processes in nature governed by physical law as well as processes constructed by humans, can be viewed as a computation, giving a uniform framework for comparing very different processes.
claims.quote: all processes, whether they are produced by human effort or occur spontaneously in nature, can be viewed as computations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Principle of Computational Equivalence: one maximal level of sophistication
claims.statement: Almost all processes whose behavior is not obviously simple correspond to computations of equivalent sophistication; there is essentially a single highest level of computational sophistication, and almost all such processes reach it regardless of how simple their rules or initial conditions are.
claims.quote: the most general is just to say that almost all processes that are not obviously simple can be viewed as computations of equivalent sophistication.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: No physical system can compute beyond cellular automata and Turing machines
claims.statement: As a law of nature, no system that can actually be constructed in our universe can carry out explicit computations more sophisticated than those of universal systems such as cellular automata and Turing machines; imaginable hypercomputers (e.g. with infinite tables of results) cannot be built.
claims.quote: no system can ever carry out explicit computations that are more sophisticated than those carried out by systems like cellular automata and Turing machines.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: An overwhelming fraction of non-simple rules are universal
claims.statement: Among all possible rules of a given type (such as cellular automata) whose behavior is not obviously simple, i.e. not repetitive or nested, the overwhelming majority are computationally universal, so universality is extremely common rather than a rare engineered property.
claims.quote: among all possible systems with behavior that is not obviously simple an overwhelming fraction are universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Rules occurring in nature are typically not specially selected
claims.statement: When no constraint such as engineering design or natural selection forces simple behavior, the rules that operate in nature are effectively selected in no special way apart from tending to be structurally simple, so they behave like randomly chosen rules and are almost always universal when their behavior is not obviously simple.
claims.quote: most rules that appear in nature can be viewed as being selected in no special way—save perhaps for the fact that the structure of the rules themselves tends to be fairly simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Rule 30 from a single cell contains every possible block
claims.statement: The pattern generated by the rule 30 cellular automaton from a single black cell appears to contain every possible block of cells eventually, so that essentially any possible computation exists somewhere within this single pattern.
claims.quote: So far as I can tell, all possible blocks eventually appear, potentially letting the pattern serve as a kind of directory of all possible computations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Complicated molecules generally do not reach minimum-energy configurations
claims.statement: Although simple molecules may settle into minimum-energy configurations, complicated molecules typically do not; they explore configurations by an explicit evolution process, so nature does not actually solve hard constraint-satisfaction problems as traditional models idealize.
claims.quote: while in simple cases complicated molecules may for example arrange themselves in configurations that minimize energy, the evidence is that in more complicated cases they typically do not.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Continuous systems cannot exceed discrete computation in practice
claims.statement: Continuous systems, including analog computers, systems described by continuous equations, and even idealized perfectly continuous systems under reasonable assumptions, cannot perform computations fundamentally more sophisticated than discrete systems like cellular automata; continuity is largely an idealization.
claims.quote: even idealized perfectly continuous systems will never in fact be able to perform fundamentally more sophisticated computations.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Equations with trigonometric functions can encode infinite computations
claims.statement: Whereas solving pure polynomial equations allows no computation beyond that of ordinary discrete systems, once trigonometric functions are allowed one can construct equations whose solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of infinitely many steps of a system like a cellular automaton.
claims.quote: as soon as one even allows trigonometric functions, for example, it turns out that it becomes possible to construct equations for which finding a solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of an infinite number of steps in the evolution of a system like a cellular automaton.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Human thinking rests on rather simple computational processes
claims.statement: The basic mechanisms of human thinking will turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes, so human thought does not perform computations beyond the level allowed by the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
claims.quote: the basic mechanisms of human thinking will in the end turn out to correspond to rather simple computational processes.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: No hidden regularity beyond repetition and nesting in rule-30-like systems
claims.statement: There is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems with complex behavior such as rule 30; beyond systems with obvious regularities like repetition and nesting, most systems are universal and computationally equivalent.
claims.quote: I have gradually come to the conclusion that there is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems, and that instead what the Principle of Computational Equivalence suggests is correct
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Complexity arises because observers are computationally equivalent to systems
claims.statement: Systems with simple rules appear complex because, once a low threshold is passed, their evolution is as computationally sophisticated as any process of perception or analysis used to study them, and this holds for any method of perception and analysis that can actually be used.
claims.quote: observers will tend to be computationally equivalent to the systems they observe—with the inevitable consequence that they will consider the behavior of such systems complex.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Computational irreducibility blocks shortcuts to predicting behavior
claims.statement: For computationally irreducible systems, even with complete knowledge of rules and initial conditions, there is no way to predict the behavior except by performing almost as many computational steps as the system's own evolution.
claims.quote: there can be no way to predict how the system will behave except by going through almost as many steps of computation as the evolution of the system itself.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Only obviously simple behavior is reducible; nearly all else is irreducible
claims.statement: Behavior that is obviously simple, such as repetitive or nested behavior, is always computationally reducible, while in practically all other cases behavior is computationally irreducible.
claims.quote: If the behavior of a system is obviously simple—and is say either repetitive or nested—then it will always be computationally reducible. But it follows from the Principle of Computational Equivalence that in practically all other cases it will be computationally irreducible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Traditional theoretical science fails where irreducibility is present
claims.statement: Traditional theoretical science, including its use of mathematical formulas, relies on computational reducibility, which is the fundamental reason it has made little progress with systems whose behavior is not quite simple and why it has tended to restrict its domain to reducible phenomena.
claims.quote: this, I believe, is the fundamental reason that traditional theoretical science has never managed to get far in studying most types of systems whose behavior is not ultimately quite simple.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Many common systems can only be understood by explicit simulation
claims.statement: Computer simulation is not merely a convenient substitute for mathematical formulas: there are many common systems whose behavior can be determined only by something like explicit simulation, and there can be no easy theory for almost any behavior that seems complex.
claims.quote: there are many common systems whose behavior cannot in the end be determined at all except by something like an explicit simulation.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Nested cellular automaton patterns can be computed in logarithmic time
claims.statement: For cellular automata with nested behavior such as elementary rules 60 and 188, the color of a cell after t steps can be found in about log2(t) steps from the base-2 digits of its position, rather than by tracing all t steps.
claims.quote: In general, to find the color of a cell after t steps of rule 188 or rule 60 evolution takes about Log[2, t] steps.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Complex-looking yet computationally reducible systems are very rare
claims.statement: Systems whose behavior looks complex but is nevertheless computationally reducible, such as the cellular automaton that generates digits of powers of 2, are very rare; in the vast majority of cases complex-looking behavior in nature and elsewhere is computationally irreducible.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that systems like this are very rare, and that in the vast majority of cases where the behavior that we see in nature and elsewhere appears to us complex it is in the end indeed associated with computational irreducibility.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Apparent free will stems from irreducible brain computation
claims.statement: The apparent freedom of human will arises because, although brain components follow definite laws, the brain's overall behavior is an irreducible computation whose outcome cannot be found by reasonable laws; no external influence, chaos, or quantum randomness is needed.
claims.quote: even though all the components of our brains presumably follow definite laws, I strongly suspect that their overall behavior corresponds to an irreducible computation whose outcome can never in effect be found by reasonable laws.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Undecidability shows up with very simple rules and initial conditions
claims.statement: Undecidability has obvious effects even in a very simple system: in a 4-color totalistic cellular automaton (code 1004600) started from simple initial conditions, some patterns die out only after over a thousand steps while others are still growing after ten million steps with no indication of their final outcome.
claims.quote: undecidability can have quite obvious effects even with a very simple underlying rule and very simple initial conditions.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Infinite-time questions about complex systems are almost always undecidable
claims.statement: For almost any system whose behavior seems complex, almost any non-trivial question about its behavior after infinitely many steps (e.g. whether a pattern dies out, becomes repetitive, or ever produces a given arrangement) is undecidable, and such undecidability should be widespread in nature.
claims.quote: for almost any system whose behavior seems to us complex almost any non-trivial question about what the system does after an infinite number of steps will be undecidable.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Post Correspondence Problem with three pairs is likely undecidable
claims.statement: Whether a set of upper/lower block pairs can be concatenated to give identical strings (the Post Correspondence Problem) is straightforward for two pairs, but already with three pairs there is computational irreducibility, making the question undecidable in general.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that even with just three pairs there is already computational irreducibility
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Exhaustive search of 2-state 2-color Turing machines finds three growth rates
claims.statement: Enumerating all 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colors shows that the maximum number of steps to finish a computation grows with input length only linearly, quadratically, or exponentially, and every exponential case has another such machine computing the same function in bounded steps.
claims.quote: it turns out that the only rates of growth that one ever sees are linear, square and exponential.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Some simple Turing machine computations require exponential effort
claims.statement: Exhaustive search of all roughly 4 billion 4-state 2-color Turing machines shows certain computations by such machines cannot be sped up by any machine of that size, suggesting that some computations specified by very simple rules require effort growing exponentially with input length.
claims.quote: there are indeed Turing machine computations that cannot actually be carried out except by spending an amount of computational effort that can increase exponentially with the length of input.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Diverse computational systems emulate each other with comparable step counts
claims.statement: Almost all the varied systems considered (cellular automata, Turing machines, substitution and other systems) can emulate each other in a comparable number of steps, typically with at most polynomial overhead such as t^2 or t^(d+1), so rates of computation do not differ greatly across systems, including presumably those in nature.
claims.quote: almost all the very varied systems in this book can actually be made to emulate each other in a quite comparable number of steps.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: P is likely different from NP
claims.statement: It is likely that in most meaningful senses there is no general way to determine whether any path of a multiway or non-deterministic system yields a given outcome in a number of steps growing only polynomially, i.e. P is not equal to NP.
claims.quote: And although it has never been established for certain it seems by now likely that in most meaningful senses there is not.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Inverse problems for rule 30 are likely NP-complete
claims.statement: Even for the rule 30 cellular automaton, deciding whether initial conditions exist that produce a given outcome after t steps (such as a vertical black stripe of a given height in the center column) is expected to be NP-complete, illustrating that simple instances of NP-complete problems are common.
claims.quote: my expectation is that asking about possible outcomes of t steps of evolution will already be NP-complete even for the rule 30 cellular automaton
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Quantum computing's exponential speedups are likely an idealization artifact
claims.statement: Although the usual formalism of quantum mechanics allows constructing quantum computers that could solve some problems exponentially faster than ordinary Turing machines, this will likely not reflect ultimate physical reality but only idealizations in current models.
claims.quote: I strongly suspect that even if this is formally the case, it will still not turn out to be a true representation of ultimate physical reality
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Inverse problems are exponentially harder than forward evolution
claims.statement: In almost any system whose behavior seems complex there is, in a fundamental sense, an almost exponential gap between the effort needed to compute behavior from given initial conditions and the effort needed to determine which initial conditions, if any, produce given behavior.
claims.quote: there really can in some fundamental sense be an almost exponential difference in the amount of computational effort needed to find the behavior of a system with given particular initial conditions, and to solve the inverse problem of determining which if any initial conditions yield particular behavior.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Computational irreducibility makes short theorems with only long proofs inevitable
claims.statement: Because the proof processes of almost every area of mathematics are computationally irreducible, adding axioms cannot remove the problem: there will essentially always be theorems that are short to state but whose shortest proofs are very long.
claims.quote: But I suspect that ultimately there is almost always computational irreducibility, and this makes it essentially inevitable that there will be short theorems that only allow long proofs.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: An irreducible multiway system cannot be both complete and consistent
claims.statement: If questions about the long-run evolution of a multiway system (an idealized axiom system) are undecidable, then the system cannot be both complete and consistent, because completeness plus consistency would give a procedure that always terminates to decide whether a string is reached.
claims.quote: So the result of this is that if the evolution of a multiway system is computationally irreducible—so that questions about its ultimate behavior are undecidable—the system cannot be both complete and consistent.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Every axiom system used in current mathematical research is universal
claims.statement: Basic logic and pure predicate logic are not universal, but adding a function or relation with more than one argument gives universality; arithmetic, set theory, group theory and ring theory are universal, and every axiom system actually used in current mathematical research is known to be universal, while heavily constrained systems such as commutative group theory and simplified real algebra and geometry are not.
claims.quote: But of the axiom systems actually used in current mathematics research every single one is now known to be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Beyond a low threshold almost every axiom system should be universal
claims.statement: The Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that, beyond a low threshold of complexity, almost any axiom system (including very simple ones) should be universal, and so should exhibit undecidability and have no general upper limit on proof length.
claims.quote: And indeed the Principle of Computational Equivalence implies that beyond some low threshold almost any axiom system should be expected to be universal.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Gödel's Theorem follows from the universality of arithmetic, shown via rule 110
claims.statement: An integer (exponential Diophantine) equation can be built whose solutions emulate the rule 110 cellular automaton; since rule 110 is universal, the axioms of arithmetic support universality, which implies Gödel's Theorem that arithmetic contains statements that cannot be proved true or false. Wolfram presents Gödel's Theorem as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
claims.quote: And with the cellular automaton being a universal one such as rule 110 this implies that the axioms of arithmetic can support universality.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Simple integer equations should exist whose lack of solutions is unprovable
claims.statement: Although known universal integer equations are very complicated (the simplest having 9 variables and an immense number of terms), there should be much simpler integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the standard axioms of arithmetic.
claims.quote: so that in fact there are in the end rather simple integer equations for which the absence of solutions can never be proved from the normal axioms of arithmetic.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Many open number-theory problems may be unprovable from arithmetic's axioms
claims.statement: A fair fraction of the unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory will turn out to be questions that cannot be answered using the standard axioms of arithmetic.
claims.quote: And it is my strong suspicion that in fact of all the current unsolved problems seriously studied in number theory a fair fraction will in the end turn out to be questions that cannot ever be answered using the normal axioms of arithmetic.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Undecidability appears in almost any area of mathematics beyond easy questions
claims.statement: Undecidability and unprovability will begin to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond questions that are always easy to answer, as a consequence of the Principle of Computational Equivalence.
claims.quote: And indeed from the Principle of Computational Equivalence I strongly believe that in general undecidability and unprovability will start to occur in practically any area of mathematics almost as soon as one goes beyond the level of questions that are always easy to answer.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Mathematics avoids undecidability by choosing questions its methods can answer
claims.statement: Undecidability and unprovability have seemed rare in mathematics because mathematics, shaped by its history, has defined itself around the questions and systems that proof-based methods can address, concentrating on limited patches of computational reducibility; so present-day mathematics is a small and uncharacteristic sample of what is possible.
claims.quote: it is that like most other fields of human inquiry mathematics has tended to define itself to be concerned with just those questions that its methods can successfully address.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Complete and consistent means exactly half of all strings are generated
claims.statement: For a multiway system serving as an axiom system, with negation any length-preserving involution on strings, the system is complete and consistent exactly when half of all possible strings of each length are eventually generated from the string representing true; more than half implies inconsistency and less than half implies incompleteness.
claims.quote: the criterion for whether a system is complete and consistent is simply that exactly half the possible strings of a given length are eventually generated if one starts from the string representing "true".
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Axiom systems used in mathematics are usually close to complete
claims.statement: The axiom systems widely used in mathematics, though usually incomplete, are typically close to complete, because they were built to describe definite kinds of objects; as a result, the alternative objects (nonstandard models) that also satisfy them, such as those for standard arithmetic, differ only in obscure ways.
claims.quote: For if one looks at axiom systems that are widely used in mathematics they almost all tend to be complete enough to prove at least a fair fraction of statements either true or false.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Most simple axiom systems admit many different operator forms
claims.statement: Enumerating simple axiom systems for a binary operator shows that the vast majority allow operators of many different forms (many models), so they are not about any one particular operator and are far from complete; only a few, such as those for logic, force essentially a single form.
claims.quote: But what the pictures on the next two pages [804, 805] show is that the vast majority of axiom systems actually allow operators with all sorts of different forms.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Very short single-axiom systems for logic exist among the simplest axiom systems
claims.statement: Propositional logic can be axiomatized in terms of Nand by a single axiom with only six Nands (found by searching small axiom systems), far shorter than textbook systems, so an axiom system for logic is likely to be found among the simplest few thousand axiom systems.
claims.quote: So what this means is that if one were just to go through a list of the simplest few thousand axiom systems one would already be quite likely to find one that represents logic.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Traditional axiom systems are not fundamentally special; others could found new fields
claims.statement: Apart from history, nothing fundamentally distinguishes the axiom systems traditionally used in mathematics (logic included), and many other axiom systems, often simple ones, could serve as foundations for new fields of mathematics as rich as the traditional ones.
claims.quote: So this leads to the conclusion that there is in a sense nothing fundamentally special about the particular axiom systems that have traditionally been used in mathematics
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Named textbook theorems of logic are those not derivable from simpler ones
claims.statement: If the theorems of basic logic are listed in order of increasing complexity, the ones that cannot be derived from simpler theorems earlier in the list are almost exactly the ones traditional textbooks single out and name as interesting.
claims.quote: And remarkably enough what I have found is that these theorems are almost exactly the ones highlighted on the previous page that have traditionally been identified as interesting.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Judgments like deep or powerful reflect the structure of the theorem network
claims.statement: Mathematicians' intuitive descriptions of theorems (difficult, powerful, surprising, deep) reflect features of the network of statements connected by theorems, and fields regarded as more successful should have more compact networks while fields full of isolated facts, such as elementary number theory, should have sparser networks.
claims.quote: And my suspicion is that our intuitive characterizations of theorems are in effect just reflections of our perception of various features of the structure of this network.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: No general definition of intelligence independent of human details
claims.statement: General features proposed as marks of intelligence (learning and memory, adaptation, abstraction) occur in systems such as simple cellular automata and fluids, so there is no workable general definition of intelligence; any usable one must be tied to specific details of human intelligence.
claims.quote: My guess is that ultimately there is not, and that in fact any workable definition of what we normally think of as intelligence will end up having to be tied to all sorts of seemingly rather specific details of human intelligence.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Proposed general features of life occur in many simple-rule systems
claims.statement: Almost any general feature proposed to characterize life, including self-organization, self-reproduction and complexity, occurs even in many systems with very simple rules, so life can only be recognized by specific shared details with life on Earth.
claims.quote: Indeed, following the discoveries in this book I have come to the conclusion that almost any general feature that one might think of as characterizing life will actually occur even in many systems with very simple rules.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Human artifacts look simple because engineering requires predictability
claims.statement: Human-made artifacts tend to look simpler than natural objects because engineers need to foresee what their systems will do, which requires computational reducibility, whereas nature has no such constraint and many natural systems are computationally irreducible.
claims.quote: And I believe the basic answer to this has to do with the fact that when we as humans set up artifacts we usually need to be able to foresee what they will do—for otherwise we have no way to tell whether they will achieve the purposes we want.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: A minimal rule for a feature hints that a system was made for a purpose
claims.statement: Since purposes can always be reinterpreted as mechanisms, purpose cannot be identified for certain from behavior; the best criterion is that a system is the minimal or optimal one producing a given feature, which suggests it was built for that purpose, as advanced technology should increasingly use minimal systems.
claims.quote: finding out that the rule for the system is the minimal or optimal one for producing that feature may make it seem more likely that at least with sufficiently advanced technology the system might have specifically been created for the purpose of exhibiting that feature.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Efficient extraterrestrial communications would show no detectable regularities
claims.statement: Signals used for communication by an advanced extraterrestrial civilization would likely be compressed to the point of showing essentially no detectable regularities, so they would look like random radio noise, and searches for sharply defined carrier frequencies would miss them; only beacons meant to be noticed would need recognizable regularities.
claims.quote: my guess is that they will exhibit essentially no detectable regularities. For any such regularity represents in a sense a redundancy or inefficiency that can be removed by the sender and receiver both using appropriate data compression.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Sophisticated computation, or primes, are not signs of intelligence
claims.statement: Producing a signal by sophisticated computation is no evidence of intelligence, because such computation is common in ordinary physical processes; for instance, turbulence in the gas around a star quickly does more computation than all of human intellectual history, and sequences such as the primes can be generated by many non-intelligent systems.
claims.quote: And indeed it seems likely that for example an ordinary physical process like fluid turbulence in the gas around a star should rather quickly do more computation than has by most measures ever been done throughout the whole course of human intellectual history.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Recognizing extraterrestrial intelligence depends on similarity to humans
claims.statement: The difficulty in finding extraterrestrial intelligence is not finding systems that compute in sophisticated ways, which are common, but finding ones whose details are similar enough to humans that we would recognize them as intelligent; somewhat generalized intelligence is likely to exist but to behave in bizarrely unhuman ways.
claims.quote: that the basic issue is not finding systems that perform sophisticated enough computations, but rather finding ones whose details happen to be similar enough to us as humans that we recognize what they do as showing intelligence.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Engineering has explored only a tiny unrepresentative fraction of possible systems
claims.statement: Traditional engineering has used only a tiny and unrepresentative fraction of possible systems and processes, those simple enough to predict, and using simple-rule systems with complex behavior will make a vast amount of new technology possible.
claims.quote: And indeed one of the things that emerges from this book is that traditional engineering has actually considered only a tiny and quite unrepresentative fraction of all the kinds of systems and processes that are in principle possible.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Simple universal rules like rule 110 could be built into computers from atoms
claims.statement: Since very simple rules such as the rule 110 cellular automaton are universal, computers could be built from many kinds of components, and a simple chemical process could plausibly assemble a rule 110-like computer at the atomic scale, with one or a few atoms per cell.
claims.quote: For while it is quite implausible that some simple chemical process could successfully assemble a traditional computer out of atoms, it seems quite plausible that this could be done for something like a rule 110 cellular automaton.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Exhaustive search is the only reliable way to find programs with given behavior
claims.statement: Because simple programs can do so many unexpected things, and computational irreducibility can make finding a behavior take irreducible work, the only reliable way to find a simple program with a desired behavior is essentially exhaustive search, so building a library of basic knowledge about simple programs is a better route to technology.
claims.quote: ultimately the only way to find what one wants is essentially just to do an exhaustive search of all possibilities.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Humans are not computationally more sophisticated than other systems in nature
claims.statement: By the Principle of Computational Equivalence, human brains, turbulent fluids, simple cellular automata and the universe as a whole all achieve the same level of computational sophistication, so humans are not fundamentally special in intelligence or complexity.
claims.quote: So this means that there is in the end no difference between the level of computational sophistication that is achieved by humans and by all sorts of other systems in nature and elsewhere.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Computational irreducibility puts permanent limits on scientific prediction
claims.statement: The Principle of Computational Equivalence and computational irreducibility show that science will never predict everything: even if the universe follows simple rules, there is in general no way to know all their consequences except by watching them unfold.
claims.quote: But the Principle of Computational Equivalence—and the phenomenon of computational irreducibility—now shows that this will never happen.
claims.chapter: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

claims.label: Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection (partial-change form)
claims.statement: The rate of increase in mean fitness of a population due to natural selection equals its additive genetic variance in fitness at that time.
claims.work: The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection
claims.chapter: The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection (1930)

claims.label: Fisher-KPP wave of advance of an advantageous gene
claims.statement: An advantageous allele spreading through a continuous population advances as a travelling wave whose speed is set by the selection coefficient and the diffusion (dispersal) rate.
claims.work: The wave of advance of advantageous genes
claims.chapter: The wave of advance of advantageous genes (1937)

claims.label: Fisher's principle of equal investment in the sexes
claims.statement: Under random mating and autosomal inheritance, selection drives parents to invest equally in sons and daughters, which gives a 1:1 sex ratio when the two cost the same.
claims.work: The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection
claims.chapter: The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection (1930)

claims.label: Fisher's infinitesimal model of quantitative inheritance
claims.statement: Continuous traits determined by many Mendelian loci of small additive effect produce the observed correlations between relatives, so biometric and Mendelian inheritance are consistent.
claims.work: The Correlation between Relatives on the Supposition of Mendelian Inheritance
claims.chapter: The Correlation between Relatives on the Supposition of Mendelian Inheritance (1919)

claims.label: Turing diffusion-driven instability
claims.statement: A homogeneous steady state of two reacting chemicals that is stable without diffusion can become unstable to spatial perturbations when the chemicals diffuse at different rates, spontaneously producing a pattern.
claims.chapter: The chemical basis of morphogenesis (1952)

claims.label: Turing wavelength selection
claims.statement: The spacing of a Turing pattern at onset is set by the reaction rates and diffusivities, not by the size of the tissue, so changing these parameters predictably changes the number of repeated elements.
claims.chapter: The chemical basis of morphogenesis (1952)

claims.label: Reaction-diffusion of morphogens accounts for biological pattern
claims.statement: Chemical substances that react and diffuse through tissue (morphogens) are sufficient to account for the main phenomena of morphogenesis.
claims.chapter: The chemical basis of morphogenesis (1952)

claims.label: Kimura fixation probability of a mutant allele
claims.statement: The probability that a mutant allele eventually fixes in a finite population depends on its initial frequency, its selective advantage and the effective population size, and equals its initial frequency when it is neutral.
claims.work: On the probability of fixation of mutant genes in a population
claims.chapter: On the probability of fixation of mutant genes in a population (1962)

claims.label: Neutral substitution rate equals the mutation rate
claims.statement: For neutral mutations the long-run rate of molecular substitution equals the mutation rate per generation, independent of population size, which yields a molecular clock.
claims.work: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level
claims.chapter: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level (1968)

claims.label: Mean time to fixation of a neutral mutant
claims.statement: A neutral mutant that does go to fixation takes on average about four times the effective population size, in generations, to do so.
claims.work: The average number of generations until fixation of a mutant gene in a finite population
claims.chapter: The average number of generations until fixation of a mutant gene in a finite population (1969)

claims.label: Neutral equilibrium heterozygosity (Kimura-Crow)
claims.statement: Under neutral mutation to new alleles and drift, expected heterozygosity reaches an equilibrium that rises with the product of effective population size and mutation rate.
claims.work: The number of alleles that can be maintained in a finite population
claims.chapter: The number of alleles that can be maintained in a finite population (1964)

claims.label: Neutral theory: most molecular substitutions are neutral
claims.statement: Most evolutionary changes at the molecular level are caused by random drift of selectively neutral or nearly neutral mutations, not by positive selection.
claims.work: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level
claims.chapter: Evolutionary Rate at the Molecular Level (1968)

claims.label: Hamilton's rule
claims.statement: A gene for social behaviour increases in frequency when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by genetic relatedness, exceeds the cost to the actor.
claims.work: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. I
claims.chapter: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. I (1964)

claims.label: Haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality
claims.statement: Because full sisters in haplodiploid species share three quarters of their genes, more than a mother shares with her offspring, haplodiploid insects are predisposed to evolve sterile worker castes.
claims.work: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. II
claims.chapter: The genetical evolution of social behaviour. II (1964)

claims.label: Local mate competition sex ratio
claims.statement: When a few mothers lay eggs on a patch and their offspring mate there before the daughters disperse, the evolutionarily stable sex ratio is female-biased, and the bias weakens as the number of mothers grows.
claims.chapter: Extraordinary Sex Ratios (1967)

claims.label: Declining force of selection with age
claims.statement: The strength of selection on survival falls with age after reproduction begins, so senescence is an inevitable outcome of natural selection.
claims.work: The moulding of senescence by natural selection
claims.chapter: The moulding of senescence by natural selection (1966)

claims.label: Evolutionarily stable strategy conditions
claims.statement: A strategy is evolutionarily stable if, once common, it cannot be invaded by any rare alternative strategy.
claims.chapter: The Logic of Animal Conflict (1973)

claims.label: Hawk-Dove mixed ESS
claims.statement: When the cost of injury exceeds the value of the contested resource, the stable outcome is a mixture in which animals escalate with probability equal to the ratio of resource value to injury cost.
claims.work: Evolution and the Theory of Games
claims.chapter: Evolution and the Theory of Games (1982)

claims.label: War of attrition ESS
claims.statement: In contests settled by display, where the animal willing to persist longer wins and costs grow with time, the stable strategy is to choose a persistence time at random from an exponential distribution whose mean equals the resource value.
claims.work: The theory of games and the evolution of animal conflicts
claims.chapter: The theory of games and the evolution of animal conflicts (1974)

claims.label: Twofold cost of sex
claims.statement: An asexual mutant female in a sexual population with equal sex ratio produces twice as many grandchildren as a sexual female, so sex needs a compensating advantage of up to twofold to persist.
claims.chapter: The Evolution of Sex (1978)

claims.label: Genetic hitchhiking (selective sweep)
claims.statement: When a favourable mutation sweeps to fixation, it reduces genetic variation at closely linked neutral sites, and the reduction is larger the tighter the linkage relative to the strength of selection.
claims.work: The hitch-hiking effect of a favourable gene
claims.chapter: The hitch-hiking effect of a favourable gene (1974)

tests.hypothesis: If Darwin's denudation argument holds, the time elapsed since the latter part of the Secondary (Mesozoic) period, i.e. since the youngest Chalk, is roughly 300 million years or more on the modern radiometrically calibrated timescale.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: the International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) chronostratigraphic boundary ages as served by the Macrostrat API (defs/intervals, timescale 'international ages'), which carries the ICS chart's numeric ages in Ma. Quantities: age of the top of the Maastrichtian (= Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary, the end of Chalk deposition) and age of the base of the Campanian (start of the youngest Chalk stages). SUPPORTS if the top-of-Maastrichtian age is >= 225 Ma (within 25% of 300 Myr, or older). Reported alongside: the base-of-Campanian age and the ratio of Darwin's 306.7 Myr to the measured age.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the top-of-Maastrichtian age is < 225 Ma (Darwin's figure is off by more than 25%). MIXED is not possible for this one-number test. INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the API cannot be reached; INCONCLUSIVE (not-operationalizable) if the API does not return a Maastrichtian interval.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'latter part of the Secondary period' is the Late Cretaceous, and 'since the late Chalk' is the time from the youngest Chalk Group strata (Campanian-Maastrichtian) to the present. The claim is a duration (about 300 million years, which he says is an underestimate of the time since the late Secondary) inferred from an assumed erosion rate; the test compares that duration with the radiometric timescale and does not test the erosion rate. Darwin himself withdrew the calculation in later editions. This follows the swarm thread's draft plan for this claim with the same 25% tolerance. READINGS CHECK (added after the result, at the hub's request; no number or threshold changed).
